question: A linen cloth bearing the apparent imprint of a crucified man has been held in northern Italy since 1578 and is venerated by some as Christ's burial shroud. In which city?
context: First documented in Lirey, France, in 1354. Carbon dating in 1988 suggested medieval origin (~1260-1390); critics dispute the sample. The Catholic Church has never officially declared its authenticity.

question: A Bavarian village has performed a passion play every ten years since vowing to do so during a 1633 plague. Which village?
context: Performances run from May to October every decade ending in zero. The text has been revised to remove antisemitic elements. The 2020 production was postponed to 2022 by COVID-19.

question: The Vatican City became the world's smallest sovereign state by the 1929 Lateran Treaty. With whom did the Holy See sign the treaty?
context: Resolved the 'Roman Question' open since 1870. The Vatican City is 44 hectares — about a fifth of a square mile. Population around 800. The pope is its absolute monarch.

question: From 1309 to 1377 the papacy resided not in Rome but in a southern French city under French royal influence. Which city?
context: The 'Babylonian Captivity of the Church' — Petrarch's phrase. Seven French popes. Catherine of Siena helped persuade Gregory XI to return to Rome in 1377. The Western Schism followed.

question: From 1378 to 1417 the Catholic Church had two — and at one point three — rival popes claiming the chair of Peter. The schism was ended by which council?
context: 1414-1418. Deposed Antipope John XXIII, accepted Gregory XII's resignation, deposed Benedict XIII, and elected Martin V. The schism left Western Christendom badly weakened.

question: Latter-day Saints teach that a complete apostasy from true Christianity took place after the apostles, requiring a restoration by Joseph Smith. By what name is this doctrine?
context: Distinguishes LDS theology from mainstream Christianity, which holds that the Holy Spirit preserved the Church through all ages. The Restoration began with Smith's 1820 First Vision.

question: Michelangelo's marble Moses in Rome shows the prophet with horns, due to a famous Vulgate translation of a Hebrew word that can also mean 'rays of light'. Which word?
context: Exodus 34:29-35. Jerome translated 'karan' as 'cornuta' — horned. The image of horned Moses recurs in medieval European art and fed later antisemitic caricatures.

question: Pope Pius XII in 1950 defined that the Virgin Mary was taken bodily into heaven at the end of her earthly life. What is this dogma called?
context: The only definition under Vatican I criteria for papal infallibility. Eastern Orthodox call the parallel feast 'the Dormition' (falling asleep). Celebrated August 15.

question: Pope Pius IX in 1854 defined that the Virgin Mary was conceived without original sin. What is this dogma called?
context: Not to be confused with the Virgin Birth (Christ's miraculous conception in Mary's womb). The Immaculate Conception is about Mary's own conception by Anne and Joachim. Defined 1854.

question: Lent begins on Ash Wednesday with the placing of ashes on worshipers' foreheads and the words 'remember that you are dust, and to dust you...' what?
context: Quoting Genesis 3:19. Forty days before Easter (excluding Sundays). The ashes are traditionally made from the burned palm fronds of the previous year's Palm Sunday.

question: The day before Ash Wednesday, marked by feasting and confession, is called Shrove Tuesday in English. The French name is what?
context: French 'Fat Tuesday'. New Orleans's celebration is the most famous in North America. 'Carnival' (from Latin 'farewell to flesh') is the broader pre-Lent festival season.

question: The Christian week of preparation for Easter, from Palm Sunday through Holy Saturday, is called what?
context: The last three days (Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday/Easter Vigil) form the Paschal Triduum — the single liturgical event at the heart of the Christian year.

question: The historical figure behind Santa Claus was a fourth-century bishop of a city in modern Turkey, known for secret gifts to a poor family's daughters. From which city?
context: c. 270-343 AD. The Dutch 'Sinterklaas' became the English 'Santa Claus'. His relics were moved to Bari, Italy in 1087, where they remain today.

question: The third-century Christian martyr behind February 14 was reportedly a Roman priest beheaded for marrying Christian couples in defiance of Claudius II. Who?
context: Martyred c. 269 AD. The Roman martyrology lists three different Valentines. The romantic associations are medieval — Chaucer's Parlement of Foules (1382) is the earliest known.

question: A fourth-century soldier-martyr became patron saint of England, Georgia, and Russia, depicted slaying a dragon. Who?
context: Martyred c. 303 AD under Diocletian. The dragon legend is medieval — the Golden Legend (c. 1260). The English Order of the Garter was founded in his name in 1348.

question: Peter's brother became patron saint of Scotland and is shown on the Saltire flag of Scotland. He was crucified on what kind of cross?
context: Tradition has him martyred in Patras, Greece, on a saltire. The Scottish national flag's white X on blue is St Andrew's saltire. Scotland claims relics of his arm bone, kneecap, finger, and tooth.

question: A French peasant girl who heard voices, led French armies to break the siege of Orleans, was captured by Burgundians, and burned by the English in 1431. Who?
context: c. 1412-1431. Aged about 19 at her death. Rehabilitated in 1456 by a posthumous trial. Canonized 1920 — the year her statue went up in every French town hall.

question: Henry II's archbishop was murdered by four knights in Canterbury Cathedral on December 29, 1170 after the king's outburst 'will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'. Who?
context: Canonized 1173 — three years later. His shrine was one of medieval Christendom's greatest pilgrimage sites. Chaucer's Canterbury Tales pilgrims travel to it. Henry VIII demolished it in 1538.

question: Medieval anchoresses were enclosed for life in a small cell attached to a church. Julian of Norwich's cell was beside which Norfolk church?
context: She took her name from the church. Revelations of Divine Love is the first known book in English by a woman (c. 1395). 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.'

question: Tradition holds that the first state to make Christianity its official religion was a Caucasus kingdom in 301 AD under King Trdat III. Which kingdom?
context: Converted by Gregory the Illuminator. The Armenian Apostolic Church traces its origins to apostles Bartholomew and Thaddaeus. Ethiopia officially Christianized c. 330 under Ezana.

question: An Athenian craftsman trapped in Crete fashioned wings of feathers and wax to escape with his son. The son flew too near what?
context: Daedalus had built Minos's labyrinth and helped Pasiphae conceive the Minotaur. Icarus's wax melted; he fell into the Icarian Sea. Daedalus reached Sicily.

question: Alexander the Great cut through (rather than untying) a complex knot at the temple of Sabazios in 333 BC. In which Phrygian town?
context: An oracle had said whoever loosened the knot would rule Asia. The 'Gordian knot' became proverbial. Alexander cut it with his sword (or by removing the pin) and went on to conquer Persia.

question: The realm of the dead who did not die in battle — those who died of disease, old age, or accident — was ruled by which female being?
context: Half-living, half-corpse appearance. Daughter of Loki. Her realm was called Helheim or Hel. Her hall was Eljudnir; her dish was Hunger; her bed was Sickbed; her doormat was Stumbling-Block.

question: A late-10th-century king of Norway, raised in Russia and a convert in England, forced Christianization on Norway and Iceland. Who?
context: King 995-1000. Probably killed at the Battle of Svolder by the kings of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway's rival Earl Erik. Iceland's peaceful 1000 AD conversion was his demand under threat.

question: Another early-11th-century king of Norway — killed at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 — became the principal patron saint of Norway after his death. Who?
context: Saint Olaf. His death made him a martyr. Miracles were reported. His body was found incorrupt. Trondheim Cathedral was built over his shrine — a major pilgrimage site of medieval northern Europe.

question: An 11th-century Danish king built a North Sea empire including Denmark, Norway, and England. Who?
context: King c. 1016-1035. The story of him commanding the tide to stop — to demonstrate to his flatterers that royal power had limits — is from Henry of Huntingdon. Pious endpoint of Viking-age Danish royal power.

question: The year 1066 is famous in English history for how many royal claimants succeeding each other on the throne?
context: Edward the Confessor died in January. Harold Godwinson succeeded. He defeated Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (September). He died at Hastings (October). William the Conqueror was crowned Christmas Day. End of Anglo-Saxon and Viking eras.

question: The vast Jewish corpus of oral law, ethics, theology, and folklore, compiled between c. 200-500 AD in two parallel versions, is called the what?
context: Greek 'didactic teaching'. Two Talmuds: the Babylonian (Bavli, c. 500 AD) and the Jerusalem (Yerushalmi, c. 400 AD). The Bavli became the central text of rabbinic Judaism. About 6,200 pages in modern editions.

question: The largest cache of ancient Hebrew manuscripts ever found was discovered in 1947 in caves near the Dead Sea. Whose collection?
context: Probably the Essenes — a Jewish ascetic community. About 980 documents discovered between 1947 and 1956 in 11 caves. Include the oldest known copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther.

question: The Second Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by which Roman general in 70 AD?
context: Vespasian had begun the campaign; Titus completed it. The Arch of Titus in Rome depicts the menorah and other temple spoils being carried off. The day of destruction is mourned as Tisha B'Av in Judaism.

question: A key architect of the Final Solution, captured by Israeli agents in Argentina in 1960, was tried in Jerusalem in 1961 and hanged. Who?
context: He was captured by Mossad agents from a bus stop in Buenos Aires. The trial was televised globally. Hannah Arendt's coverage produced her phrase 'the banality of evil'. Israel's only judicial execution.

question: After the Holocaust, the modern state of Israel was founded by UN partition. In what year did David Ben-Gurion proclaim independence?
context: May 14, 1948. The Arab-Israeli war began the next day. Six Arab armies attacked; Israel survived. The 1947 UN Partition plan would have created a Jewish and a Palestinian state; only Israel emerged.

question: The Jewish prayer recited by mourners — praising God's name without mentioning death — is in Aramaic. What is it called?
context: Said by mourners daily for eleven months after the death of a parent, and on yahrzeit (death anniversaries). Origin in the 1st-2nd centuries AD. Joyful in content, mournful in occasion.

question: The central declaration of Jewish faith — 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One' — is called the what?
context: Deuteronomy 6:4. Recited morning and evening; affixed to door-posts (the mezuzah) and arms (the tefillin). The dying Rabbi Akiva's final word, while being flayed by the Romans, was the long final note of 'One'.

question: Once in his life, every able Muslim must make a pilgrimage to Mecca. What is the pilgrimage called?
context: Performed during the month Dhul Hijjah. Rituals include circling the Kaaba seven times, running between the hills of Safa and Marwa, throwing stones at pillars representing Satan, sacrificing an animal at Mina.

question: The last pharaoh of Egypt — who allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony before being defeated by Octavian — was killed (probably by her own hand) in 30 BC. Who?
context: Reigned 51-30 BC. Of Greek (Ptolemaic) descent — the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian. After Antony's defeat at Actium (31 BC), they both died by suicide. Egypt became a Roman province under Octavian (Augustus).

question: Mesopotamian temples were built as massive stepped pyramids — towers reaching up toward the sky-god's abode. What were they called?
context: Tower of Babel: probably the Etemenanki ziggurat of Babylon. Hundreds of ziggurats stretched from Sumer to Assyria. The best-preserved example is the Ziggurat of Ur, partly restored by Saddam Hussein.

question: In March 1997 a cult of 39 followers committed suicide in San Diego — they believed they were boarding a UFO behind a passing comet. Which comet?
context: Marshall Applewhite (Ti) and Bonnie Nettles (Do) had founded the group decades earlier. They wore matching Nike sneakers. The website Heaven's Gate is still online — maintained by remaining adherents.

question: In April 1993 federal agents stormed the compound of a religious cult in Texas; fire broke out and 76 cult members died including their leader. The leader was named what?
context: Vernon Howell legally changed his name. Branch Davidians (offshoot of Seventh-day Adventists). The siege lasted 51 days. Investigation continues on the fire's origin — accidental or deliberate. A formative event in 1990s American distrust of federal power.

question: An Icelandic book — written in the 12th and 13th centuries — records the names of about 400 settlers of Iceland and the lands they took. What is its title?
context: 'Book of Settlements'. Contains valuable genealogical, geographical, and ethnographic information for early Iceland (c. 870-930). Some scholars suggest it inspired the development of the family sagas.

question: The holiest day of the Jewish year — a 25-hour fast of atonement on the tenth day of Tishrei — is called what?
context: Hebrew 'Day of Atonement'. Falls in autumn (September or October). The shofar (ram's horn) sounds to close the day. Even non-observant Jews often fast and attend synagogue on Yom Kippur.

question: Genesis 1 opens with the spirit of God hovering over the formless deep. Across six days God speaks the cosmos into being — light, sky, sea, land, plants, sun and moon, creatures — and on the seventh he rests. What Hebrew verb opens the book?
context: Bereshit gives Genesis its Hebrew name. The repeated 'and God saw that it was good' frames creation as orderly, intentional, and morally weighted.

question: Genesis 3: the cunning serpent told the first woman that eating the forbidden fruit would not bring death but make her like God, knowing good and evil. She ate and gave to her husband; their eyes were opened. What did they sew to cover themselves?
context: After the fall, God himself made them garments of skin — the first death in scripture. The expulsion from Eden grounds Christian doctrine of original sin.

question: Genesis 4: a younger brother's flock-offering was accepted but the elder's grain-offering was not. The elder rose against his brother in a field and killed him — humanity's first murder. What was God's question to the killer?
context: Cain's reply 'Am I my brother's keeper?' became proverbial. God marked him so no one would kill him in vengeance, and he wandered east of Eden in the land of Nod.

question: Genesis 18: three visitors told Abraham the cities of the plain would be destroyed for their wickedness. Abraham bargained — would God spare them for fifty righteous? Forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? — finally settling at what number?
context: Not even ten were found. Lot fled with his family; his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt. Sulfur and fire fell on Sodom and Gomorrah.

question: Genesis 39: the favored Hebrew slave rose to manage all of Potiphar's household. Potiphar's wife pursued him daily; when he fled her bedroom she kept his cloak as false evidence and accused him of attempted rape. What happened to him?
context: Joseph rose again in prison, interpreting dreams. The famine of seven fat and seven lean years brought his brothers begging for grain — leading to one of scripture's great reconciliation scenes.

question: In the wilderness between Egypt and Sinai, Israel complained of hunger. Each morning a thin flake covered the ground like frost — sweet, white, tasting of honey wafers. The people asked 'man hu' — 'what is it?' What was it called?
context: Exodus 16. Each gathered an omer, doubling on the sixth day for the Sabbath. Quail covered the camp in the evenings. The ark later held a jar of manna as a sign of provision.

question: Numbers 16: a Levite cousin of Moses led 250 community leaders in revolt, declaring all the assembly holy and demanding the priesthood. Moses said God would choose. The ground opened, swallowing the rebels alive into Sheol. Who led the revolt?
context: Dathan and Abiram joined Korah; fire from God consumed the 250. The next day a plague killed 14,700 who grumbled. Aaron stood with the censer between the living and the dead, and the plague stopped.

question: Judges 7: a hesitant judge twice tested God with a wool fleece (wet while ground was dry; dry while ground was wet). God then trimmed his army from 22,000 down to 300 to defeat the Midianites with trumpets, jars, and torches. Who was he?
context: The 300 were those who lapped water like dogs rather than kneeling. Gideon refused kingship: 'The Lord shall rule over you.' His ephod, sadly, became a snare to Israel.

question: 1 Samuel 3: a boy serving in the Shiloh tabernacle heard a voice in the night. Three times he ran to the old priest Eli, who finally taught him to say 'Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.' Who was the boy?
context: Samuel became the last judge and first great prophet of Israel — anointing both Saul and David as kings. His mother Hannah had prayed for him at Shiloh while Eli watched.

question: 1 Samuel 18: King Saul's son loved the young harpist 'as his own soul' and gave him his robe, sword, bow, and belt — risking his crown to warn him of Saul's murderous intent. When he died in battle, David lamented their love. Who was the prince?
context: Jonathan died with Saul at Mount Gilboa fighting the Philistines. David wept: 'Your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.' David later cared for Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth.

question: After David had Uriah killed, the prophet came to court with a story: a rich man with vast flocks stole a poor man's only beloved ewe lamb to feed a guest. 'That man deserves to die!' said David. The prophet answered, 'You are the man.' Who was he?
context: 2 Samuel 12. David repented (Psalm 51 is his cry of contrition). The first son of Bathsheba died; the second was Solomon. Nathan also helped install Solomon over Adonijah at David's death.

question: 1 Kings 19: after slaughtering Baal's prophets and fleeing Jezebel's vengeance, the prophet sat under a juniper tree wishing to die. At Horeb a great wind, then earthquake, then fire passed — but God was not in them. In what was God?
context: 1 Kings 19:12. Elijah covered his face with his mantle and went out to the cave mouth. God recommissioned him and revealed there were yet 7,000 in Israel who had not bowed to Baal.

question: 2 Kings 2: as Elijah and Elisha walked together east of the Jordan, a chariot of fire with horses of fire separated them. The elder prophet ascended in a whirlwind to heaven. What did his successor pick up from the ground?
context: Elisha had asked for a double portion of his spirit. With the mantle he struck the Jordan and the waters parted. Jewish tradition keeps a chair for Elijah at every Passover seder and circumcision.

question: 2 Kings 5: an Aramean commander rode to Israel for healing of his skin disease. The prophet Elisha sent word to dip seven times in the Jordan. Naaman raged — Damascus had better rivers! — but his servants reasoned with him. What was healed?
context: His skin became like that of a young child. Naaman became a worshipper of Israel's God, asking for two mule-loads of soil to take home. Elisha refused payment; his servant Gehazi grasped for it and inherited the leprosy.

question: Isaiah 53 portrays a 'man of sorrows, acquainted with grief' who was 'wounded for our transgressions' and 'led as a lamb to the slaughter'. Christians read this as foretelling Christ; Jewish tradition reads the servant as which figure?
context: The 'suffering servant songs' (chapters 42, 49, 50, 52-53) are among the most contested passages in scripture. Handel's 'Messiah' wove them into Christian liturgy permanently.

question: Daniel 2: King Nebuchadnezzar saw a great statue with head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet of clay. A stone struck it and grew into a mountain filling the earth. Daniel said the gold head was who?
context: Successive empires: silver=Persia, bronze=Greece, iron=Rome (traditional). The stone is God's eternal kingdom. Apocalyptic literature begins with Daniel's visions of beasts and the Ancient of Days.

question: After the exile, a Persian king's cupbearer asked leave to rebuild Jerusalem's broken walls. He inspected the ruins by night, organized work in 52 days, half guarding while half built. Who was the cupbearer?
context: King Artaxerxes I sent him as governor in 445 BC. Ezra the scribe meanwhile re-instituted the Torah, reading it from a wooden platform to the gathered exiles who wept at hearing the law.

question: After losing children, livestock, and health, Job sat in ashes scraping his sores with a potsherd. Three friends came to comfort him but argued he must have sinned. After 37 chapters of dialogue, who finally spoke from where?
context: God's speech from the whirlwind asks Job rhetorical questions about creation — Leviathan, Behemoth, the morning stars. Job covers his mouth: 'I have heard of you, but now my eye sees you.'

question: Called as a youth in 627 BC, the 'weeping prophet' watched Jerusalem fall to Babylon in 586 BC. His scroll was cut and burned by King Jehoiakim — so his scribe Baruch wrote it again. Tradition says he wrote Lamentations. Who was he?
context: Jeremiah was thrown into a muddy cistern, taken to Egypt against his will, and (by later tradition) stoned to death there. The 'new covenant' prophecy (Jeremiah 31) became central to Christian theology.

question: Luke 2: a Roman census ordered by Caesar Augustus required Joseph to travel from Nazareth to his ancestral town. Mary was great with child. They found no room at the inn, so the newborn was laid in a manger — a feeding trough. In what town?
context: Bethlehem ('house of bread') fulfilled Micah 5:2. Shepherds came at angelic announcement. The early church set the date December 25 by the third century — possibly displacing Roman Saturnalia.

question: Luke 2: shepherds keeping watch over their flocks by night were terrified when the glory of the Lord shone around them. An angel announced glad tidings of great joy. Then a multitude of the heavenly host sang — what?
choices: 'Worthy is the Lamb that was slain'
context: Latin 'Gloria in excelsis Deo' became the second-oldest Christian hymn after the Sanctus. Shepherds, lowest of the laboring poor, are the first to hear the gospel — a theological pattern Luke develops throughout.

question: Matthew 2: warned by the magi's snub, Herod the Great ordered the killing of every male child two years old and under in Bethlehem and its district. Joseph fled with Mary and Jesus to where, warned by an angel in a dream?
context: Matthew sees this fulfilling Hosea 11:1: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' The flight to Egypt anchors Christianity's earliest geographic spread. Herod died c. 4 BC; the family returned and settled in Nazareth.

question: A wild man in camel's hair, eating locusts and wild honey, preached repentance at the Jordan River and baptized crowds. He pointed beyond himself: 'I am not worthy to untie his sandal.' Who was he?
context: Mark 1:6. Son of Zechariah the priest and Elizabeth — Mary's relative. Herod Antipas later beheaded him at Salome's request. Jesus said no one born of women was greater than John.

question: After his baptism, the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness 40 days. The devil tempted him to turn stones to bread, to leap from the temple pinnacle, and to bow for all the kingdoms of the world. With what did Jesus answer each?
context: Each reply begins 'It is written'. 'Man shall not live by bread alone' (Deut 8:3). 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test' (Deut 6:16). 'Worship the Lord your God and serve him only' (Deut 6:13).

question: John 3: a Pharisee and member of the ruling council came to Jesus by night. Jesus told him 'Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.' The Pharisee asked how a man could enter his mother's womb a second time. Who was he?
context: Greek 'gennethe anothen' means both 'born again' and 'born from above'. Nicodemus later brought 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes to anoint Jesus's body. The passage contains John 3:16.

question: John 4: at noon by Jacob's well in Sychar, Jesus asked a woman for water. He told her he could give living water, then named her five husbands and current partner. Astonished, she dropped her water jar and ran. To which people did she belong?
context: Samaritans were half-Israelite, half-Gentile, holding only the Pentateuch and worshipping at Mount Gerizim — despised by Jews. Her testimony brought a whole town to faith. Jesus stayed two days.

question: Matthew 14: in the fourth watch of the night, the disciples saw a figure walking on the storm-tossed Sea of Galilee. They cried out in terror — a ghost! Jesus said 'Take heart; it is I.' One disciple stepped out, walked, then began to sink. Who?
context: Peter cried 'Lord, save me!' Jesus reached out and caught him: 'O you of little faith, why did you doubt?' The wind ceased when they entered the boat. The disciples worshipped: 'Truly you are the Son of God.'

question: Matthew 17: Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. There he was transfigured — his face shone like the sun, his clothes became dazzling white. Two figures from Israel's past appeared and talked with him. Who were they?
context: Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) bear witness to Christ. Peter wanted to build three tabernacles; a cloud overshadowed them and the Father's voice came: 'This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.'

question: Days before Passover, Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed donkey colt, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. Crowds spread garments and palm branches on the road, shouting 'Hosanna to the Son of David!' What does 'Hosanna' mean?
context: Hebrew 'hoshia-na'. The same crowds would cry 'Crucify him!' five days later. Palm Sunday opens Holy Week — Christianity's most sacred season, climaxing in Easter.

question: Approaching Passover, Jesus entered the temple courts and overturned the tables of money changers and the seats of those selling doves. With a whip of cords he drove them out. Quoting Isaiah, he said the temple was meant to be what?
answer: 'A house of prayer for all nations'
choices: 'A house of prayer for all nations'
'A pillar and ground of the truth'
context: Mark 11:17. The money-changers exchanged Roman coins (with imperial images) for temple shekels. Sacrificial animals were sold at markup. Jesus called it 'a den of robbers' — Jeremiah 7:11.

question: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said 'This is my body, given for you.' Then he took the cup: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood.' This is the institution narrative of which sacrament?
context: 1 Corinthians 11 and the synoptic gospels. Catholic doctrine holds transubstantiation; Lutherans hold consubstantiation; Reformed hold spiritual presence; Zwinglians hold memorial only. The Christian center of gravity.

question: On the Mount of Olives, in a garden of olive presses, Jesus prayed 'Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will but yours be done.' He sweated as it were great drops of blood. What did the disciples do nearby?
context: Greek 'Gethsemane' means 'oil press'. Peter, James, and John — the same three from the Transfiguration — could not watch one hour. An angel from heaven strengthened him. Then the torches and the kiss.

question: Matthew 26: a member of the Twelve went to the chief priests and asked 'What will you give me if I deliver him over?' They counted out thirty pieces of silver. He returned them, threw them in the temple, and hanged himself. Who?
context: The price of a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32). The priests bought the Potter's Field for burial of foreigners — called Akeldama ('field of blood'). Judas's kiss in Gethsemane became the archetype of betrayal.

question: Pontius Pilate, finding no guilt in Jesus, tried to release him. The crowd cried 'Crucify him!' Pilate took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying 'I am innocent of this man's blood.' The crowd answered with what fateful cry?
answer: 'His blood be on us and on our children'
choices: 'His blood be on us and on our children'
context: Matthew 27:25. Used through history to justify Christian anti-Semitism. Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965) explicitly repudiated the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the crucifixion.

question: On Easter evening, two disciples walked the seven miles from Jerusalem to Emmaus. A stranger joined them and explained the scriptures concerning the Messiah from Moses and the prophets. They recognized him only when he did what?
answer: Broke bread with them at table
choices: Broke bread with them at table
Showed them the wounds in his hands
Walked with them through closed doors
context: Luke 24. 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked with us?' Once they recognized him, he vanished. They ran back the seven miles that night to Jerusalem to tell the eleven. Cleopas is named; the other unnamed.

question: John 20: a disciple absent on Easter night refused to believe the others' reports. 'Unless I see the print of the nails and put my hand in his side, I will not believe.' A week later Jesus appeared and invited him to do exactly that. Who?
context: Thomas confessed 'My Lord and my God!' — the highest Christological confession in the gospels. Tradition says he carried Christianity to India, where Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their origin to him.

question: Acts 1: after appearing to his disciples over 40 days teaching about the kingdom, Jesus led them out near Bethany. He lifted his hands and blessed them; as he blessed them he was carried up into a cloud. Two men in white asked what?
answer: 'Why do you stand looking into heaven?'
choices: 'Why do you stand looking into heaven?'
'Whom are you seeking in the clouds?'
'Is it not the Lord who departs?'
'Where is your faith, men of Galilee?'
context: The Ascension is celebrated 40 days after Easter. The 'two men in white' promised he would return in the same way. Christ's session at the Father's right hand became central to Christology.

question: On a Galilean hillside, Jesus delivered the longest block of teaching in the gospels — Matthew 5-7. It opens with eight blessings: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit... those who mourn... the meek...' What are these blessings collectively called?
context: Latin 'beatitudo' — blessedness. The sermon includes the Lord's Prayer, the salt and light sayings, instructions on prayer, fasting, almsgiving, anxiety, and judgment. The most-quoted ethical teaching in Western history.

question: Asked how to pray, Jesus gave a short prayer beginning 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.' Catholics call it the Pater Noster. Protestants often call it what?
context: Matthew 6 and Luke 11. Six petitions for Catholics, seven counting 'deliver us from evil' separately for Protestants. The doxology 'For thine is the kingdom' was added by the early church and appears in the Didache.

question: Luke 15: a younger son demanded his inheritance early, squandered it on riotous living in a far country, came to himself in a pigsty, and turned home. His father saw him coming far off and ran to meet him. What did the father order?
answer: The fatted calf, the best robe, a ring
choices: The fatted calf, the best robe, a ring
The bread of affliction and bitter herbs
context: The greatest of Jesus's parables. The elder brother's resentment is the parable's second move — Rembrandt's late painting catches the father's exhausted embrace. The Greek word is 'asotos' — 'wasteful' more than 'prodigal'.

question: Luke 10: a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers. A priest passed by on the other side; so did a Levite. A despised foreigner stopped, bound his wounds, took him to an inn, and paid for his care. From where was the rescuer?
context: Jesus told the parable to answer the question 'Who is my neighbor?' Samaritans were the religious enemies of the Jews — making the answer scandalous. 'Go and do likewise.'

question: In a parable of seeds and soils, the same seed lands on a path (birds eat it), rocky ground (withered), among thorns (choked), and good soil (multiplies thirty, sixty, hundredfold). The seed represents what?
context: Mark 4, Matthew 13. Jesus explained it privately to the disciples. Augustine, Origen, and others used it as a hermeneutic for varieties of human response to revelation. Closes with: 'He who has ears, let him hear.'

question: At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples 'Who do people say I am?' Some said John the Baptist, some Elijah, some Jeremiah. 'But who do you say I am?' One disciple answered first. What did he say?
answer: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God'
choices: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God'
'You are the Lamb of God who takes away sin'
'You are the bread that came down from heaven'
'You are the resurrection and the life'
context: Matthew 16:16. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. Jesus replied 'You are Peter (Petros), and on this rock (petra) I will build my church' — Catholic foundation for papal primacy.

question: After feeding the 5,000, Jesus said 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger.' This is the first of seven 'I am' (ego eimi) statements in which gospel?
context: John's seven: bread of life, light of the world, gate for the sheep, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way truth and life, true vine. Each echoes Exodus 3:14: 'I AM has sent me to you.'

question: Approaching Lazarus's tomb at Bethany, Jesus said to Martha 'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.' What did Martha confess?
answer: 'You are the Christ, the Son of God'
choices: 'You are the Christ, the Son of God'
'You are my Lord and my God'
'You are the prophet who was to come'
context: John 11:27. Martha's confession matches Peter's at Caesarea Philippi. Often overlooked because Mary gets the contemplative scene at Jesus's feet — but Martha makes the great Christological confession.

question: At the Last Supper Thomas asked 'Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?' Jesus answered 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.' This is found in which gospel?
context: The verse is central to Christian exclusivism. Inclusivists (Karl Rahner's 'anonymous Christianity', for example) interpret 'through me' to include those who follow Christ's pattern without naming him.

question: The most quoted verse in the Bible, often called the 'gospel in miniature', begins 'For God so loved the world that he gave...' Whom did he give?
context: John 3:16 — spoken to Nicodemus by night. 'That whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.' Martin Luther called this 'the gospel in miniature'. Held up on signs at sporting events worldwide.

question: After the resurrection on a mountain in Galilee, Jesus told the eleven 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.' Baptize them in whose name?
choices: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
context: Matthew 28:18-20. The Trinitarian baptismal formula. The 'great commission' became the charter of Christian missions — driving everything from Paul to William Carey to modern evangelicalism.

question: Acts 2: 50 days after Passover, the disciples were gathered in one place. A sound like a rushing mighty wind filled the house. Divided tongues as of fire rested on each. They began to speak in other languages. What was the festival?
context: Greek 'pentekoste' — fiftieth day. The Jewish Feast of Weeks commemorated giving of the law at Sinai. Christian tradition: the Holy Spirit given to the church. 3,000 baptized that day after Peter's sermon.

question: Acts 7: a deacon and powerful preacher rehearsed Israel's history before the Sanhedrin and accused them of resisting the Holy Spirit. They stoned him outside Jerusalem. As he died he prayed 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.' Who watched?
context: Saul (later Paul) held the cloaks of the witnesses. Stephen is venerated as the protomartyr — December 26 in Western calendars. His face had shone 'like the face of an angel' as he spoke.

question: Acts 9: a fierce persecutor of Christians traveled to Damascus with warrants for arrests. Near the city a light from heaven flashed; he fell to the ground. A voice asked 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' Blind for three days, then baptized by whom?
context: Saul of Tarsus — Pharisee, Roman citizen, student of Gamaliel. Renamed Paul after his conversion. Wrote 13 (or 14, counting Hebrews) New Testament letters and conducted three great missionary journeys.

question: Acts 17: Paul, distressed at Athenian idolatry, was brought before the philosophical court on Mars Hill. He told them he had seen an altar inscribed 'To an unknown god' and proceeded to proclaim him. Whom did he quote from Greek poets?
context: Acts 17:28. He quoted both Epimenides and Aratus's Phaenomena. Most converted no one notable — Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris are the named exceptions.

question: Acts 27-28: as a prisoner sailing to Rome under appeal to Caesar, Paul's ship was caught in a fierce northeaster called Euraquilo. After 14 days adrift they ran aground on an island. Paul shook a viper from his hand without harm. What island?
context: 276 souls survived. Paul healed Publius's father and many others on Malta. He reached Rome in early 60 AD and stayed two years under house arrest, preaching openly. Tradition: beheaded under Nero around 64-67 AD.

question: Paul's most famous passage — read at countless weddings — begins 'If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but have not love, I am a noisy gong.' What is the famous triad with which it ends?
answer: Faith, hope, love — the greatest is love
choices: Faith, hope, love — the greatest is love
context: 1 Corinthians 13. Probably written from Ephesus c. 55 AD to the troubled Corinthian church. 'Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude.' The hymn to agape.

question: Ephesians 6: Paul tells believers to put on the whole armor of God. Belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, feet shod with the gospel of peace, shield of faith, helmet of salvation. What is the sword?
answer: The Spirit, which is the word of God
choices: The Spirit, which is the word of God
context: Roman legionary kit metaphorized. Paul wrote from prison in Rome, likely chained to a soldier whose gear he saw daily. The passage shaped martial Christian imagination from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress to modern devotionals.

question: Bishop of Smyrna and disciple of John the apostle, at age 86 he was arrested in Roman persecution around 155 AD. Told to revile Christ to save his life, he replied 'Eighty-six years have I served him; he has done me no wrong.' What was his fate?
context: When the flames did not consume him, he was stabbed. The Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest Christian martyr account outside the New Testament. He links the apostolic generation to the patristic.

question: A North African church father who wrote in Latin (rather than Greek), defended Christians in the 'Apology' around 197 AD, coined 'Trinity' (trinitas), and famously said 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of...' what?
context: Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155-220 AD). Later embraced the rigorist Montanist movement. His Latin theological vocabulary — substance, person, sacrament — still shapes Western Christianity.

question: In 312 AD before the battle of the Milvian Bridge against Maxentius, the emperor saw a vision — a cross of light in the sky with the words 'In this sign, conquer' (in hoc signo vinces). He marked the chi-rho on his soldiers' shields and won. Who?
context: The next year Constantine's Edict of Milan (313 AD) legalized Christianity. He convened the Council of Nicaea (325). He was baptized only on his deathbed in 337. The first 'Christian' emperor — though pagan religion remained legal.

question: Two emperors met in northern Italy and agreed to grant religious toleration to Christians and return confiscated church property throughout the empire. Constantine ruled the West; his co-author ruled the East. What was the agreement called?
context: Constantine and Licinius, 313 AD. Christianity went from persecuted minority to legal religion. Theodosius I made it the state religion in 380 AD. Within a century paganism was banned and the empire was officially Christian.

question: In 325 AD Constantine summoned bishops to a city in Bithynia to settle a dispute about Christ's divinity. The presbyter Arius taught that the Son was a created being. The council declared the Son 'homoousios' (one substance) with the Father. Where?
context: About 300 bishops attended. Athanasius (then a deacon) opposed Arius. The Nicene Creed emerged. Arius and two bishops who refused to sign were exiled. The controversy raged for another half-century — Athanasius exiled five times.

question: In 451 AD a council in a Bithynian city defined Christ as 'truly God and truly man... in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.' Which council?
context: The Chalcedonian Definition responded to both Nestorianism (two persons) and monophysitism (one nature). Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac) rejected Chalcedon — schism that continues today.

question: A 32-year-old African rhetorician sat weeping under a fig tree in a Milan garden in 386 AD, agonized by his moral inability. He heard a child chanting 'tolle lege' — 'take up and read'. He opened Paul's letter to the Romans at random. Who was he?
context: He read Romans 13:13-14: 'Not in revelry and drunkenness... but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.' Augustine traces the scene in Book 8 of the Confessions — Western autobiography is born.

question: Around 397-400 AD a North African bishop wrote his spiritual autobiography in 13 books, addressed directly to God: 'You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.' What is the title?
context: The Confessions inaugurated Western autobiography. Augustine traced his theft of pears as a boy, his sojourn with Manicheans, his mistress and son Adeodatus, his mother Monica's tears, his conversion under the fig tree.

question: After Alaric's Goths sacked Rome in 410 AD, pagans blamed the abandoned gods. A North African bishop spent 13 years writing a 22-book reply contrasting two cities — the City of Man (love of self to contempt of God) and the City of God (love of God to contempt of self). Who?
context: De Civitate Dei (413-426 AD). Founded Christian political theology. Earthly empires rise and fall, but the City of God endures eternally. Augustine died as Vandals besieged Hippo in 430 AD.

question: From a cave in Bethlehem, a fierce scholar spent 23 years (382-405 AD) translating the Bible from Hebrew and Greek into Latin — the standard text of the Western church for 1,000 years. What is the translation called?
context: Latin 'vulgata' — 'common'. Jerome ('Hieronymus') was famously irascible. Tradition paints him with a lion (he extracted a thorn from its paw) and a skull. His Vulgate became the Council of Trent's official text.

question: In 529 AD, an Italian noble's son founded a monastery on a hilltop south of Rome and wrote a Rule that became the foundation of Western monasticism — balancing prayer, manual labor, and sacred reading. The motto: 'ora et labora'. Who?
context: Monte Cassino. The Rule of Benedict (73 chapters) emphasized moderation, stability, obedience, and humility. Benedict's twin sister Scholastica founded the women's order. They are buried together at Monte Cassino.

question: In 664 AD a synod in Northumbria, England, decided whether Roman or Celtic Christianity would shape the English church — particularly the dating of Easter and the tonsure. King Oswiu chose Rome. Where did they meet?
context: Wilfrid argued for Rome's universality; Colman defended Iona's tradition. The decision aligned England with continental Christianity. Lindisfarne (founded by Aidan from Iona) and Iona itself eventually accepted the Roman date.

question: On Christmas Day 800 AD in Saint Peter's Basilica, Pope Leo III crowned a Frankish king Holy Roman Emperor — the first 'emperor of the Romans' in the West since 476. Who was crowned?
context: Charlemagne (Karl der Grosse) had defended Leo III against Roman rivals. The crowning shocked Constantinople — there was an Eastern emperor. The Carolingian renaissance revived Latin learning and created a Christian Western Europe.

question: In 1095 Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade at Clermont, calling Christian knights to liberate Jerusalem from Muslim rule. After three years of brutal marching, on July 15, 1099, the crusaders breached the walls. What happened next?
answer: A massacre of Muslims and Jews in the city
choices: A massacre of Muslims and Jews in the city
Surrender of the Holy Sepulchre keys
context: Crusader chronicles boast of blood up to horses' bridles. The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem held until 1187 (Saladin recaptured the city). The First Crusade also triggered the Rhineland massacres of Jews in 1096.

question: A 14th-century Dominican mystic and Paris theologian preached the birth of God in the soul and the abandonment of self into divine ground. Some of his propositions were condemned posthumously in 1329 by Pope John XXII. Who?
context: (c.1260-1328). His Rhineland mysticism shaped Tauler, Suso, the Theologia Germanica, and indirectly Luther. The 'spark of the soul' (Seelenfunklein) and 'gelassenheit' (releasement) entered later German philosophy through Heidegger.

question: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried an Italian astronomer for heresy for teaching that the earth moves around the sun, contrary to the apparent sense of scripture. He recanted and was sentenced to house arrest for life. Who?
context: Galileo (1564-1642). Pope John Paul II formally acknowledged the church's error in 1992. The Galileo affair became a paradigmatic case of religion-vs-science conflict (though the actual history is more tangled than the legend).

question: On Friday, October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of all Knights Templar in his kingdom. Tortured into confessing heresy, sodomy, and idolatry, the last Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned alive in Paris in 1314. Who pressured?
context: Philip was deeply in debt to the order. Clement (the first Avignon pope) was politically dependent on France. The order was suppressed in 1312. Friday the 13th's association with bad luck partly stems from this date.

question: An Oxford theologian and forerunner of the Reformation taught in the late 14th century that scripture was the supreme authority and translated the Bible from Vulgate into Middle English. His followers were called 'mumblers'. Who?
context: Wycliffe (c.1320-1384). The Council of Constance condemned him posthumously in 1415; his bones were exhumed and burned. He inspired Jan Hus in Bohemia. The Lollards persisted as English dissenters into the Reformation.

question: A Czech priest and rector of Prague University, condemned at the Council of Constance under a safe-conduct that was then revoked, was burned at the stake July 6, 1415. His last words: 'In a hundred years a swan will come.' Who?
context: The 'swan' was understood by Luther a century later to mean himself. Hus opposed indulgences, communion in one kind for laity, and clerical wealth. The Hussite wars (1419-1434) followed his death — Bohemia held out against the empire.

question: Around 1455 in Mainz, a German goldsmith perfected movable-type printing and produced an edition of the Latin Vulgate Bible — about 180 copies, 1,286 pages, in two volumes. The book transformed Europe. Who was he?
context: About 49 copies survive in some form. Without Gutenberg, no Reformation: Luther's tracts and German Bible spread by printing press at unprecedented speed. The Information Revolution begins 500 years before computers.

question: A Dutch humanist scholar published the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516 (with parallel Latin), giving reformers a fresh text from which to translate. He famously laid 'the egg that Luther hatched'. Who?
context: Erasmus (c.1466-1536) remained Catholic, opposed Luther on free will in De Libero Arbitrio (1524), but his text — Textus Receptus — and his satire ('In Praise of Folly', 1509) helped destabilize medieval Catholicism.

question: In April 1521, Martin Luther stood before Emperor Charles V at the imperial Diet in Worms and was ordered to recant his writings. After a day's reflection he refused, ending (per legend) 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders.' What does it mean?
answer: 'Here I stand, I can do no other'
choices: 'Here I stand, I can do no other'
'I will not be moved by men'
context: The exact words are debated — but the substance is well-attested. Luther was declared outlaw by the Edict of Worms. Frederick the Wise hid him at the Wartburg castle, where he translated the New Testament into German in 11 weeks.

question: Hidden as 'Junker Jorg' at the Wartburg in 1521-22, Martin Luther translated the New Testament from Erasmus's Greek text into German in 11 weeks. The complete German Bible (with Old Testament) was published in 1534. Why was this revolutionary?
answer: Lay people could now read scripture directly
choices: Lay people could now read scripture directly
The pope had forbidden Bible translation
The Latin Vulgate was poorly translated
Greek and Hebrew were unknown in Germany
context: Luther's German Bible shaped the modern German language much as the King James Version (1611) shaped English. Bible reading in vernacular became the engine of Protestant piety, literacy, and dissent.

question: In 1525 the former Augustinian friar married a former Cistercian nun who had escaped her convent (smuggled out in a fish barrel) two years earlier. Their marriage modeled Protestant clerical family life. Who did Luther marry?
context: Together they had six children (three survived to adulthood). 'Kathie' managed their Wittenberg household — the former Black Cloister gifted by the elector — and helped reform domestic Christianity. Luther: 'I would not exchange my Kathie for France and Venice.'

question: In October 1529 Philip of Hesse brought Luther and Zwingli together at his Marburg castle to unify the Reformation. They agreed on 14 articles. The 15th — on what — they could not. Communion split the Reformation permanently.
context: Luther chalked 'Hoc est corpus meum' ('This is my body') on the table and insisted Christ was bodily present. Zwingli held the elements were memorial signs. The split between Lutheran and Reformed branches dates from Marburg.

question: In 1553 a Spanish physician and anti-Trinitarian arrived in Geneva, was arrested, tried, and burned at the stake October 27. John Calvin had warned him not to come and supported the death sentence. Who was the heretic?
context: Servetus had also discovered pulmonary circulation. Calvin requested beheading rather than burning; the council refused. The execution shocked humanists; Sebastian Castellio's 'Whether Heretics Are to Be Persecuted' (1554) made the case for tolerance.

question: A fiery Scottish Calvinist exiled to Geneva returned home in 1559 and preached the Scottish Reformation. He confronted Mary Queen of Scots in five legendary audiences. He published 'First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women'. Who?
context: (c.1514-1572). Knox founded Scottish Presbyterianism. The 'monstrous regiment' meant 'unnatural rule' by women — aimed at Mary Tudor, Mary of Guise, and Mary Stuart. Embarrassed John Calvin when Elizabeth I took the English throne.

question: The English archbishop of Canterbury who guided Henry VIII's break with Rome and produced the first English-language liturgy in 1549, revised in 1552. Burned at the stake October 1556 under Mary I, after recanting and re-recanting. Who?
context: (1489-1556). At the stake he thrust his right hand — which had signed the recantations — into the flames first. The Book of Common Prayer (1662 revision) is the foundation of Anglican worship worldwide.

question: In 1534 the English Parliament passed an Act declaring the king (not the pope) the 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England. The break with Rome was over an annulment of which marriage?
answer: Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon
choices: Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon
Henry's marriage to Anne of Cleves
context: Catherine had failed to produce a male heir. The pope refused annulment. Henry made himself head of the church to annul his own marriage. He married Anne Boleyn (then four others). Thomas More and Bishop Fisher were executed for refusing the oath.

question: Between 1536 and 1541 Henry VIII and Thomas Cromwell dissolved over 800 English and Welsh monasteries, transferring vast wealth to the Crown and gentry. What spiritual losses did England sustain?
answer: Centers of learning, hospitality, and charity to the poor
choices: Centers of learning, hospitality, and charity to the poor
context: Libraries scattered or lost. Hospitals and almshouses for the poor disappeared. Pilgrimage shrines (Becket's at Canterbury, Walsingham) demolished. The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) revolted against this — and was crushed.

question: An English priest fled to the Continent to translate the New Testament from Greek into English (printed 1526) and the Pentateuch from Hebrew (1530). Betrayed in Antwerp, he was strangled and burned in 1536. Last words: 'Lord, open the King of England's eyes.' Who?
context: King Henry VIII authorized an English Bible three years after Tyndale's death. About 83% of the King James New Testament and 76% of the Old Testament is Tyndale's wording. He gave English 'Jehovah', 'Passover', 'scapegoat', 'mercy seat'.

question: Authorized by King James I in 1604 and published in 1611, this Bible was the work of 47 scholars in six committees at Westminster, Oxford, and Cambridge. It became the dominant English Bible for over 300 years. What is its common name?
context: Built heavily on Tyndale (76-83%). The KJV shaped English literature — Shakespeare, Milton, Bunyan, Lincoln, Melville, Dickinson, King — to a degree paralleled only by Homer's hold on Greek.

question: In 1620 a small ship carried 102 English Separatist 'Pilgrims' (and other passengers) from Plymouth to Massachusetts. Before landing they signed a compact for self-government. What was the ship?
context: Half died the first winter. Squanto (Tisquantum) and the Wampanoag taught them to plant corn. The 1621 harvest feast became Thanksgiving in American memory. The Mayflower Compact was a foundational document of American democracy.

question: On May 24, 1738, an Anglican priest attending a Moravian meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, felt his heart 'strangely warmed' while a reader was explaining Luther's preface to Romans. The man founded Methodism. Who?
context: John (1703-1791) and his brother Charles (the great hymn-writer) founded Methodism. Field preaching to coal miners and weavers — sometimes 20,000 at a time. Wesley rode 250,000 miles preaching across Britain.

question: A cross-eyed Anglican preacher with an extraordinary voice traveled the American colonies seven times (1739-1770), preaching outdoors to crowds of 20,000 in fields and streets. Benjamin Franklin tested his voice's reach. The First Great Awakening's central figure. Who?
context: (1714-1770). Methodist Calvinist (versus Wesley's Arminian). Whitefield's preaching tour of 1739-41 shook colonial religion. He preached 18,000 sermons total. Died in Newburyport, Massachusetts, mid-tour at 55.

question: An evangelical Anglican member of Parliament, converted in 1785, made the abolition of the British slave trade his life's work. After 20 years of campaigning, the Slave Trade Act passed in 1807. Who?
context: (1759-1833). The full abolition of slavery in the British Empire passed three days before he died (Slavery Abolition Act 1833). His ally Hannah More wrote the popular tracts; Clarkson gathered the evidence; Wilberforce led in Parliament.

question: In 301 AD a kingdom in the Caucasus became the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion — 80 years before Rome. The bishop who converted King Trdat III is venerated as 'Enlightener'. Who?
context: Trdat III had imprisoned Gregory in a pit for 13 years before Gregory's prayers cured the king's madness. Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet around 405 AD to translate scripture. Armenia rejected Chalcedon — Oriental Orthodox.

question: A German Lutheran pastor and former U-boat commander spent eight years in Sachsenhausen and Dachau for opposing Nazi religious policy. After the war he wrote a poem that became famous: 'First they came for the socialists...' Who?
context: (1892-1984). Niemoller co-founded the Confessing Church with Bonhoeffer and Barth. The 'First they came' poem appears in many versions; he attributed it to the failures of complicity. He campaigned for nuclear disarmament after the war.

question: An Oxford English literature don, atheist since youth, was reluctantly converted to theism in 1929 ('the most reluctant convert in all England') and to Christianity in 1931 after a conversation with Tolkien. Author of Mere Christianity. Who?
context: (1898-1963). Lewis's conversion happened on a motorcycle ride to Whipsnade Zoo. He gave BBC wartime broadcasts that became 'Mere Christianity' (1952). The Chronicles of Narnia (1950-56) and the Space Trilogy followed.

question: An Albanian-born Catholic nun founded the Missionaries of Charity in 1950 in Calcutta to serve 'the poorest of the poor'. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonized in 2016. Who?
context: (1910-1997). Born in Skopje (Ottoman Empire, now North Macedonia). The Missionaries of Charity operate in 130+ countries. Her published private letters (2007) revealed decades of spiritual darkness — a 'dark night of the soul' she carried in secret.

question: Central Christian doctrine: one God in three coeternal, coequal persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Latin formula: 'three persons (personae) in one substance (substantia)'. What technical Greek term is also used?
context: The Cappadocian Fathers (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa) developed this vocabulary in the 4th century. Trinitarian orthodoxy stands against modalism (one God in three masks), Arianism (Son created), and tritheism (three gods).

question: Catholic dogma defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at Trent: in the Eucharist, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood. The visible 'accidents' remain. What is this doctrine called?
context: Aquinas worked out the philosophy using Aristotelian categories. Lutherans hold consubstantiation; Zwinglians hold a memorial view; Calvinists hold spiritual real presence. Anglicans embrace mystery.

question: Martin Luther rejected Roman transubstantiation but insisted on Christ's real bodily presence in the Eucharist — 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine. At Marburg 1529 he chalked 'Hoc est corpus meum' ('This is my body') on the table. The Lutheran position?
context: Luther and Zwingli could not agree on this at Marburg, fracturing the Reformation. The Formula of Concord (1577) clarified the Lutheran view. The term 'consubstantiation' is sometimes resisted by Lutherans themselves as imprecise.

question: Approaching Thebes, a young man encountered a winged monster with a lion's body and a woman's head who killed any who could not solve her riddle: 'What walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon, and three at evening?' He answered: 'Man.' Who?
context: Oedipus. The Sphinx threw herself from a cliff. Oedipus reigned in Thebes — having unknowingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta. Sophocles's Oedipus Tyrannus (c. 429 BC) dramatized the unraveling. The name means 'swollen foot'.

question: After the British Mandate ended on May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed an independent Jewish state in Tel Aviv. Five Arab states invaded within hours. The state survived. What was founded?
context: The first Jewish polity in 1,878 years (since 70 AD). The 1967 Six-Day War gave Israel control of Jerusalem's Old City, Sinai, the West Bank, and the Golan. Yom Kippur War 1973. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict remains unresolved into the 21st century.

question: A 6th-5th century BC Chinese teacher gathered disciples and taught social order through ritual propriety (li), benevolence (ren), and filial piety (xiao). Compiled posthumously by disciples into a book of sayings. Who, and what book?
context: Confucius (Kong Fuzi, c. 551-479 BC). The Analects (Lunyu). Confucian thought shaped Chinese (and Korean, Japanese, Vietnamese) social life for 2,500 years through the imperial examination system (in effect for 1,300 years). 'When you know a thing, hold that you know it; when you do not, allow you do not — this is knowledge.'

question: The Celtic festival marking the end of harvest and beginning of winter — when the veil between the worlds of the living and the dead was thinnest. Christianized as the eve of All Saints. What was the name?
context: Samhain (pronounced 'sow-in'). October 31. The four Celtic quarter-days: Samhain, Imbolc (February), Beltane (May), Lughnasadh (August). Catholic All Saints' Day (November 1) and All Souls' Day (November 2) absorbed Samhain in Ireland. American Halloween descends from Irish immigration.

question: From February to April 1993 in Texas, the FBI besieged a Branch Davidian compound led by a charismatic apocalyptic preacher. After 51 days the FBI assault used tanks; fires destroyed the building. About 76 followers died including the leader. Who?
context: Vernon Howell renamed himself David Koresh. The Branch Davidians had split from Seventh-day Adventism. The Waco event radicalized American anti-government militias — Timothy McVeigh cited Waco when he bombed the Oklahoma City federal building exactly two years later (April 19, 1995).

question: In March 1997 in Rancho Santa Fe, California, 39 members of a UFO-millennarian cult killed themselves with phenobarbital in vodka, believing a spaceship trailing the Hale-Bopp comet would carry their souls. They wore matching tracksuits and Nike sneakers. Who led them?
context: Heaven's Gate. Marshall Applewhite ('Do') had been the leader since Nettles ('Ti') died in 1985. The cult had been around for 22 years. They had castrated some members. Their website is still maintained (deliberately) by surviving sympathizers — eerie internet artifact.

question: Genesis 32: Jacob, alone at the ford of the Jabbok before meeting his brother Esau, wrestles a stranger till daybreak. The stranger strikes Jacob's hip. What does Jacob demand before letting him go?
answer: A blessing — and is renamed Israel ('strives with God'), walking with a limp for the rest of his life.
choices: A blessing — and is renamed Israel ('strives with God'), walking with a limp for the rest of his life.
Esau's forgiveness in advance, so the morning meeting will pass in peace at the riverbank.
The return of the birthright bought from Esau with stew, now disputed after years apart.
A name change for his sons, so the twelve tribes would not carry his deceiver's name.
context: Peniel ('face of God') is what Jacob names the place — saying he saw God face to face and lived. The wound and renaming together founded the Jewish national name.

question: Exodus 3: a fugitive Hebrew who killed an Egyptian and fled to Midian sees a bush burning unconsumed. The voice sends him back to Pharaoh. Asked for a name, what does the voice answer?
answer: 'I AM WHO I AM' — Hebrew *ehyeh asher ehyeh* — the divine name later rendered as YHWH.
choices: 'I AM WHO I AM' — Hebrew *ehyeh asher ehyeh* — the divine name later rendered as YHWH.
'I am the God of Abraham — you shall need no further name beyond what was spoken to your fathers.'
'My name is hidden in the mountain — when you lead the people there, it will be given on stone.'
'I am Adonai, Lord of hosts — speak this name to Pharaoh and his magicians will know whom they oppose.'
context: Exodus 3:14 — the central self-disclosure of the God of Israel. Aquinas and Maimonides both read it as 'pure being,' grounding centuries of metaphysical reflection on God as existence itself.

question: 1 Samuel 17: a nine-foot champion of Gath has challenged Israel's army for forty days. A shepherd boy delivering bread to his brothers volunteers. What does he refuse before going out?
answer: Saul's armor — too heavy and untested; he goes with his sling and five smooth stones from the brook.
choices: Saul's armor — too heavy and untested; he goes with his sling and five smooth stones from the brook.
Money from the king's purse, insisting the victory must fall to the God of Israel alone.
The use of any weapon — taking only his shepherd's staff to provoke the giant into striking first.
A blessing from the high priest, saying his anointing must wait until the giant is felled.
context: David. One stone struck Goliath's forehead and the Philistines fled. The story became Western culture's archetype of the small overcoming the great — Michelangelo's David in Florence has stood for the idea for five centuries.

question: Exodus 12: ninth plague has passed; the tenth will kill Egypt's firstborn in a single night. Israelite households are told to do something so the plague passes over them. What?
answer: Slaughter a lamb without blemish and paint its blood on the doorposts and lintel of every Hebrew house.
choices: Slaughter a lamb without blemish and paint its blood on the doorposts and lintel of every Hebrew house.
Carve the divine name in Hebrew letters across the door, marking the household for the angel of mercy.
Light a seven-branched lamp inside the house and keep it burning from dusk until the cock first crows.
Recite the names of the patriarchs over the threshold while standing in unleavened bread up to the ankles.
context: Passover — Pesach. Eaten standing, sandals on, staffs in hand. Israel keeps the festival every spring; Christian tradition reads the Last Supper as a Passover meal, with Christ as the unblemished lamb.

question: 2 Samuel 11 records David's affair with Bathsheba while her husband Uriah is at the front. She conceives. David recalls Uriah hoping he will sleep with his wife and hide the paternity; Uriah refuses. What does David then arrange?
answer: Uriah carries a sealed letter to Joab ordering Joab to place him where the fighting is fiercest, then withdraw.
choices: Uriah carries a sealed letter to Joab ordering Joab to place him where the fighting is fiercest, then withdraw.
Uriah is poisoned at a banquet thrown in his honor by the king, with the wine-bearer dismissed in silence.
Uriah is exiled to a frontier garrison on the pretext of a promotion, never to return alive.
Uriah is drowned crossing the Jordan in floodwater, the riverbank guard quietly told to look away.
context: Nathan confronts David with the parable of the rich man who took the poor man's lamb. David repents in Psalm 51 — 'create in me a clean heart' — but the firstborn dies. Solomon is the second son of Bathsheba.

question: Numbers 22: Balaam, a foreign prophet hired to curse Israel, rides to the job; his donkey balks three times. When his eyes are opened, what does he see?
answer: An angel of the LORD with a drawn sword standing in the road — what the donkey had been seeing all along.
choices: An angel of the LORD with a drawn sword standing in the road — what the donkey had been seeing all along.
A cherub like the one guarding Eden after Adam and Eve had been expelled from the garden.
A pillar of fire blocking the path, the same sign that had led Israel by night across the wilderness.
The shade of Moses, freshly buried on Mount Nebo, warning him not to curse what God had blessed.
context: Balaam blesses Israel four times instead of cursing, including 'a star shall come out of Jacob' — read in Christian tradition as a Messianic prophecy. The talking donkey is one of the strangest scenes in the Hebrew Bible.

question: 2 Kings 2 has Elijah walking with Elisha toward Bethel. Something separates them and Elijah is taken up. Elisha cries — 'My father! My father!' What is the vehicle of departure?
answer: A chariot of fire with horses of fire — and Elijah is carried up by a whirlwind into heaven.
choices: A chariot of fire with horses of fire — and Elijah is carried up by a whirlwind into heaven.
A pillar of cloud descending from above, the same cloud that had led Israel out of Egypt long before.
A great wind from the wilderness, like the one that had driven the locust plague over Pharaoh's lands.
A boat of white birds bearing him out across the river and beyond the visible edge of the wilderness.
context: Elisha takes up Elijah's mantle, strikes the Jordan, and the waters part — confirming the prophetic succession. Elijah's not-dying grounded his returning role in Jewish and Christian eschatology, including at the Mount of Transfiguration.

question: Esther: Xerxes' Jewish queen, raised by her cousin Mordecai, learns that the vizier Haman has obtained a decree to exterminate all Jews on a single day. What does Mordecai say to make her act?
answer: 'Who knows whether you have come to royal dignity for such a time as this?' — perhaps God placed you here for exactly this.
choices: 'Who knows whether you have come to royal dignity for such a time as this?' — perhaps God placed you here for exactly this.
'The God of Abraham requires nothing less than the queen's own life given for the people of the covenant.'
'If you refuse, the daughters of Judah throughout Persia will rise without you, and your shame remembered.'
'The kings of Israel have always answered when the lot was cast against them — refuse now and be cut off.'
context: Esther fasts three days, approaches Xerxes uninvited (a capital offense), and exposes Haman. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. The festival of Purim — 'lots,' from the lot Haman cast — commemorates the deliverance.

question: Luke 1: a young woman in Galilean Nazareth receives an angelic visit promising she will bear a son to be called Jesus. She asks how, since she is a virgin. What does the angel answer?
answer: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' — nothing is impossible with God.
choices: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' — nothing is impossible with God.
'Your kinsman John, born of the barren, will be a sign to you, and the rest you shall know in fasting.'
'A great wind shall pass through Nazareth at the new moon, and you shall know the time of your conception.'
'You shall touch the rod of Aaron in the temple at Jerusalem, and the bloom will testify to your favor.'
context: The Annunciation. Mary's reply — 'let it be unto me according to your word' — became the model of consenting faith. Christmas dating reflects this scene: March 25 (Annunciation) plus nine months gives December 25.

question: John 13: on the night before his death, Jesus rises from supper, lays aside his outer garment, ties a towel around himself, and pours water into a basin. Peter objects when his turn comes. What is Jesus doing?
answer: Washing the disciples' feet — a slave's task — saying they must do the same for one another after he is gone.
choices: Washing the disciples' feet — a slave's task — saying they must do the same for one another after he is gone.
Anointing the disciples' heads with oil to consecrate them for the work they will do after his departure.
Carrying water for the Passover meal himself, in a sign that he refuses the lordship the disciples ascribed.
Mixing wine with water for the cup he will pass — a domestic ritual the head of the table normally avoids.
context: John's foot-washing replaces the institution of the Eucharist in his Last Supper narrative. The act is John's summary of the entire incarnation: God taking the form of a slave. Catholic Holy Thursday liturgy reenacts it.

question: Mark 14: at the night trial before Caiaphas, witnesses disagree. The high priest finally asks Jesus directly: 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' What does Jesus answer?
answer: 'I am — and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, coming with the clouds of heaven.'
choices: 'I am — and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, coming with the clouds of heaven.'
'You have said so — and the Father has spoken thrice in your hearing, and you have not turned.'
'I have answered already — the Sanhedrin's verdict is written on the inner wall of the temple before me.'
'The blessing of Abraham is upon you — but the Son of Man comes by a road you have not prepared.'
context: Caiaphas tears his robes and cries blasphemy. The reply combines Daniel 7 (Son of Man with clouds) and Psalm 110 (seated at the right hand). In Matthew, Jesus says 'you have said so'; Mark's 'I am' is the most direct claim in the gospels.

question: Matthew 27: a Roman centurion stood opposite Jesus and witnessed how he cried out and died. He had presumably overseen many executions. What does he say when Jesus dies?
answer: 'Truly this man was the Son of God' — the first Gentile confession of Christ in the synoptic gospels.
choices: 'Truly this man was the Son of God' — the first Gentile confession of Christ in the synoptic gospels.
'Truly this man was a king of Israel' — recognizing the inscription Pilate had ordered placed on the cross.
'Truly the temple veil has been torn' — alluding to the simultaneous tearing reported by the gospel.
'Truly the gods of Rome are silent' — admitting the imperial cult could not match what he had seen.
context: Mark has the same line. Luke has 'truly this man was righteous.' Named Longinus in later tradition; a relic claimed as his spear is venerated in St. Peter's Basilica. The first model of Gentile faith.

question: Luke 24: two disciples walk from Jerusalem to Emmaus on the third day. A stranger joins them and interprets the scriptures concerning Jesus. When do they recognize him?
answer: In the breaking of bread at table that evening — and at that moment he vanishes from their sight.
choices: In the breaking of bread at table that evening — and at that moment he vanishes from their sight.
When they reach the village and a child cries out his name, knowing him from earlier travels in Galilee.
When he removes his cloak at the door and the wounds on his hands and feet are revealed in the lamplight.
When they pass a stream and he refuses to drink, as he had at Jacob's well in Samaria long before.
context: The road to Emmaus. Luke uses the same fourfold sequence — took, blessed, broke, gave — used at the Last Supper. The pattern grounded Christian eucharistic theology for centuries.

question: Matthew 5's Beatitudes open the Sermon on the Mount: who is *makarios* ('blessed') and what they will inherit. The first promises the kingdom of heaven. Who receives it?
answer: The poor in spirit — those who recognize their spiritual poverty, not those rich in religious confidence.
choices: The poor in spirit — those who recognize their spiritual poverty, not those rich in religious confidence.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, since their longing for justice will be filled.
Those who keep the commandments from their youth, since their lifelong fidelity will be rewarded.
Those who tithe carefully of their grain, since their offerings will rise like incense in remembrance.
context: Matthew gives nine Beatitudes; Luke 6 gives four (paired with four 'woes'). The sermon includes the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule, 'love your enemies,' and 'judge not.' The most extended block of Jesus's teaching.

question: Luke 15 contains three parables about lost things: a sheep, a coin, and a son. The third tells of a younger son who demands his inheritance, wastes it on dissolute living, and ends up feeding pigs. When he 'comes to himself,' what does he do?
answer: Rises and goes to his father, planning to say he has sinned and is no longer worthy to be called a son.
choices: Rises and goes to his father, planning to say he has sinned and is no longer worthy to be called a son.
Sells his last possession to buy a ticket home, vowing in his heart never to ask for what he does not earn.
Hires himself out to the swineherd until he has earned enough to repay his father and return as a freedman.
Joins a band of bandits to seize back his inheritance from the older brother who is now its sole holder.
context: The Prodigal Son. The father runs to him while he is 'still a long way off' — a level of joy that scandalized the elder brother. Rembrandt's painting in the Hermitage is among the most-reproduced religious images in the world.

question: Matthew 16: Jesus at Caesarea Philippi asks who people say he is — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah. Then he asks the disciples directly. Who answers, and what does he say?
answer: Simon Peter: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' — earning the renaming and the promise of the keys.
choices: Simon Peter: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' — earning the renaming and the promise of the keys.
Andrew: 'You are the prophet greater than Moses, of whom the Law foretold' — and is praised for his humility.
John: 'You are the bridegroom of Israel, of whom we are the friends' — anticipating his gospel's imagery.
Nathanael: 'You are the king the angels in Jacob's ladder ascended toward' — recalling John 1.
context: Peter's confession is the hinge of Matthew. Jesus says 'flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,' renames him Petros, gives him the keys of the kingdom. The same Peter denies him three times within days.

question: Matthew 16: after Peter's confession, Jesus gives him a new name and a promise. The promise has been read for two millennia as the basis of one tradition's claim about papal authority. What does Jesus give Peter?
answer: 'The keys of the kingdom of heaven — whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.'
choices: 'The keys of the kingdom of heaven — whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.'
'The seat of Moses at Jerusalem, that you may teach in his stead until the consummation of the age.'
'The mantle of Elijah at Carmel, that the prophets of the kingdom may know whom to follow.'
'The rod of Aaron and the staff of the shepherd, that the flock and the sanctuary have one keeper.'
