context: 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church' (Matthew 16:18). Catholic tradition reads 'this rock' as Peter himself; many Protestants read it as his confession of Christ. The verse is inscribed in 5-foot Greek letters around the dome of St. Peter's Basilica.

question: John 8: Jesus declares of the patriarchs, 'before Abraham was, I AM' — echoing the divine name at the burning bush. Across John he uses 'I am' in seven extended metaphors. Which of the following is one?
answer: 'I am the good shepherd — the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.'
choices: 'I am the good shepherd — the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.'
'I am the gate of judgment — by me kings rise and fall in their generations.'
'I am the cornerstone — what the builders rejected is laid upon the foundation.'
'I am the rock in the wilderness — strike me and waters of life will pour out.'
context: Johannine 'I am' statements: bread of life, light of the world, gate, good shepherd, resurrection, way/truth/life, true vine. Together they form the structural backbone of John's high Christology — Jesus appropriating to himself the divine name.

question: Acts 2: the disciples are gathered in Jerusalem fifty days after Passover, on Shavuot/Pentecost. A sudden sound from heaven fills the house, and tongues like fire rest on each. What follows?
answer: They speak in other tongues, and Jews from many nations hear their own languages and ask what it means.
choices: They speak in other tongues, and Jews from many nations hear their own languages and ask what it means.
A pillar of cloud forms above the upper room, visible across Jerusalem, drawing a crowd to the city gates.
Each disciple receives a parchment naming the region to which he is sent, sealed in a wax color of its own.
They walk through the temple courts blessing the priests, who fall to their knees and join the apostles.
context: Peter preaches the first Christian sermon, quoting Joel 2 — 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.' About three thousand are baptized. Pentecost is reckoned by most traditions as the birthday of the church.

question: Acts 7: Stephen the deacon, on trial before the Sanhedrin, gives a long retelling of Israel's history ending with the charge that the court has killed the prophets and now the Righteous One. The court erupts. How does he die?
answer: Dragged outside the city and stoned, while a young man named Saul holds the cloaks of those throwing the stones.
choices: Dragged outside the city and stoned, while a young man named Saul holds the cloaks of those throwing the stones.
Beheaded by a soldier of Herod's guard at the gate of the temple, like John the Baptist before him.
Crucified on a hill outside Jerusalem alongside two zealots, beneath an inscription naming his offenses.
Thrown from the southwest corner of the temple platform, the same height the second temptation had set.
context: Stephen is the first Christian martyr. He prays as he dies — 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — echoing Jesus on the cross. Saul of Tarsus, present at the stoning, will be on the road to Damascus in the next chapter.

question: Acts 17: Paul on the Areopagus at Athens, surrounded by Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. He begins not from scripture but from an altar he has passed. What is its inscription?
answer: 'To an unknown god' — which Paul takes as his point of contact, declaring he will proclaim that god.
choices: 'To an unknown god' — which Paul takes as his point of contact, declaring he will proclaim that god.
'To the god of the Hebrews' — placed by traders who had heard of the temple at Jerusalem.
'To the gods of Olympus' — a generic dedication Paul argues conceals what the philosophers truly seek.
'To the god who creates' — which Paul welcomes as nearly the right name for the maker of all things.
context: Paul quotes Aratus ('we are his offspring') and Epimenides ('in him we live, move, and have our being'). Most mock him at the mention of resurrection, but a few — including Dionysius the Areopagite — believe.

question: 1 Corinthians 13 — written by Paul to a divided church in Corinth around AD 54 — is the most famous chapter on love in Western literature. It opens by saying gifts without love are nothing. What three things does the chapter end by saying remain?
answer: Faith, hope, and love — and the greatest of these is love.
choices: Faith, hope, and love — and the greatest of these is love.
Wisdom, knowledge, and prophecy — but knowledge will pass away, and only love endures.
Grace, mercy, and peace — the threefold blessing that opens many of Paul's letters.
Word, sacrament, and prayer — the three pillars of the apostolic community in its persecution.
context: Read at countless weddings, often without recognition of its original target — the Corinthians' jealousy, factionalism, and pride in spiritual gifts. The Greek *agape* is rendered 'charity' in the KJV and 'love' in modern translations.

question: Revelation, written by John on Patmos around AD 95 under Domitian, opens with letters to seven churches and turns to a vision of the heavenly throne room. Around the throne four living creatures cry day and night. What do they say?
answer: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.'
choices: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.'
'Worthy is the Lamb that was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might.'
'Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.'
'Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns over all flesh forever.'
context: Revelation borrows heavily from Daniel and Ezekiel — the four living creatures combine Ezekiel 1's chariot with Isaiah 6's seraphim. The threefold 'holy' is the Sanctus of Christian liturgy, sung in every Eucharist since at least the fourth century.

question: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was burned around AD 155 for refusing to offer incense to the emperor. The Roman governor pleaded with the old bishop to save himself with a small concession. What did Polycarp answer?
answer: 'Eighty-six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong — how then can I blaspheme my King?'
choices: 'Eighty-six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong — how then can I blaspheme my King?'
'I have not lived these years to surrender the cross at the gate where Stephen first crossed it.'
'The fire you threaten lasts an hour; the fire I am promised lasts forever — choose which I should fear.'
'The emperor's name is a coin; the name of Christ is a country — too old to change my citizenship.'
context: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* is the earliest extant Christian martyr narrative outside the New Testament. Polycarp was a disciple of John the Apostle; the chain through Irenaeus to the second-century church was central to early Christian self-understanding.

question: Tertullian, writing in Carthage around AD 197, watched the Roman state execute Christians and noted that persecution made the church grow. He coined a phrase that became one of Christianity's most-quoted slogans. What was it?
answer: 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.'
choices: 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.'
'The bread of the persecuted is the wheat of the kingdom.'
'The chains of the saints are the keys of the heathen.'
'The graves of the witnesses are the gates of the gospel.'
context: Tertullian's *Apology*, addressed to Roman provincial governors. He later joined the Montanist movement and was condemned, but the Latin theological vocabulary he created — *Trinitas, persona, substantia* — became the toolkit for orthodox doctrine.

question: In 325 AD Constantine convened a council at Nicaea in Asia Minor to settle a Christological dispute. The Egyptian presbyter Arius taught that the Son was a creature of the Father — divine but created. The council rejected this. What term did it use to define the relationship?
answer: Homoousios — 'of one substance' or 'of the same essence' as the Father, not a created being.
choices: Homoousios — 'of one substance' or 'of the same essence' as the Father, not a created being.
Homoiousios — 'of similar substance' but not identical essence, a position later rejected as half-Arian.
Hypostasis — three distinct persons in the Godhead, a term clarified at later councils.
Theotokos — bearer of God, applied to Mary the mother of Jesus, defined at Ephesus in 431.
context: Arianism persisted in the East and among Germanic Christians for centuries. Athanasius defended *homoousios* through five exiles. The controversy effectively ended at Constantinople 381, producing the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed used in liturgy today.

question: In 529 AD an Italian monk of noble birth retreated to Monte Cassino and founded a monastery. He composed a Rule of about 73 short chapters that became the template for Western monasticism for fifteen centuries. The Rule's most famous motto is two Latin words. What are they?
answer: *Ora et labora* — 'pray and work,' the twin pillars of Benedictine life.
choices: *Ora et labora* — 'pray and work,' the twin pillars of Benedictine life.
*Pax et bonum* — 'peace and good,' the greeting that became the Franciscan motto.
*Ad maiorem Dei gloriam* — 'to the greater glory of God,' the Jesuit motto coined a thousand years later.
*Fiat lux* — 'let there be light,' the opening words of Genesis used as Oxford's motto.
context: Benedict of Nursia's Rule balanced prayer, manual labor, study, and stability. Benedictine monasteries preserved classical learning through the Dark Ages — copying manuscripts that would otherwise have been lost — and trained generations of bishops, scholars, and rulers.

question: In January 1077, Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa for three days, awaiting Pope Gregory VII to lift his excommunication. The dispute was over the right to appoint bishops. What is it called?
answer: The Investiture Controversy — over whether the emperor or the pope had authority to invest bishops with their offices.
choices: The Investiture Controversy — over whether the emperor or the pope had authority to invest bishops with their offices.
The Filioque Controversy — over whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son.
The Iconoclastic Controversy — over whether images of Christ and the saints could be venerated in churches.
The Donation of Constantine — over whether a fourth-century imperial grant to the papacy was authentic.
context: Henry's penance was political theater that secured short-term absolution. The fundamental dispute lasted until 1122. 'Go to Canossa' came to mean 'submit humiliatingly' — adopted by Bismarck in 1872: '*Nach Canossa gehen wir nicht*' — we shall not go to Canossa.

question: In 1204 the Fourth Crusade — originally bound for Egypt — was diverted by Venetian creditors and Byzantine intrigue to Constantinople. The Latin army stormed and sacked the Christian capital of the East. One quartet of plunder ended up on Venice's facade. What is it?
answer: Four bronze horses looted from the Hippodrome and placed on the facade of St. Mark's Basilica.
choices: Four bronze horses looted from the Hippodrome and placed on the facade of St. Mark's Basilica.
*Lapis Negra* tablets taken from the Bucoleon Palace, now in the Vatican Museums.
*Pala d'Oro* gold altarpiece, given by the Doge to King Louis IX, now in the Louvre.
*Throne of Charlemagne* re-fashioned from Byzantine silver, now in Aachen Cathedral.
context: The sack of Constantinople was one of the great scandals of medieval Christianity. Pope John Paul II formally apologized in 2001. The bronze horses had stood in Constantinople for almost a millennium before being shipped to Venice; they remain on St. Mark's facade.

question: Francis of Assisi (d. 1226), son of a wealthy cloth merchant, renounced his inheritance in the public square at age 25, returning even his clothes to his father. He founded an order committed to absolute poverty. What did he call poverty?
answer: Lady Poverty — addressed as a noble lady in the chivalric tradition of his youth.
choices: Lady Poverty — addressed as a noble lady in the chivalric tradition of his youth.
Sister Want — paired with 'Brother Hunger' in the language of family.
Mistress Need — addressed as the teacher of every other virtue in turn.
Mother Earth — confused by later readers with his actual 'Sister Earth' from the Canticle.
context: Francis received the stigmata on Mount La Verna in 1224 — the first recorded case in Christian history. The Franciscans became one of the great mendicant orders alongside the Dominicans founded by Dominic Guzmán in 1216.

question: Aquinas's *Summa* opens with five proofs of God's existence — the *quinque viae*. The first argues from motion: nothing moves itself; an infinite regress is impossible; there must be an unmoved mover. What does Aquinas call this terminus?
answer: 'And this everyone understands to be God.' — the formula concluding each of the five ways.
choices: 'And this everyone understands to be God.' — the formula concluding each of the five ways.
'And this is the first principle of being.' — the Aristotelian formula Aquinas borrows directly.
'And this is the cause of causes.' — the Avicennan formula Aquinas inherits from Islamic sources.
'And this is the necessary being.' — the formula made famous later by Leibniz.
context: The five ways: motion, efficient causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final cause. Aquinas drew on Aristotle (mediated through Averroes) and Avicenna. His arguments remain points of reference in natural theology, defended by analytic philosophers like Edward Feser.

question: On October 13, 1307 King Philip IV ordered the simultaneous arrest of every Knight Templar. The Templars had been the fighting monastic order of the First Crusade and had become wealthy bankers. What was the king's motive?
answer: Debt — Philip owed the Templars vast sums and used heresy charges to seize their assets and erase the debts.
choices: Debt — Philip owed the Templars vast sums and used heresy charges to seize their assets and erase the debts.
Heresy — Philip genuinely believed reports the Templars had been spitting on the cross during initiations.
Treason — Philip had intercepted Templar correspondence suggesting an alliance with the Saracens against him.
Schism — Philip's confessor had warned him the order had broken with Rome and was operating independently.
context: Many Templars confessed under torture; the order was dissolved in 1312; Grand Master Jacques de Molay was burned at the stake in Paris in 1314. The Friday-the-13th bad-luck association traces to this arrest, though it was popularized only in the 19th century.

question: Catherine of Siena (d. 1380), a lay Dominican tertiary, never married, never entered a convent, and lived at home in Tuscany. From there she conducted a campaign that drew her into European politics. What did she persuade Pope Gregory XI to do in 1377?
answer: Return the papacy from Avignon to Rome — ending nearly seventy years of the 'Babylonian Captivity' of the popes.
choices: Return the papacy from Avignon to Rome — ending nearly seventy years of the 'Babylonian Captivity' of the popes.
Convene a general council in Constance to resolve the Western Schism that had divided the church.
Excommunicate the Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV for interference in episcopal appointments in Bohemia.
Found a new mendicant order for widows and unmarried women, larger than the Beguines of the Low Countries.
context: Catherine's *Dialogue of Divine Providence*, dictated in mystical ecstasy, is a Tuscan-Italian classic. She was named Doctor of the Church in 1970 — one of the first two women so designated. She and Francis of Assisi are patrons of Italy.

question: An anchoress walled into a cell attached to a parish church in Norwich wrote *Revelations of Divine Love* — sixteen 'showings' she received during a near-fatal illness around 1373. One image became famous — God holding a small thing in his hand. What was it?
answer: Something the size of a hazelnut — 'all that is made' — which endures because God loves it.
choices: Something the size of a hazelnut — 'all that is made' — which endures because God loves it.
An empty cup — 'the world's sufficiency' — which fills as the soul comes to receive.
A coin marked with the king's image — 'the human heart' — which God turns and reads.
A flame in a glass globe — 'the soul's life' — which would go out if God lifted his hand.
context: Julian of Norwich, whose real name we do not know. Her phrase 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' is among the most-quoted lines in English mysticism. T. S. Eliot built it into the close of *Little Gidding*.

question: On April 18, 1521, Martin Luther stood before the Diet of Worms — the imperial assembly — asked to recant his writings. He requested a day; the next day he refused, with words that echoed for four centuries. What did he say?
answer: 'Unless I am convinced by Scripture and plain reason, I cannot and will not recant. Here I stand. I can do no other.'
choices: 'Unless I am convinced by Scripture and plain reason, I cannot and will not recant. Here I stand. I can do no other.'
'I would rather die than betray the conscience of any man who has read these books with fear of God.'
'The pope is the antichrist of the latter days, and I shall be silent only when the trumpet sounds the last.'
'Let the emperor strike — the gospel preaches itself, and a thousand monks cannot now unburn this fire.'
context: Charles V placed Luther under the imperial ban. Frederick the Wise had Luther 'kidnapped' to the Wartburg Castle, where Luther translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks. That translation reshaped German as profoundly as the KJV shaped English.

question: The wars of religion in Germany (1618–1648) — the Thirty Years' War — killed an estimated 4–8 million people, a higher per-capita death toll than World War I in the affected lands. The war began with a Protestant action in Prague. What was the trigger?
answer: The Defenestration of Prague — Bohemian Protestants threw two imperial regents out a castle window.
choices: The Defenestration of Prague — Bohemian Protestants threw two imperial regents out a castle window.
The Edict of Restitution — Ferdinand II ordered the return of Catholic property seized since 1552.
The Battle of White Mountain — imperial forces crushed the Bohemian Protestant army outside Prague.
The Sack of Magdeburg — Tilly's imperial army massacred 20,000 of the city's 25,000 inhabitants.
context: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the war and established *cuius regio, eius religio* — the ruler decides his territory's religion. Westphalia is often dated as the start of the modern state system. The carnage soured Europeans on confessional warfare for generations.

question: In Northampton on July 8, 1741, a Congregational minister preached on Deuteronomy 32:35 — 'their foot shall slide.' The sermon depicted humans dangled by God over hell like a spider over a flame. What was its title?
answer: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — Jonathan Edwards's most famous sermon, central to the First Great Awakening.
choices: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — Jonathan Edwards's most famous sermon, central to the First Great Awakening.
'The Christian Hope' — Edwards's better-known sermon at his Yale commencement four years earlier.
'A Faithful Narrative' — Edwards's earlier description of the Northampton revival of 1734–35.
'The Religious Affections' — Edwards's 1746 treatise on how to distinguish genuine spiritual experience.
context: Edwards was one of the most subtle theological minds in American history — a careful reader of Locke and Newton as well as Calvin. His later writings (*Freedom of the Will*, *True Virtue*) shaped American intellectual culture. Princeton honors him.

question: In 1620 a small group of English Separatists, after twelve years in Leiden, sailed for the New World on a single ship. They reached Cape Cod, signed a compact before disembarking, settled at Plymouth, and lost half their number the first winter. What was the ship called?
answer: The Mayflower — 102 passengers; the compact signed in November 1620 is foundational to American political tradition.
choices: The Mayflower — 102 passengers; the compact signed in November 1620 is foundational to American political tradition.
The Arbella — flagship of John Winthrop's larger 1630 Massachusetts Bay fleet of eleven ships.
The Susan Constant — the largest of the three Jamestown ships that landed in Virginia in 1607.
The Half Moon — Henry Hudson's 1609 ship of Dutch exploration up what became the Hudson River.
context: The Pilgrims' Plymouth Colony merged with the larger Puritan Massachusetts Bay. Their Thanksgiving with the Wampanoag in fall 1621 became the basis for the American national holiday established by Lincoln in 1863. Plymouth Rock became a pilgrimage site by 1774.

question: In April 1945, a German Lutheran pastor was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on Hitler's personal order. He had been involved in plots to assassinate the dictator. His prison letters became one of the great 20th-century Christian texts. Who?
answer: Dietrich Bonhoeffer — author of *The Cost of Discipleship* (1937) and *Letters and Papers from Prison*.
choices: Dietrich Bonhoeffer — author of *The Cost of Discipleship* (1937) and *Letters and Papers from Prison*.
Karl Barth — Swiss Reformed theologian whose Barmen Declaration of 1934 opposed Nazi ideology in the church.
Martin Niemöller — German Lutheran pastor jailed in concentration camps but who survived to write 'First they came...'
Hans Lilje — Lutheran bishop of Hannover, jailed but freed before the end of the war.
context: Bonhoeffer was 39. His phrase 'cheap grace versus costly grace' became central to a generation's Christian ethics. He had returned voluntarily from safety in New York in 1939 because, as he wrote, he could not 'share the trials of this time with my people' from abroad.

question: C. S. Lewis, Oxford Fellow in English literature and a World War I veteran, was an atheist until his early thirties. Two evenings on Addison's Walk in 1931 with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson set the stage. Where did the final conversion happen?
answer: On a motorcycle journey to Whipsnade Zoo with his brother Warren — 'when we set out I did not believe; when we reached the zoo I did.'
choices: On a motorcycle journey to Whipsnade Zoo with his brother Warren — 'when we set out I did not believe; when we reached the zoo I did.'
In Magdalen College Chapel during a Christmas Eve Eucharist that he attended for the music.
In a hospital bed at the Wingfield Convalescent Hospital after being treated for trench fever.
In a thatched cottage in the Cotswolds during a reading party with G. K. Chesterton's friends.
context: Lewis described himself as 'the most reluctant convert in all England.' He became one of the 20th century's most influential lay Christian writers — *Mere Christianity*, *The Problem of Pain*, *The Screwtape Letters*, and Narnia. He died on November 22, 1963 — the same day as Kennedy and Aldous Huxley.

question: On July 18, 1870, the First Vatican Council passed the dogma of papal infallibility 533–2 in St. Peter's Basilica. Lightning is said to have flashed at that moment. The dogma is narrower than popular caricature suggests. Under what conditions does it apply?
answer: When the pope speaks *ex cathedra* — from the chair, on faith or morals, binding the whole church.
choices: When the pope speaks *ex cathedra* — from the chair, on faith or morals, binding the whole church.
On any utterance in any encyclical or apostolic letter signed personally by the reigning pope.
Whenever the pope addresses bishops in plenary session in St. Peter's Basilica with the College of Cardinals.
When the pope sits enthroned with the *tiara* on his head during the solemn Easter audience.
context: Vatican I closed early because of the Franco-Prussian War; Italian troops entered Rome in September 1870, ending the Papal States. Two formal *ex cathedra* definitions: the Immaculate Conception (Pius IX, 1854 — before the dogma was defined) and the Assumption (Pius XII, 1950).

question: In 1962 Pope John XXIII — a 78-year-old elected as a 'caretaker' — convened a council to 'throw open the windows of the church.' He died in 1963; the council continued until December 1965. What is it called?
answer: The Second Vatican Council — Vatican II — the most significant Catholic council since Trent.
choices: The Second Vatican Council — Vatican II — the most significant Catholic council since Trent.
The Council of Trent II — a renewed Counter-Reformation effort coordinated with Protestant observers.
The Synod of the Apostolic Constitution — a smaller body of bishops convened only for liturgical reform.
The First Roman Synod — a national-level meeting before any global ecumenical council could be planned.
context: Vatican II's documents — *Dei Verbum, Lumen Gentium, Gaudium et Spes, Nostra Aetate* — reformed Catholic worship (Mass in vernacular languages), strengthened biblical scholarship, opened ecumenical dialogue, and recognized religious freedom.

question: On October 16, 1978, the College of Cardinals elected a 58-year-old Pole as pope — the first non-Italian since the Dutch Adrian VI in 1522, and the first from Eastern Europe. He took the name of his immediate predecessor, who had reigned 33 days. Who was he?
answer: Karol Wojtyła — Pope John Paul II, who held the papacy until April 2, 2005.
choices: Karol Wojtyła — Pope John Paul II, who held the papacy until April 2, 2005.
Stefan Wyszyński — Polish primate and Wojtyła's mentor, often confused in early reports as the elected pope.
Albino Luciani — the John Paul I he succeeded, who had died after 33 days in mysterious circumstances.
Giovanni Benelli — the Italian cardinal who had been the front-runner before the conclave deadlocked.
context: John Paul II's papacy of nearly 27 years was the second-longest in history. He played a major role in undermining Soviet power in Eastern Europe; survived an assassination attempt in 1981; canonized more saints than all previous popes combined; and made the papacy a global pulpit.

question: In 1521 Cortés took Tenochtitlán; Spanish friars then undertook the conversion of millions. One image, said to have appeared to the Nahua peasant Juan Diego in December 1531, became central. What is it?
answer: The Virgin of Guadalupe — appearing on Tepeyac hill, her image imprinted on Juan Diego's tilma cloak.
choices: The Virgin of Guadalupe — appearing on Tepeyac hill, her image imprinted on Juan Diego's tilma cloak.
The Cross of Caravaca — a double-barred crucifix said to have been delivered by angels to Spanish friars.
The Black Christ of Esquipulas — a dark-wood statue of crucified Christ revered across Central America.
The Lord of Miracles of Lima — a fresco of Christ painted by an Angolan slave that survived earthquakes.
context: Guadalupe became the national symbol of Mexico — carried on banners in the 1810 independence revolt under Father Hidalgo, and in the 1910 revolution by Zapata's army. Her feast day (December 12) draws millions of pilgrims to her basilica north of Mexico City, the most-visited Catholic shrine in the world.

question: Anselm of Canterbury, in his 1098 treatise *Cur Deus Homo* ('Why God Became Man'), set out an influential theory of why Christ had to die. Human sin had infinitely offended God's honor; only an infinite payment by a being fully God and fully man could discharge the debt. What is this theory called?
answer: Satisfaction theory — Christ's death satisfies the debt humans owed to God's offended honor.
choices: Satisfaction theory — Christ's death satisfies the debt humans owed to God's offended honor.
Ransom theory — Christ's death is paid to Satan, who held humanity captive after the Fall.
Penal substitution — Christ bears the penal punishment for human sin in our place.
Christus Victor — Christ's death and resurrection is a cosmic victory over the powers of evil.
context: Anselm's theory replaced the older 'ransom to Satan' model dominant in patristic and early medieval thought. Reformation theology sharpened satisfaction into penal substitution. Gustaf Aulén's *Christus Victor* (1931) sparked a recovery of the earlier model.

question: In Catholic eucharistic theology defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at Trent, the bread and wine at consecration become the body and blood of Christ. The 'substance' changes while the 'accidents' (appearance, taste) remain. What is this called?
answer: Transubstantiation — using Aristotelian substance/accident metaphysics, codified by Aquinas.
choices: Transubstantiation — using Aristotelian substance/accident metaphysics, codified by Aquinas.
Consubstantiation — Luther's formulation, in which Christ is present 'in, with, and under' the bread.
Sacramental union — Luther's actual term, sometimes confused with the Catholic doctrine.
Real presence — a broader term used by Anglicans for various sub-views including the via media.
context: Lutherans hold a 'sacramental union' (bread + body together); Reformed hold a spiritual real presence; Zwingli's Swiss reform held the Eucharist as memorial only. The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 between Luther and Zwingli failed over this point, dividing magisterial Protestantism.

question: On June 22, 1633, before the Roman Inquisition, an elderly Italian astronomer was forced to read aloud a recantation of his teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun. He had published *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* the previous year. Tradition holds he muttered something after rising. What?
answer: *Eppur si muove* — 'and yet it moves' — referring to the Earth.
choices: *Eppur si muove* — 'and yet it moves' — referring to the Earth.
*Veritas vincit* — 'truth conquers' — the motto later used by John Hus before being burned.
*Audi alteram partem* — 'hear the other side' — a legal maxim recommending judicial fairness.
*Numero, pondere, mensura* — 'by number, weight, and measure' — Galileo's mathematical creed.
context: Galileo lived under house arrest until his death in 1642. The trial became symbolic of religion versus science, though historians now see a more complex picture: Galileo had powerful patrons in the church, his theology was orthodox, and the proximate cause was political conflict with Pope Urban VIII. John Paul II expressed regret in 1992.

question: The sale of indulgences reached its scandalous height in 1517 under a Dominican friar raising funds for St. Peter's. His jingle — 'as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs' — provoked the 95 Theses. Who?
answer: Johann Tetzel — operating in Saxony just across the river from Wittenberg.
choices: Johann Tetzel — operating in Saxony just across the river from Wittenberg.
Cardinal Cajetan — the Dominican theologian who later examined Luther at Augsburg.
Albrecht of Brandenburg — the archbishop who held the indulgence concession to repay his banker.
Pope Leo X — the Medici pope (Giovanni di Lorenzo) who reigned during the indulgence campaign.
context: Tetzel is the unforgettable name; Albrecht of Brandenburg and the Fuggers' banking house were the financial mechanism; Leo X was the pope. Tetzel was disowned by Rome after the scandal broke. The Catholic Church reformed indulgence practice at Trent (1563) and Paul VI further reformed it in 1967.

question: On July 6, 1415, the Czech priest and reformer Jan Hus, having traveled to the Council of Constance under imperial safe-conduct, was condemned for heresy and burned at the stake. The safe-conduct had been revoked on the grounds that no faith need be kept with heretics. What were his last reported words?
answer: 'In a hundred years, God will raise up a man whose call for reform cannot be suppressed.' (Apocryphal but persistent.)
choices: 'In a hundred years, God will raise up a man whose call for reform cannot be suppressed.' (Apocryphal but persistent.)
'Truth conquers all' — *Veritas vincit* — the Czech national motto today.
'Forgive them, for they know not what they do' — adapted from Christ's words on the cross.
'The God of Wycliffe is mightier than the council of Constance'.
context: Luther in 1517 noted that Hus had been condemned for opinions he himself now held. The Czech Hussite movement persisted; the Moravian Brethren, descendants of Hus's reformers, played a key role in 18th-century Pietism, including John Wesley's Aldersgate experience. Hus is a Czech national hero.

question: On St. Bartholomew's Day, August 24, 1572, in Paris, an organized massacre of French Protestants (Huguenots) began at the order of the queen mother Catherine de' Medici, with the consent of Charles IX. Coligny was killed in his bed. The massacre spread for weeks. What was the approximate death toll?
answer: 5,000 to 10,000 Huguenots killed in Paris and provincial cities combined.
choices: 5,000 to 10,000 Huguenots killed in Paris and provincial cities combined.
30,000 to 50,000 Huguenots killed, comparable to the larger pogroms of the early modern period.
1,000 to 2,000 Huguenots killed, mostly in Paris and a few major Protestant centers.
200 to 500 Huguenots killed — the casualties were inflated in later Protestant pamphlets.
context: Pope Gregory XIII reportedly celebrated the news with a Te Deum and commissioned commemorative medallions — actions that remained a stain on Catholic-Protestant memory for centuries. The French wars of religion (1562–1598) ended with the Edict of Nantes (1598), granting Huguenots toleration. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685.

question: Augustine of Hippo's mother followed her son for years, weeping over his Manichaean phase and his concubinage, praying for his conversion — until a Milanese bishop assured her that 'the son of so many tears' could not be lost. She lived to see him baptized at the 386 Easter Vigil. Who?
answer: Monica — eventually canonized; patroness of mothers, married women, and converts.
choices: Monica — eventually canonized; patroness of mothers, married women, and converts.
Helena — mother of Constantine, who found relics of the True Cross in Jerusalem around 326.
Macrina — sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who shaped both Cappadocian Fathers theologically.
Felicity — early African martyr (203 AD), often paired with Perpetua in Christian liturgy.
context: Monica's deathbed scene at the port of Ostia, recounted in *Confessions* Book 9, is one of the great mother-son scenes in Western literature. Her shared mystical vision with Augustine — 'on we went, conversing of things eternal' — has been a touchstone for Christian spirituality.

question: On May 30, 1431, in the marketplace of Rouen in English-occupied Normandy, a nineteen-year-old French peasant girl was burned at the stake as a heretic. She had led the French army to victory at Orléans in 1429, attended the coronation of Charles VII at Reims, and been captured at Compiègne in 1430. Who?
answer: Joan of Arc — *Jeanne d'Arc* — rehabilitated by a papal court in 1456 and canonized in 1920.
choices: Joan of Arc — *Jeanne d'Arc* — rehabilitated by a papal court in 1456 and canonized in 1920.
Catherine of Siena — the lay Dominican who persuaded Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome.
Margery Kempe — the English mystic and pilgrim whose 1430s autobiography survives.
Christine de Pizan — the French intellectual whose *Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc* celebrated the maid.
context: Joan's trial transcripts survive — she defended herself with remarkable presence of mind against trained ecclesiastical lawyers. The English burned her three times to make sure no relic survived; her ashes were thrown into the Seine. Her rehabilitation came under Charles VII's later reign; her canonization was a French national event in 1920.

question: Maximilian Kolbe, a Polish Franciscan, volunteered in Auschwitz to take the place of a stranger condemned to starvation. He led the condemned men in prayer; when last alive he was killed by carbolic acid. Why did the man whose place he had taken survive the war?
answer: Franciszek Gajowniczek lived until 1995 — present at Kolbe's canonization in Rome in 1982.
choices: Franciszek Gajowniczek lived until 1995 — present at Kolbe's canonization in Rome in 1982.
Tadeusz Borkowski lived another two months but died of typhus before liberation.
Stanisław Lewandowski escaped Auschwitz the following spring and joined the Polish resistance.
Józef Wojtyła — no relation to the future pope — survived and emigrated to Canada in 1948.
context: John Paul II — himself a Pole — canonized Kolbe in 1982 with Gajowniczek present. Kolbe's act is among the clearest modern Christian witnesses of laying down one's life for another. He had run a major Marian publishing operation in Poland before the war and sheltered Jewish refugees at his friary at Niepokalanów.

question: Genesis 1 opens with a refrain — 'and God saw that it was good' — repeated for each day of creation. On the sixth day, after creating humans in his image, the formula is intensified. What does God say?
answer: 'And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.'
choices: 'And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.'
'And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was finished perfectly.'
'And God saw what he had made, and rested from his labors before evening.'
'And God saw the man and the woman, and blessed them with the breath of life forever.'
context: Genesis 1 — the seven-day creation account — is one of two distinct creation narratives in the opening chapters. The other (Genesis 2) is more anthropomorphic: God forms Adam from dust and breathes life into him, then plants Eden. The two accounts have driven theological reflection for centuries.

question: Genesis 3 has the serpent telling Eve that on the day she eats the forbidden fruit she will not die — instead her eyes will be opened. After eating, the couple covers themselves and hides. When God walks in the garden, what is Adam's reply?
answer: 'I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.'
choices: 'I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.'
'The fruit was sweet to my taste, and I did not know that it was forbidden to me alone.'
'The woman urged me, and I yielded only because she was given to me as a helper.'
'The earth has cried out under my feet, and I have hidden myself in the hour of judgment.'
context: God curses the serpent, the woman, and the man in turn. Christian tradition reads 'I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed' (3:15) as the *protoevangelium* — the first gospel — foreshadowing Christ's defeat of evil.

question: Genesis 4 has Cain offering produce of the ground and Abel offering the firstborn of his flock. God respects Abel's offering but not Cain's. Cain leads Abel into the field and kills him. When God asks where Abel is, what is Cain's famous reply?
answer: 'I do not know — am I my brother's keeper?'
choices: 'I do not know — am I my brother's keeper?'
'He is fallen in the field — the earth has drunk his blood.'
'He has wandered from me — go ask the wilderness, where the wind blows.'
'Has he not gone up to your throne? Why does the LORD ask his own?'
context: Hebrews 11 contrasts Abel — who offered 'by faith' — with Cain. 'Am I my brother's keeper?' has become English shorthand for the refusal of moral obligation. Cain is exiled to Nod, founds a city, and his descendants invent music and metalwork.

question: Genesis 11 places humanity after the flood building a tower 'with its top in the heavens' to make a name for themselves. God comes down to see, and decides to do something to scatter them. What?
answer: Confuse their language so they no longer understand each other, scattering them across the face of the earth.
choices: Confuse their language so they no longer understand each other, scattering them across the face of the earth.
Send a great wind to topple the tower, after which they cannot agree on whether to rebuild.
Strike the builders with a plague that singles out the architects, who alone could direct the project.
Reverse the seasons for a year so the bricks of the tower cannot harden against winter rain.
context: Babel — Hebrew *Bavel*, Greek *Babylon*, etymologized in the text as 'confused.' The story is theologically rich: pride and unity in defiance of God, scattering into the nations of the table that opens chapter 10. Pentecost (Acts 2) is read as the reversal of Babel.

question: Exodus 20 records the giving of the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. The first commandment opens with the declaration 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.' What does it then forbid?
answer: 'You shall have no other gods before me.'
choices: 'You shall have no other gods before me.'
'You shall not make for yourself a graven image of anything in heaven or on earth.'
'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain.'
'Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.'
context: Catholics and Lutherans combine the first two into one and split the tenth (covet wife / covet possessions). Reformed and Eastern Orthodox traditions count them as Exodus does, with the prohibition of graven images as the separate second commandment. The numbering reflects deep theological disagreement.

question: 1 Kings 17: the prophet Elijah confronts King Ahab and announces a drought. The LORD then sends Elijah east of the Jordan to the Brook Cherith, where he drinks from the brook and is fed by what?
answer: Ravens — who bring him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening.
choices: Ravens — who bring him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening.
Eagles — who carry food from the king's table while flying above the wilderness valley.
A widow's son who finds him by accident and feeds him from his family's diminishing store.
Wild deer — who lead him to a hidden cistern and bring grain from a wilderness farm by night.
context: When the brook dries up, Elijah is sent to Zarephath in pagan Sidon, where a starving widow shares her last meal with him and her jar of meal and cruse of oil do not fail. The widow's son falls ill and dies; Elijah revives him. The Sidonian widow's faith becomes a Jewish reference for foreign believers.

question: Isaiah 6 records the prophet's call: the year King Uzziah died (740 BC), Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up, his train filling the temple. Seraphim with six wings cry 'Holy, Holy, Holy' to one another. Isaiah cries out — what?
answer: 'Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, dwelling among a people of unclean lips.'
choices: 'Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, dwelling among a people of unclean lips.'
'Spare me, O LORD, that I may pour out the offering of my hands at your altar in the morning.'
'Set a watchman on the wall of Jerusalem, that he may see the chariots of Egypt and Assyria.'
'Have I deserved this, O LORD? Did my father sin against you, or did I myself depart from your way?'
context: A seraph touches Isaiah's lips with a coal from the altar; his guilt is taken away. The LORD asks 'whom shall I send?' Isaiah answers 'Here am I; send me.' The scene became the model for Christian commissioning liturgies — and for the Sanctus of every Eucharistic prayer.

question: Isaiah 53 — describes a figure who 'has no form or majesty,' is 'despised and rejected,' 'a man of sorrows acquainted with grief.' This figure is wounded for transgressions, bruised for iniquities. What does the chapter say happens by his stripes?
answer: 'By his stripes we are healed' — Christian tradition reads this as the foundational prophecy of Christ.
choices: 'By his stripes we are healed' — Christian tradition reads this as the foundational prophecy of Christ.
'By his stripes the nation is gathered' — Jewish tradition reads this as the suffering of Israel as a whole.
'By his stripes the temple is purified' — a third-temple reading that became messianic in late Second Temple Judaism.
'By his stripes the king is anointed' — a coronation reading favored in the Royal Psalms.
context: Isaiah 53 is among the most quoted Old Testament passages in the New Testament — including 1 Peter 2:24 and Acts 8 (Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch). The 'Servant' is identified variously in Judaism (Israel, the prophet, an individual messiah) and unanimously in Christianity with Jesus.

question: The book of Ecclesiastes opens with a famous refrain attributed to 'the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem' (traditionally Solomon). The book's view of human life under the sun is bleak. What is its opening cry?
answer: 'Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.'
choices: 'Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.'
'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom — and to depart from evil is understanding.'
'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want — he makes me lie down in green pastures.'
'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'
context: *Hevel havalim*, hakkol hevel.* 'Vanity' translates *hevel* — 'breath' or 'vapor.' The Preacher (Qoheleth) examines pleasure, wisdom, work, and wealth, finding nothing that endures. The book ends with 'fear God and keep his commandments — for this is the whole duty of man.'

question: Psalm 23, attributed to David, opens with a metaphor that has shaped Western devotional language for three millennia. What is the opening line?
answer: 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.'
choices: 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.'
'Out of the depths have I cried to you, O LORD; LORD, hear my voice.'
'How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face?'
'I lift up my eyes to the hills — from where does my help come?'
context: The 23rd psalm is read at most Christian funerals and many Jewish ones. Its valley 'of the shadow of death' (*tsalmavet*) and 'rod and staff' (the shepherd's two tools) shaped countless hymns and poems. The translation history runs through Tyndale, Geneva, KJV, BCP, and modern versions.

question: Paul's letter to the Galatians (c. AD 49) opens with sharp anger: he had founded these churches in Asia Minor, and after his departure other teachers had convinced the Galatians that Gentile converts had to be circumcised. What does Paul call this teaching?
answer: 'A different gospel — which is not another' — and he pronounces a curse on anyone preaching it.
choices: 'A different gospel — which is not another' — and he pronounces a curse on anyone preaching it.
'A small misunderstanding' — easily corrected once the matter is brought before the apostles.
'A Pharisaic remnant' — to be tolerated as the Galatians grow in maturity over years.
'A wisdom from God' — Paul allows that the teaching is permissible if pastorally needed.
context: Galatians is the most polemical of Paul's letters. He insists Christians are 'justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law.' The argument shaped Luther's Reformation: Luther's Galatians lectures of 1531 were translated and reread in every later Protestant revival.

question: Romans, written around AD 57 from Corinth, is Paul's most systematic letter. It opens with the gospel as 'the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes,' then a long argument for universal sin and free justification. Chapter 8 ends with a triumph. What?
answer: 'Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers... shall separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.'
choices: 'Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers... shall separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.'
'Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves — be wise as serpents.'
'Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all we ask or think, to him be glory.'
'You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.'
context: Romans 8 is the high point of the letter. It moves from 'no condemnation' through life in the Spirit, the groaning of creation awaiting redemption, the unbreakable chain of foreknowledge-predestination-justification-glorification, and ends with the triumphant assurance Paul puts in twelve specific dangers.

question: Ephesians 6 closes with the famous metaphor of the Christian's armor — belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the gospel, shield of faith, helmet of salvation, sword of the Spirit. What is the sword identified as?
answer: 'The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.'
choices: 'The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.'
'The sword of the Lord and of Gideon' — Old Testament battle cry.
'The sword of judgment, gleaming in the hand of the righteous judge.'
'The sword of Solomon, which divides the truth from the falsehood.'
context: The armor metaphor draws on Isaiah 11 and 59 ('he put on righteousness as a breastplate'). Wesley's hymn 'Soldiers of Christ Arise,' Bunyan's *Pilgrim's Progress*, and centuries of Christian devotional language built on this imagery. The sword is *the word* — the only offensive weapon in the list.

question: Philippians 2, written by Paul from prison around AD 62, contains an early Christian hymn celebrating Christ — who, 'being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped' but emptied himself. What term names this self-emptying?
answer: Kenosis — *ekenōsen* in Greek — 'he emptied himself' — the basis of 'kenotic Christology.'
choices: Kenosis — *ekenōsen* in Greek — 'he emptied himself' — the basis of 'kenotic Christology.'
Hypostasis — referring to the persons of the Godhead, not specifically to Christ's self-emptying.
Theosis — the divinization of the believer in Eastern Christianity, the opposite of kenosis.
Apophasis — negative or 'unsaying' theology, a separate strand of mystical reflection.
context: Philippians 2:6–11 is widely regarded as a pre-Pauline hymn. It moves from incarnation through obedience unto death (even death on a cross) to exaltation — 'every knee shall bow.' Modern 'kenotic theology' (e.g., 19th-century British divines) drew systematically on this passage.

question: James, traditionally attributed to James the brother of Jesus (the leader of the Jerusalem church), takes a position on faith and works that Luther found troubling. The letter argues a man is justified by works and not by faith alone. Luther called James what?
answer: 'A right strawy epistle' — *eine recht strohern Epistel* — though he kept it in his Bible.
choices: 'A right strawy epistle' — *eine recht strohern Epistel* — though he kept it in his Bible.
'The Petrine corrective' — a pastoral letter useful for those misreading Paul on grace.
'The Greek apocrypha' — denying its apostolicity and removing it from his New Testament.
'The lost Gospel' — speculating that it preserved sayings of Jesus omitted from the canonical four.
context: Luther never removed James from his canon. He acknowledged its difficulty alongside Paul (Romans 4 — 'Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness'). Catholic tradition reconciles them by distinguishing initial justification (by faith) from continuing justification (cooperating with grace, including good works).

question: Acts 8 records Philip the deacon being sent south from Jerusalem on the desert road to Gaza. He encounters a court official from a foreign queen, riding in a chariot and reading Isaiah aloud. Philip joins him. What does the official ask?
answer: 'How can I understand, unless someone guides me?' — opening the way to baptism at the next pool of water.
choices: 'How can I understand, unless someone guides me?' — opening the way to baptism at the next pool of water.
'How can I be saved, unless I journey to Jerusalem first?' — which Philip gently disabuses him of.
'How can my queen approve, unless I bring her a witness?' — which Philip provides in himself.
'How can I read of the suffering servant, when our courts have no songs of grief?' — which Philip explains.
context: The Ethiopian eunuch is among the earliest non-Jewish converts in Acts — the gospel reaching the southern reaches of the known world. Ethiopian Christian tradition claims this scene as the origin of African Christianity, and the foundation for the Aksumite kingdom's later official conversion under King Ezana.

question: Acts 10 has the Roman centurion Cornelius, stationed at Caesarea, receiving a vision of an angel. At the same time Peter at Joppa is on a roof, hungry, when he has his own vision — a sheet lowered from heaven full of clean and unclean animals, with the command 'rise, kill, and eat.' What is the lesson?
answer: 'What God has made clean, do not call common' — opening the gospel to Gentiles without circumcision.
choices: 'What God has made clean, do not call common' — opening the gospel to Gentiles without circumcision.
'What the LORD has set apart, treat as holy' — the priestly distinction Peter must now keep.
'What the law has decreed unclean, the prophet must purify'.
'What you see in vision, hold for a sign' — the dream-interpretation role Peter must now play.
context: Cornelius and his household are baptized. The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) confirms the principle that Gentiles need not become Jews to enter the church. Peter's vision is the hinge moment of the Acts narrative — from a Jewish sect into a universal mission.

question: The Society of Friends, founded in 17th-century England by George Fox, rejected liturgy, clergy, and oaths, and worshipped in silence broken only when someone felt 'moved' to speak. The group came to be called by a nickname derived from Fox's instruction to magistrates. What was it?
answer: Quakers — Fox told the judges to 'tremble at the word of the Lord.'
choices: Quakers — Fox told the judges to 'tremble at the word of the Lord.'
Shakers — from their characteristic shaking during ecstatic worship, an offshoot of Quakerism.
Ranters — from the energetic preaching style of one earlier 17th-century radical sect.
Diggers — from the agrarian socialist communes founded by Gerard Winstanley after the war.
context: William Penn, an English Quaker, founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a haven for the persecuted. Quakers were prominent in the abolitionist movement (John Woolman, Lucretia Mott, Levi Coffin) and in Underground Railroad operations. The American Friends Service Committee won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947.

question: On December 1, 1955, an African-American Methodist woman refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a Montgomery, Alabama bus. The boycott that followed launched the modern civil rights movement and made a young pastor. — a national figure. Who was she?
answer: Rosa Parks — secretary of the Montgomery NAACP, deliberately chosen as a respectable plaintiff.
choices: Rosa Parks — secretary of the Montgomery NAACP, deliberately chosen as a respectable plaintiff.
Claudette Colvin — also arrested in Montgomery in 1955, but considered less suitable as a plaintiff.
Daisy Bates — president of the Arkansas NAACP, leading the Little Rock Nine integration in 1957.
Septima Clark — South Carolina educator who taught literacy classes for voting rights through SCLC.
context: Parks was not a tired old seamstress (as later mythology has it) but a trained civil rights activist who had attended the Highlander Folk School. Her arrest was not the first such refusal — Colvin had refused months earlier — but Parks was the test case the NAACP chose. The Montgomery Improvement Association elected King its president.

question: Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570–475 BC), a presocratic philosopher, made a striking critique of anthropomorphic religion. Mortals, he wrote, made the gods in their own image: Ethiopians' gods were dark and snub-nosed, Thracians' gods were red-haired and blue-eyed. What conclusion did he draw?
answer: If horses and oxen could draw, their gods would be horses and oxen — implying there is one true god, very unlike them.
choices: If horses and oxen could draw, their gods would be horses and oxen — implying there is one true god, very unlike them.
Greek polytheism is the only correct religion; foreign gods are inventions.
All religions are equally false; the philosopher must abandon all of them.
Religions are political tools; the philosopher must support whichever fits the constitution.
context: Xenophanes was a transitional figure between mythological and philosophical theology in Greek thought. His critique of anthropomorphism was developed by Plato (in *Republic* Book 10's attack on poetic theology) and the Stoics, and reached Christianity through Clement of Alexandria and the Cappadocian Fathers.

question: Socrates was condemned to death in 399 BC by an Athenian jury of 501. The charges were impiety and corrupting the youth. He was accused specifically of not believing in the city's gods. What did he claim to have heard since childhood?
answer: An inner *daimonion* — a divine voice that warned him against wrong actions but never told him what to do.
choices: An inner *daimonion* — a divine voice that warned him against wrong actions but never told him what to do.
The Muses singing in his ear, dictating his philosophy to him as he walked the agora.
Apollo's oracle, repeated daily to him by a priestess hidden in a private chamber.
Pythagoras's posthumous instructions, transmitted through the air to his successor.
context: Plato's *Apology* records Socrates's defense and the *daimonion*. Socrates accepted execution by hemlock rather than fleeing. His religious framework — taken seriously by his followers — was neither orthodox Athenian piety nor outright atheism but a personal theology of providence and judgment. Plato and Xenophon both wrote *Apologies* of Socrates.

question: Aristotle in his *Metaphysics* argued for a 'Unmoved Mover' (*kinoun akinēton*) — a being that causes motion without itself being moved, the final cause of all change in the cosmos. What does this being do?
answer: It contemplates only itself, since to contemplate anything less would be beneath it; it moves all by being loved.
choices: It contemplates only itself, since to contemplate anything less would be beneath it; it moves all by being loved.
It creates the world from nothing in time, then withdraws to rest from labor on the seventh day.
It directs each event by particular acts of providence, choosing winners and losers individually.
It dwells in three persons cooperating, communing eternally in love among themselves.
context: Aristotle's Unmoved Mover became the philosophical god of medieval theology — Aquinas's First Way is a direct development. The doctrine is famously unsatisfying as a religious deity: it does not know us, love us, or providentially act for us. Christian appropriation required adding everything that makes a god worthy of worship.

question: Iceland accepted Christianity in 1000 — but on terms that allowed certain pagan practices to continue. The law-speaker Thorgeir, a heathen himself, was asked to decide the matter to avoid civil war. What did he do?
answer: Lay under a cloak for a day and a night, emerged, and decided for Christianity with private pagan exceptions.
choices: Lay under a cloak for a day and a night, emerged, and decided for Christianity with private pagan exceptions.
Cast lots before the Althing, declaring he would abide by the result whatever it was.
Consulted with both Christian and pagan priests, then summarized their cases for the Althing to vote.
Walked to the temple at Uppsala in Sweden to ask the gods directly, returning with their verdict.
context: Thorgeir's exceptions: pagans could keep household worship privately, exposure of unwanted infants was still allowed, eating horse meat (a pagan religious practice) was still permitted. The Althing's collective conversion through one man's judgment is unique in medieval Europe — and the exceptions were withdrawn over the following decades.

question: Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), born in Córdoba and later court physician to Saladin in Egypt, produced one of the great works of medieval Jewish thought — a 14-book code of Jewish law in clear Hebrew. What is it called?
answer: *Mishneh Torah* — 'second to the Torah,' a comprehensive code organized topically.
choices: *Mishneh Torah* — 'second to the Torah,' a comprehensive code organized topically.
*Guide for the Perplexed* — Maimonides' philosophical work for those troubled by reason and faith.
*Sefer ha-Bahir* — but this is a 12th-century kabbalistic text, not by Maimonides.
*Zohar* — but the Zohar is a 13th-century mystical text, not Maimonides'.
context: Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed* (in Arabic) reconciled Jewish theology with Aristotelian philosophy and was studied by Aquinas. His 'Thirteen Principles of Faith' became a standard formulation of Jewish belief. His tomb in Tiberias still draws pilgrims; his Hebrew was so clear that his code became standard reference for Jewish law for centuries.

question: Kabbalah — Jewish mystical tradition — was developed especially in 13th-century Spain. Its central text claimed to be ancient but was largely composed by Moses de León in the 1280s. What is it called?
answer: The Zohar — 'Splendor,' attributed pseudonymously to the 2nd-century rabbi Simeon bar Yohai.
choices: The Zohar — 'Splendor,' attributed pseudonymously to the 2nd-century rabbi Simeon bar Yohai.
The Talmud — but the Talmud is the legal/halakhic foundation, not the mystical one.
The Midrash — but Midrash is a genre of biblical interpretation, not specifically mystical.
The Mishneh Torah — but this is Maimonides' legal code, philosophically rather than mystically inclined.
context: Kabbalah developed further in 16th-century Safed (in the Galilee) under Isaac Luria — 'Lurianic Kabbalah' with its doctrines of *tzimtzum* (divine contraction), *shevirat ha-kelim* (breaking of the vessels), and *tikkun olam* (repair of the world). Lurianic ideas spread through European Jewry and shaped Hasidism in the 18th century.

question: Reginald Pole (1500–1558), an English cardinal in Rome and a contender to be pope at the conclave of 1549 (he lost by one vote), was archbishop of Canterbury under Mary I and oversaw the burning of Protestants. He died the same day as Mary herself, November 17, 1558. Who succeeded both?
answer: Elizabeth I as queen and Matthew Parker as archbishop — restoring the Protestant settlement.
choices: Elizabeth I as queen and Matthew Parker as archbishop — restoring the Protestant settlement.
Mary Queen of Scots as queen — but she became queen consort of France in 1559, not of England.
Catherine of Aragon — but Catherine had died in 1536, decades before Mary's death.
Edward VI — but Edward had been Mary's predecessor, not successor.
context: Pole's death on the same day as Mary's effectively ended the Catholic restoration in England. Elizabeth's accession in 1558 began the long Elizabethan settlement of moderate Protestantism. Pole's reputation has been complicated by historians — he was a serious Catholic reformer (associate of the *Spirituali* and a near-pope) as well as the architect of English Counter-Reformation burnings.

question: Søren Kierkegaard, in *Fear and Trembling* (1843), reflected on the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) as the central image of faith. The 'Knight of Faith' — Abraham — does what no ethical universalism can sanction. The book is built around a stunning paradox. What?
answer: The 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — faith may demand what universal ethics forbids.
choices: The 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — faith may demand what universal ethics forbids.
The 'incognito of the divine' — God's address is always disguised in the ordinary.
The 'leap into the irrational' — but Kierkegaard never uses this phrase; it is later misattribution.
The 'subjective truth' — faith is a question of the believer's existence, not propositional content.
context: Kierkegaard's Abraham hesitates between three days' journey to Moriah. The terror of being asked to kill his son cannot be communicated to the village — every parent would condemn him. Yet Abraham obeys. Kierkegaard's reading became central to 20th-century existentialism and Christian theology. His attack on the comfortable 'Christendom' of his time still resonates.

question: The Phoenix — a mythological bird of great age that died in flames and rose from the ashes — was known to Greek sources from Egyptian originals. Herodotus described it. How long did it live, according to most ancient sources?
answer: 500 years — after which it built a spice-nest, was consumed in fire, and rose again from the ashes.
choices: 500 years — after which it built a spice-nest, was consumed in fire, and rose again from the ashes.
100 years — making its renewals frequent and witnessed in a normal human lifetime.
1,000 years — making the bird truly extraordinary and a once-in-an-age phenomenon.
Forever — the Phoenix never actually died, the funeral pyre being a metaphor.
context: The Phoenix entered Christian symbolism as a figure of the resurrection — Clement of Rome (1 Clement, c. 95 AD) cites it as evidence of the natural plausibility of bodily resurrection. The myth appears in art and literature from Persia to China to medieval Europe, sometimes amalgamated with the Chinese fenghuang and other 'firebird' images.

question: The 'Tale of Sinuhe' — composed c. 1900 BC during the Egyptian Middle Kingdom — is one of the oldest surviving fictions in any language. It tells of an Egyptian noble who flees to the Levant after a coup, prospers there, and returns home to be reburied properly. What religious concern dominates?
answer: Returning to Egypt to receive proper burial — the afterlife depended on it.
choices: Returning to Egypt to receive proper burial — the afterlife depended on it.
Securing the king's pardon — the only path back to honor at court.
Marrying his daughters to Egyptian nobles — preserving lineage and inheritance.
Bringing his foreign goods home — to enrich his ancestral village and family.
context: Sinuhe's career in Asia is told vividly, but the urgent need for proper Egyptian burial — return to one's tomb, mummification, the funerary rituals — drives the narrative. The Egyptian view of the afterlife was deeply tied to bodily preservation in the homeland. The 'Tale of Sinuhe' is the foundational text of Egyptian literature.

question: Augustine's *Confessions* (c. 397 AD) is widely called the first Western autobiography. It begins with a famous prayer-paradox addressed to God. What is it?
answer: 'You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.'
choices: 'You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.'
'O God, who hast prepared for them that love thee good things, which pass man's understanding.'
'Lord, I believe; help thou my unbelief — confess my sin and turn my heart.'
'In the beginning, O Lord, all was darkness, and the form of my own soul was without shape.'
context: *Confessions* Book 1, opening. The phrase 'inquietum est cor nostrum' — 'our heart is restless' — has been quoted more than nearly any other line from Augustine. The *Confessions* invented the genre of spiritual autobiography for the West; Rousseau's *Confessions* (1782) modeled itself on the title, even as it departed from Augustine's theological frame. Petrarch carried Augustine in his pocket.

question: Augustine's *City of God* (begun 413 AD) was written in response to a specific event. What?
answer: Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in August 410 — the first sack of the city in nearly 800 years.
choices: Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in August 410 — the first sack of the city in nearly 800 years.
The death of Theodosius in 395 — splitting the empire and weakening Christian Rome.
The Vandal arrival in North Africa in 429 — Augustine's home province under siege.
Constantine's death in 337 — leading to Arian dispute and ecclesiastical disorder.
context: Pagans blamed Christianity for the sack — the gods, they said, had abandoned Rome because Rome had abandoned them. Augustine responded with the great work distinguishing the 'city of God' (the people of faith across history) from the 'city of man' (worldly political organizations, which rise and fall). *De Civitate Dei* runs to 22 books; it shaped Western Christian thought about politics, history, and providence for over a millennium.

question: Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179) was a German Benedictine abbess who recorded visions she had been having since childhood. What was the title of her first major work?
answer: *Scivias* — 'Know the Ways' — completed 1151, with vivid illustrations of her visions.
choices: *Scivias* — 'Know the Ways' — completed 1151, with vivid illustrations of her visions.
*Causae et Curae* — but this is her medical treatise, not her visionary work.
*Physica* — but Physica is her natural science treatise on plants and minerals.
*Ordo Virtutum* — but this is her morality play, an early example of medieval drama.
context: Hildegard's range was extraordinary: theology, visions, medicine, music composition, drama, herbalism, language invention (she created *Lingua Ignota* — a private liturgical language). Her music has been widely recorded in the late 20th century. Pope Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 2012 — only the fourth woman to receive that title (after Teresa of Avila, Catherine of Siena, Thérèse of Lisieux).

question: Aquinas's *Summa Theologica* (1265-1274) opened with his 'Five Ways' — five proofs of God's existence. What is the first?
answer: The argument from motion — everything moving is moved by another, traced back to an unmoved mover.
choices: The argument from motion — everything moving is moved by another, traced back to an unmoved mover.
The argument from gradation — beings vary in goodness; the gradation requires a maximally good being.
The argument from contingency — everything contingent depends on something necessary.
The argument from final cause — everything tends toward an end, requiring an intelligent designer.
context: Aquinas's five ways: motion, efficient causation, contingency/necessity, gradation, and teleology. They drew on Aristotle (the Unmoved Mover) and the Islamic philosopher Avicenna. The first three are versions of cosmological argument; the fourth is ontological-axiological; the fifth is teleological. They are among the most-discussed arguments in Western philosophy.

question: Thomas Aquinas, on December 6, 1273, while saying Mass, had an experience that ended his theological writing. He never finished his *Summa Theologica*. What did he say?
answer: 'Such things have been revealed to me that all I have written seems like straw.'
choices: 'Such things have been revealed to me that all I have written seems like straw.'
'The Lord has shown me the road; I can write no more, only follow.'
'My pen is empty; let another finish what God has given me to begin.'
Both A and C are reported in different sources; the experience itself is well-attested.
context: Aquinas died March 7, 1274, traveling to the Council of Lyon. The unfinished *Summa* breaks off mid-question in Part III. The 'straw' experience has been variously interpreted — as mystical, as physical breakdown, as a stroke. Aquinas's life was overwhelmingly intellectual; his end is the moment when the theologian-philosopher exceeds even his own intellectual achievements.

question: Jan Hus (1369-1415), a Bohemian priest who preached reform a century before Luther, was promised safe-conduct to the Council of Constance to defend his teachings. What happened?
answer: He was tried, condemned, and burned at the stake July 6, 1415 — the safe-conduct was disregarded.
choices: He was tried, condemned, and burned at the stake July 6, 1415 — the safe-conduct was disregarded.
He defended himself successfully; the Council found him orthodox and he returned to Prague.
He fled the Council overnight, returning to Bohemia where he died in his own bed.
He converted his accusers; the Council reformed itself and ended the Avignon papacy.
context: Hus's burning was a foundational moment for the later Reformation — Luther studied him carefully and called himself a 'Hussite without knowing it.' Hus's followers — the Hussites — fought a successful series of wars against Catholic armies in Bohemia for two decades. The Moravian Brethren and the modern Czech Republic both trace religious identity partly to him. Hus is the only protestant on the Czech Republic's commemorative calendar of national heroes.

question: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) was the Catholic Church's response to the Reformation. What did it definitively affirm?
answer: Both scripture and tradition as authoritative; seven sacraments; transubstantiation; justification by faith and works.
choices: Both scripture and tradition as authoritative; seven sacraments; transubstantiation; justification by faith and works.
Sola scriptura — adopting the Protestant view that only the Bible is authoritative.
The reduction of seven sacraments to two — baptism and Eucharist — matching the Protestant churches.
The complete abolition of papal authority — handing decision-making to the bishops as a council.
context: Trent's decrees defined Roman Catholicism for the next four hundred years, until Vatican II (1962-1965). The Council ran in three periods over 18 years. It also reformed clerical discipline, established seminaries, and produced standardized liturgy. The 'Counter-Reformation' phase of Catholic history — institutional rigor and missionary expansion — substantially follows Trent's framework.

question: George Whitefield (1714-1770), the great English revivalist of the 18th century, made seven preaching tours of America. What was distinctive about his preaching style?
answer: Open-air preaching to crowds of tens of thousands, with dramatic voice and gesture; Benjamin Franklin tested how far his voice carried.
choices: Open-air preaching to crowds of tens of thousands, with dramatic voice and gesture; Benjamin Franklin tested how far his voice carried.
Whispered intimate sermons to small groups, refusing to preach to crowds of more than a hundred.
Always preached in Latin, requiring translators in colonial settings.
Refused to preach outside Anglican churches, limiting his American audience.
context: Whitefield's preaching innovations — outdoor crowds, dramatic delivery, transatlantic celebrity — transformed Anglo-American evangelical religion. Franklin's *Autobiography* recounts measuring Whitefield's voice carriage in Philadelphia. Whitefield helped found Methodism with the Wesleys, but split with them on Calvinism. He owned slaves and supported slavery — a serious moral failure named honestly in modern accounts of the Great Awakening.

question: The Second Great Awakening (c. 1790-1840) produced major reform movements. What was Lyman Beecher's particular cause?
answer: Temperance — preaching against alcohol, founding the American Temperance Society in 1826.
choices: Temperance — preaching against alcohol, founding the American Temperance Society in 1826.
Abolition — but Beecher was cautious on abolition; his daughter Harriet Beecher Stowe was the bolder voice.
Women's rights — but this was the work of Stanton, Mott, and others; not Beecher.
Public education — but this was Horace Mann's work, contemporary but separate.
context: The Beecher family was the great evangelical-reform dynasty of 19th-century America. Lyman Beecher father, then sons Henry Ward Beecher (preacher and abolitionist) and Edward Beecher, then daughters Catharine Beecher (educator) and Harriet Beecher Stowe (*Uncle Tom's Cabin*, 1852). The Second Great Awakening's energy moved directly into causes including temperance, abolition, women's rights, prison reform, and public education.

question: John Henry Newman (1801-1890), Anglican turned Catholic, was the leading mind of the Oxford Movement. His 1845 conversion shook English religious life. What did he later write to defend his integrity?
answer: *Apologia Pro Vita Sua* (1864) — a religious autobiography written in response to Charles Kingsley's attack.
choices: *Apologia Pro Vita Sua* (1864) — a religious autobiography written in response to Charles Kingsley's attack.
*The Grammar of Assent* (1870) — but this is his philosophy of religious belief, not the autobiography.
*The Idea of a University* (1852) — but this is his philosophy of education.
*Loss and Gain* (1848) — but this is his autobiographical novel, distinct from the *Apologia*.
context: Kingsley had accused Newman of dishonesty in his Roman Catholic conversion. The *Apologia* (1864) traced Newman's intellectual development from boyhood Calvinist to Anglican high churchman to Catholic. It transformed English attitudes toward Catholics by showing the conversion as the rigorous outcome of deep thinking. Newman was made a cardinal in 1879, canonized 2019. The Oxford Oratory in his honor preserves his memory.

question: Vatican I (1869-1870), called by Pope Pius IX, defined a doctrine that has been controversial within Catholicism ever since. What?
answer: Papal infallibility — the Pope, when speaking *ex cathedra* on faith and morals, is preserved from error.
choices: Papal infallibility — the Pope, when speaking *ex cathedra* on faith and morals, is preserved from error.
Mary's Immaculate Conception — but this was defined by Pius IX in 1854, before Vatican I.
Papal supremacy over secular rulers — but this was medieval, not 19th-century Catholic doctrine.
The Trinity as three persons — but this was defined at Nicaea in 325, not at Vatican I.
context: The 1870 definition of papal infallibility came at the same time the Pope was losing his temporal power in Italy — the Italian unification reduced him to the prisoner of the Vatican. Some Catholics (the 'Old Catholics') broke with Rome over the definition. The dogma is narrow in actual application — only one infallible pronouncement (Mary's Assumption, 1950) has been formally declared since 1870. The exact conditions for infallibility have been debated by Catholic theologians ever since.

question: Pope Pius X (1903-1914) launched a major anti-modernist campaign. What was the 1907 encyclical that articulated his position?
answer: *Pascendi Dominici Gregis* — condemning Modernism as 'the synthesis of all heresies.'
choices: *Pascendi Dominici Gregis* — condemning Modernism as 'the synthesis of all heresies.'
*Rerum Novarum* — but this was Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical on labor and capital.
*Mit Brennender Sorge* — but this was Pius XI's 1937 condemnation of Nazi racism.
*Pacem in Terris* — but this was John XXIII's 1963 encyclical on peace, post-Vatican II.
context: *Pascendi Dominici Gregis* was a sustained intellectual assault on Catholic biblical scholars and theologians who had been engaging with Protestant historical-critical methods. Suspected modernists were required to take the Anti-Modernist Oath (1910). The campaign chilled Catholic biblical and theological scholarship for fifty years. Vatican II (1962-1965) partly reversed the constraint, encouraging modern scholarship while preserving traditional doctrine.

question: Karl Barth's *Epistle to the Romans* (1922 second edition) launched what is called 'dialectical theology.' What was his main target?
answer: 19th-century liberal Protestantism, especially its accommodation with German nationalism and Kulturprotestantismus.
