Paul's letter to the Galatians, possibly contemporaneous, presents the issue with greater theological force: justification by faith, not by works of the law.

question: Around 155 AD, Polycarp — bishop of Smyrna, said to have been a disciple of the apostle John himself — was arrested during a wave of persecution. He was about 86. Brought before the proconsul in the stadium, he was urged to swear by the genius of Caesar, curse Christ, and be released. The proconsul threatened him with wild beasts, then with fire. What was Polycarp's famous reply?
answer: 'Eighty and six years have I served him, and he hath done me no wrong: how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?'
choices: 'Eighty and six years have I served him, and he hath done me no wrong: how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?'
'I am old and my voice fails: send me wild beasts that they may hasten what years have left undone in me'
'Thy fire is cold compared to the eternal fire prepared for the wicked: cast me in and I shall feel no warmth'
'Thy Caesar reigneth but a season: my King reigneth forever in the heavens far above the realm of Rome'
context: The Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. 155) is the earliest extra-biblical Christian martyrdom account preserved in full. The proconsul ordered him burned; the flames reportedly formed an arch around him; a soldier was sent to stab him with a dagger. Polycarp links the apostolic generation to the second-century church — a direct chain back to John.

question: Athanasius (c. 296-373) was bishop of Alexandria from 328 until his death — except for the five exiles totaling 17 years that emperors imposed on him for his refusal to compromise the Nicene faith. Throughout this period, Arian or semi-Arian emperors held the imperial throne; most bishops capitulated. Athanasius did not. A famous Latin phrase summarizes his career. What is it?
answer: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world — celebrating his lonely stand for orthodoxy
choices: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world — celebrating his lonely stand for orthodoxy
Athanasius pro Deo — Athanasius for God — emphasizing his theological positivity rather than opposition
Athanasius Patriarcha — Athanasius the Patriarch — emphasizing his episcopal authority over Egypt
Athanasius semper victor — Athanasius ever victorious — emphasizing his eventual triumph at councils
context: Athanasius's 'On the Incarnation' (c. 318) remains the classic statement of why God became man. His Festal Letter of 367 is the first list to enumerate exactly the 27 books of the New Testament canon as we have them. His persistence is widely credited with preserving Nicene orthodoxy through fifty years of Arian imperial pressure.

question: Augustine of Hippo (354-430) is the most influential theologian in Western Christianity. Born in Thagaste in Roman North Africa to a pagan father and Christian mother Monica, he received a classical education. As a young man he abandoned Christianity for Manichaeism for nine years; he took a concubine and had a son. He moved to Milan as imperial rhetor in 384. There he encountered an exceptional bishop. Who?
answer: Ambrose of Milan — whose preaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections and prepared his Christian conversion
choices: Ambrose of Milan — whose preaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections and prepared his Christian conversion
Jerome of Bethlehem — translator of the Vulgate, who happened to be passing through on a mission to consult the imperial court
Hilary of Poitiers — bishop and theologian who personally received Augustine into the catechumenate before his conversion
Damasus of Rome — the pope who commissioned the Vulgate and welcomed Augustine to Rome for instruction in the faith
context: Ambrose (c. 339-397) — provincial governor turned bishop by popular acclamation — was the preacher whose teaching dissolved Augustine's Manichaean objections to Genesis. Ambrose baptized Augustine at the Easter vigil 387. The Latin hymns Ambrose wrote (Te Deum etc.) shaped Western liturgy; his confrontations with the emperor Theodosius established a principle of ecclesiastical independence from imperial power.

question: In August 386 AD, Augustine was 31, imperial rhetor in Milan, tormented by his inability to break from concubinage despite intellectual conviction of Christian truth. In the garden of his lodging, he flung himself under a fig tree weeping. He heard a child's voice chanting 'tolle lege' — 'take up and read.' Taking it as divine command, he opened Paul's letters at random. What did he read?
answer: Romans 13:13-14 — 'not in chambering and wantonness... but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' — and the doubt was resolved
choices: Romans 13:13-14 — 'not in chambering and wantonness... but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' — and the doubt was resolved
Galatians 5:22 — the fruits of the Spirit — and he immediately began a new ascetic life of teaching and prayer
1 Corinthians 13 — the love chapter — and he wept over his lost years before turning to compose hymns to charity
Philippians 4:13 — 'I can do all things through Christ' — and he rose to his feet healed of his sexual compulsions
context: Augustine recounts the garden conversion in Confessions Book 8 — one of the foundational texts of Western autobiography. The 'tolle lege' moment is among the most-painted scenes in Christian art. Augustine was baptized by Ambrose the following Easter vigil (April 24-25, 387). His mother Monica died at Ostia later that year, content that her prayers were answered.

question: In April 1204, the army of the Fourth Crusade — diverted from its planned attack on Muslim Egypt — sacked Constantinople, the capital of Byzantine (Eastern Christian) civilization. The crusaders had been bankrolled by Venice; the doge Enrico Dandolo (over 90, blind) led the assault. The city was looted for three days. Holy relics were carried west. What was the lasting consequence for Christian unity?
answer: Permanent rupture between Catholic and Orthodox churches — the Great Schism of 1054 was now sealed in blood
choices: Permanent rupture between Catholic and Orthodox churches — the Great Schism of 1054 was now sealed in blood
Restoration of Christian unity — Orthodox patriarch acknowledged Roman primacy as a result of military defeat
Conversion of Russia to Catholicism — the Russian church transferred allegiance from Constantinople to Rome
Unification of all eastern Christianity under a single Latin patriarch ruling from Constantinople for 60 years
context: The 1204 sack of Constantinople deepened the 1054 schism beyond healing — Orthodox Christians have never forgotten it. The Latin Empire of Constantinople (1204-1261) ruled from the looted city until the Byzantines recovered it. Many of the great works of art (the Horses of San Marco, the Pala d'Oro) and relics now in Venice came from the sack.

question: Julian of Norwich (c. 1343-after 1416) was an English anchoress — a woman enclosed for life in a cell attached to a church. In May 1373, at age 30, she received a series of sixteen visions (or 'showings') during a near-fatal illness. She wrote a short account immediately; she later expanded a fuller text after twenty years of contemplation. Her Revelations of Divine Love is the first known book in English written by a woman. What is her most famous phrase?
answer: 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — Christ's reassurance to her in the visions
choices: 'All shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — Christ's reassurance to her in the visions
'Love is patient, love is kind' — a phrase she actually adapted from 1 Corinthians 13 with attribution
'Now I shall be all in love' — her dying words recorded by her companion at the anchorhold
'In Christ I find my life' — her abridged life-motto inscribed on the wall of her Norwich cell
context: T. S. Eliot quoted 'all shall be well' in 'Little Gidding' (Four Quartets, 1942). Julian's striking image of Christ as Mother and her theology of the never-failing love of God have made her unusually appealing to modern readers. Her anchorhold survives at the Church of St. Julian, Norwich (rebuilt after WWII bombing); pilgrims visit regularly.

question: Meister Eckhart (c. 1260-1328) was a German Dominican preacher and mystical theologian whose vernacular sermons in Middle High German made him one of the most original voices in medieval Christianity. He preached on detachment (Abgeschiedenheit), the birth of the Word in the soul, and the depths of the Godhead. Some of his statements alarmed church authorities; he was posthumously condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329. Of what was he accused?
answer: Pantheism — apparently dissolving the Creator-creature distinction in language about the soul's union with God
choices: Pantheism — apparently dissolving the Creator-creature distinction in language about the soul's union with God
Pelagianism — denying the necessity of grace by emphasizing the soul's natural capacity for divine union
Donatism — denying the validity of sacraments performed by unworthy priests in his German diocese
Iconoclasm — denying the legitimacy of religious images, particularly in the Frankfurt Dominican houses
context: Eckhart's bold language — 'the eye with which I see God is the eye with which God sees me' — was vulnerable to misinterpretation. His defenders argue he was misunderstood; modern scholarship has largely rehabilitated him. He influenced the German mystics Tauler and Suso, the Theologia Germanica (later quoted by Luther), and modern interpreters from Schopenhauer to Heidegger.

question: On July 6, 1415, the Czech priest Jan Hus — rector of Charles University in Prague, preacher in the Bethlehem Chapel, critic of Church abuses — was burned at Constance. Emperor Sigismund had promised safe conduct. Hus had drawn on John Wycliffe's earlier teachings against indulgences and clerical wealth. What movement did his death ignite?
answer: The Hussite Wars (1419-1434) — Czech Hussite armies, led by Jan Žižka, repeatedly defeated imperial crusades sent against them
choices: The Hussite Wars (1419-1434) — Czech Hussite armies, led by Jan Žižka, repeatedly defeated imperial crusades sent against them
The First Lutheran Crusade — a unified German Protestant response that proved decades premature and was crushed quickly
The Catholic Counter-Reformation — Trent's reforms were initiated in direct response to Hus's death within the same year
The Jesuit Order — Ignatius of Loyola founded the order specifically to counter the Hussite legacy in Eastern Europe
context: Hus's death (despite Sigismund's safe-conduct, which the council ruled void for heretics) outraged Bohemia. The Hussite Wars saw Jan Žižka's wagenburg tactics defeat five papal crusades. The Compactata of 1436 gave Bohemia communion in both kinds (bread and wine for laity) and tolerated some Hussite practices. Luther later said 'We are all Hussites without knowing it.'

question: On April 17-18, 1521, at the Diet of Worms, Emperor Charles V demanded that Martin Luther — who had now been excommunicated by Pope Leo X (Decet Romanum Pontificem, January 1521) — recant his teachings. A pile of his books lay on a table. Luther asked for one day to consider. The next day, he refused. According to the most famous version of his words, what did he say?
answer: 'Here I stand, I can do no other; my conscience is captive to the Word of God; to act against conscience is neither right nor safe'
choices: 'Here I stand, I can do no other; my conscience is captive to the Word of God; to act against conscience is neither right nor safe'
'I will not recant, for the Pope is the Antichrist, and the Antichrist's authority can compel no Christian conscience'
'My books shall remain unburned, for they testify to the truth of Christ against the false church of indulgences'
'I appeal to the next general council, which alone has authority to judge between me and the bishop of Rome'
context: Modern scholarship doubts the precise 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders' formulation appeared in the original 1521 records — but Luther did refuse to recant unless convinced by scripture or evident reason. Charles V issued the Edict of Worms (May 25, 1521) declaring Luther an outlaw. Luther's protector Elector Frederick the Wise had him spirited away to Wartburg Castle for safety.

question: In 1524-1525, German peasants in southern and central Germany rose in armed revolt — the Peasants' War, the largest popular uprising in Europe before the French Revolution. Their Twelve Articles drew on Luther's language of Christian freedom, demanding social reforms. Perhaps 100,000 peasants died. Luther's response shocked many sympathizers. What did he write?
answer: 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes of Peasants' (May 1525) — urging princes to 'stab, slay, kill' the rebels mercilessly
choices: 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes of Peasants' (May 1525) — urging princes to 'stab, slay, kill' the rebels mercilessly
'In Defense of the Wretched Peasants' (May 1525) — calling on princes to grant the Twelve Articles by Christian charity
'Concerning the Two Kingdoms' (May 1525) — refusing comment on temporal politics as outside the gospel's scope
'A Lament for the Slain' (May 1525) — mourning the peasant dead while regretfully accepting their need for suppression
context: Luther's 'Against the Murdering, Thieving Hordes' is among the most controversial documents of the Reformation. He had urged moderation earlier, but the peasant atrocities at Weinsberg (April 1525) hardened him. The text helped lose the peasant cause but secured princely support for the Reformation. The 'two kingdoms' distinction — secular sword distinct from spiritual gospel — was Luther's framework.

question: From October 1-3, 1529, at Marburg Castle, Philip of Hesse — a Protestant prince hoping to unite the Reformation against Catholic powers — sponsored a meeting between Luther, Zwingli, and other reformers. They agreed on 14 of 15 articles of faith. They could not agree on the 15th, regarding the Eucharist. Luther reportedly wrote on the table in chalk a Latin phrase from Christ's institution. What did he write?
answer: 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'This is my body' — insisting on the literal meaning against Zwingli's symbolic reading
choices: 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'This is my body' — insisting on the literal meaning against Zwingli's symbolic reading
'Sola fide' — 'By faith alone' — insisting on justification as the foundation of all sacramental theology
'Caro non prodest' — 'The flesh profits nothing' — Zwingli's countertext that Luther reportedly used to mock him
'Tu es Petrus' — 'You are Peter' — the Catholic papal text that Luther mockingly applied to Zwingli's claim
context: Luther insisted on the literal interpretation of 'Hoc est corpus meum' — 'this IS my body.' Zwingli insisted 'est' meant 'signifies.' Without agreement on Eucharist, the Protestant front was permanently divided. Marburg's failure was a structural disaster — the Reformation produced Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist movements that fought each other as fiercely as they fought Rome.

question: John Knox (c. 1514-1572) founded Scottish Presbyterianism — Calvin's most fiery disciple. Originally a Catholic priest, he converted in the 1540s, served as a Marian galley slave (1547-1549), and lived in Geneva (1556-1558) absorbing Calvin's theology. Returning to Scotland in 1559, he led the Reformation. What was his most famous polemical work, directed against whom?
answer: The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) — against female rulers Mary Tudor and Mary Stuart
choices: The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) — against female rulers Mary Tudor and Mary Stuart
The Scots Confession (1560) — Scotland's first Reformed confession, which Knox principally drafted with five others
The Book of Discipline (1561) — establishing Presbyterian church governance throughout Scotland by parish and synod
The History of the Reformation in Scotland — published posthumously, covering events from Hamilton's martyrdom to 1567
context: The First Blast (1558) attacked female rule generally and Catholic queens Mary I of England and Mary of Guise of Scotland specifically. The title meant 'monstrous regiment' as 'unnatural rule.' Awkwardly, Elizabeth I came to the throne the same year — and never forgave Knox the polemic. His confrontations with Mary Queen of Scots after 1561 became legendary.

question: In January 1604, at the Hampton Court Conference after James VI of Scotland became James I of England, the Puritan John Reynolds proposed a new authorized Bible. James approved; the work went to 47 scholars in six companies at Oxford, Cambridge, and Westminster. They began work in 1607 and completed in 1611. What was the principal aim, and what made the King James distinctive?
answer: An authorized text for public worship — readable aloud, dignified, drawing heavily on Tyndale (NT) and the Geneva (OT)
choices: An authorized text for public worship — readable aloud, dignified, drawing heavily on Tyndale (NT) and the Geneva (OT)
A scholarly text from original languages — replacing the Latin Vulgate for academic theological study primarily
A simple text for the common people — written in deliberately plain colloquial English of the early 17th century
A Puritan text — replacing the Bishops' Bible favored by the Anglican establishment with a Reformed alternative
context: The King James Version (or Authorized Version, AV) shaped English religious and literary language for 350+ years. About 75% of its NT comes from Tyndale; its phrasings ('through a glass darkly,' 'the powers that be,' 'a thorn in the flesh') saturate English usage. Modern critical editions correct its textual base; for literary power and historical influence it remains unmatched in English religious translation.

question: In 1630, a much larger Puritan migration arrived in New England — about 700 settlers on 11 ships, led by John Winthrop. Unlike the earlier Pilgrim Separatists, the Massachusetts Bay Puritans regarded themselves as still part of the Church of England, intending to establish a model 'pure' church. On board the Arbella in 1630, Winthrop gave a famous sermon. What was its central image?
answer: 'A city upon a hill' — Matthew 5:14 applied to the colony as a Christian model the eyes of the world would watch
choices: 'A city upon a hill' — Matthew 5:14 applied to the colony as a Christian model the eyes of the world would watch
'A burning bush' — Exodus 3 applied to the colony as a beacon of Reformation faith in the wilderness
'A new Jerusalem' — Revelation 21 applied to the colony as the eschatological community fulfilling prophecy
'A righteous remnant' — Isaiah 10 applied to the colony as the survivors of the Old England Antichrist persecution
context: Winthrop's 'Model of Christian Charity' delivered the 'city upon a hill' phrase later quoted by John F. Kennedy and Ronald Reagan. The Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630) grew rapidly; by 1640 about 20,000 Puritans had crossed the Atlantic. The colony established Congregationalist churches, town meeting governance, Harvard College (1636), and Salem (where the witch trials occurred in 1692).

question: On March 25, 1807, the British Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, ending British participation in the Atlantic slave trade. The principal architect of the political campaign — sustained over twenty years (his first bill was 1789) — was an evangelical Anglican MP and friend of William Pitt the Younger. He was supported by a Christian network known as the Clapham Sect. Who was he?
answer: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical conversion in 1785 turned him to abolitionism and 'reformation of manners'
choices: William Wilberforce — whose evangelical conversion in 1785 turned him to abolitionism and 'reformation of manners'
Lord Mansfield — Chief Justice whose 1772 Somerset v. Stewart ruling effectively ended slavery in England itself
John Newton — former slave-ship captain turned Anglican curate who wrote 'Amazing Grace' (1779) on his conversion
Granville Sharp — abolitionist lawyer who brought the Somerset case and helped Wilberforce on the parliamentary campaign
context: Wilberforce's twenty-year campaign for abolition is one of the great moral political victories of modern history. The Slave Trade Act 1807 ended British trade; the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 (passed three days before Wilberforce's death) emancipated slaves throughout the British Empire. The Clapham Sect — evangelical Anglicans pooling effort across causes — pioneered many techniques of modern political activism.

question: Around 1820, a 14-year-old upstate New York farm boy named Joseph Smith Jr. (1805-1844) — caught up in the religious revivals of the 'Burned-Over District' and confused by competing claims of denominations — went into a grove of trees on his family's farm near Manchester, NY, to pray about which church to join. He later reported a vision. What did he claim?
answer: The Father and the Son appeared to him in pillars of light; he was told to join none of the existing churches
choices: The Father and the Son appeared to him in pillars of light; he was told to join none of the existing churches
An angel named Moroni appeared to him with golden plates; this was actually three years later in September 1823
He saw the resurrected Christ standing on a stone altar offering him a new testament for the American continent
He received the gift of tongues and began prophesying in Hebrew; this was actually witnessed by his father Joseph Sr.
context: Smith's 'First Vision' (recounted in 1832, 1835, 1838, and 1842 with various details) became foundational for Mormonism. Three years later (September 21, 1823), Smith reported the angel Moroni appearing and directing him to golden plates containing the Book of Mormon, which he claimed to translate and publish in 1830. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) considers Smith its founding prophet.

question: After Joseph Smith Jr.'s 1844 lynching at Carthage, Illinois, the Latter-day Saints were left fractured and embattled. The largest faction followed Brigham Young (1801-1877), president of the Quorum of the Twelve, who led the Mormons west across the plains in one of the largest religious migrations in American history. On July 24, 1847, Young arrived in the Great Salt Lake Valley with the vanguard company. What did he reportedly say?
answer: 'This is the place' — directing the settlement of what became Salt Lake City in then-Mexican territory
choices: 'This is the place' — directing the settlement of what became Salt Lake City in then-Mexican territory
'The desert shall blossom as the rose' — quoting Isaiah 35:1 as commission for irrigation and cultivation
'Here we build the Temple' — pointing to the site of the future Salt Lake Temple (built 1853-1893)
'We are Israel come home' — declaring the Salt Lake basin a new promised land for the Saints
context: Young's 'This is the place' (later commemorated in This Is The Place Heritage Park in Salt Lake City) marked the founding of Mormon Utah. The territory was Mexican until the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) made it American. Young served as territorial governor 1850-1857; succeeded as church president by John Taylor in 1880. The polygamy controversy with the federal government dominated late 19th-century Utah politics.

question: On October 11, 1962, Pope John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council, having called it in January 1959 to widespread surprise (he had been elected as a transitional 'caretaker' pope at age 76). Four sessions ran from 1962 through December 1965 (Paul VI succeeded John XXIII in 1963). The council produced 16 documents reshaping Catholic life. What was John XXIII's word for the council's purpose?
answer: Aggiornamento — 'bringing up to date' — opening the church to dialogue with the modern world
choices: Aggiornamento — 'bringing up to date' — opening the church to dialogue with the modern world
Anathema — 'curse' — condemning modernist heresies that had infiltrated the church since Vatican I
Anamnesis — 'remembering' — restoring liturgical and patristic practices that had been forgotten
Acclamatio — 'acclamation' — emphasizing lay involvement in the assembly of the Eucharistic liturgy
context: Vatican II's major documents — Lumen Gentium (the church), Dei Verbum (revelation), Sacrosanctum Concilium (liturgy), Gaudium et Spes (the church in the modern world), Nostra Aetate (non-Christian religions), Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom) — reshaped Catholic life. The Mass moved to vernacular languages; relations with other Christians and non-Christians transformed.

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906-1945) was a German Lutheran pastor, theologian, and resistance figure. After 1933 he opposed the Nazi co-optation of the German church, helping found the Confessing Church (Barmen Declaration, 1934). He ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde. In 1939 he chose to return from safety in New York to Germany. He participated in the resistance and the July 20, 1944 assassination plot against Hitler. What was his fate?
answer: Arrested April 1943; hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp April 9, 1945 — two weeks before liberation
choices: Arrested April 1943; hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp April 9, 1945 — two weeks before liberation
Escaped to Switzerland in October 1944 after the failed plot; spent the post-war decade writing prison letters
Survived the war in hiding; emigrated to America in 1946 and taught at Union Theological Seminary until 1955
Captured at the Swiss border January 1945; held in Berlin until killed in the Soviet artillery shelling of April 1945
context: Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenbürg by special SS order on Hitler's direct command, April 9, 1945 — the camp was liberated by US forces April 23. His Letters and Papers from Prison (published 1951) and The Cost of Discipleship (1937) became Christian classics. His 'religionless Christianity' phrase from prison provoked decades of theological debate. The 1944 plot's failure cost him his life.

question: C. S. Lewis (1898-1963), Oxford literary scholar, described his 1929 acceptance of theism as 'the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.' Two years later (September 1931), on a long conversation in the Magdalen College grounds with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson, his final conversion to Christianity occurred. The next morning he experienced something distinctive. What was it?
answer: Riding on his brother Warnie's motorcycle sidecar to Whipsnade Zoo, he arrived believing what he had not believed when they set out
choices: Riding on his brother Warnie's motorcycle sidecar to Whipsnade Zoo, he arrived believing what he had not believed when they set out
Writing The Pilgrim's Regress in a single weekend in his Magdalen College rooms recounting his entire spiritual journey
Receiving Confirmation from the Anglican bishop of Oxford in a private ceremony arranged by his college chaplain
Preaching his first sermon at the Magdalen College chapel on the text 'Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief'
context: Lewis's motorcycle-to-the-zoo conversion (September 28, 1931) is recounted in Surprised by Joy. He went on to become the most influential lay Christian writer of the 20th century in English — Mere Christianity (1952), The Screwtape Letters (1942), the Chronicles of Narnia (1950-1956), The Problem of Pain (1940). His friend Tolkien remained Catholic; Lewis returned to the Anglican Church of his Belfast childhood.

question: J. R. R. Tolkien (1892-1973), Oxford philologist and friend of C. S. Lewis, was a devout Catholic whose religious faith infuses his fictional creation Middle-earth without ever appearing explicitly. The Lord of the Rings (published 1954-1955) was, he wrote in a letter, 'a fundamentally religious and Catholic work; unconsciously so at first, but consciously in the revision.' What specifically Catholic element did Tolkien attribute his deepest source to?
answer: The Eucharist — specifically the Blessed Sacrament as the inspiration for the lembas wayfaring bread of the Elves
choices: The Eucharist — specifically the Blessed Sacrament as the inspiration for the lembas wayfaring bread of the Elves
The Rosary — the prayer he said daily and which structures the chapter rhythms of the Lord of the Rings
The Mass — specifically the Latin Tridentine Mass which he attended and refused to abandon after Vatican II
The papacy — the papal infallibility of 1870 specifically inspired the resistance to Sauron's One Ring
context: Tolkien wrote in Letter 213 (1958): 'I am a Christian (which can be deduced from my stories), and in fact a Roman Catholic.' Letter 250 (1963) cited the Blessed Sacrament. The 'three things that Christianity has done for me' he listed elsewhere as the Blessed Sacrament, the Mass, the Holy Mother. He was instrumental in C. S. Lewis's 1931 conversion to Christianity; they remained close friends until Tolkien's distress at Lewis's marriage in 1956.

question: Reformed (Calvinist) theology was systematized in response to Arminian challenges at the Synod of Dort (1618-1619). The synod's findings were later organized in the English-speaking world by the acronym TULIP. The 'T' stands for Total Depravity. What does this doctrine actually teach?
answer: Every aspect of human nature is corrupted by sin; humans cannot will spiritual good without God's prior grace
choices: Every aspect of human nature is corrupted by sin; humans cannot will spiritual good without God's prior grace
Every human action is as wicked as it could possibly be; humans are unable to perform any genuine moral good
All humans are equally and absolutely depraved; no distinction in degrees of sin can be made among persons
The total depraved population of humanity outnumbers the elect by an unknown but very large fixed ratio
context: Total depravity does NOT teach humans are as bad as they could be — only that no part of fallen human nature is untouched by sin's corruption. The doctrine is sometimes called 'total inability' to clarify: humans cannot, on their own, turn to God. Critics charge it makes God responsible for choosing not to save those he could have. Defenders charge alternatives make salvation depend partly on human will, denying salvation by grace alone.

question: At the Althing in the year 1000 AD (June 23, by traditional dating), Iceland made a decision unique among European Christianizations. The country had been divided between pagans and Christians; civil war was threatened. The decision was put to one man — the Lawspeaker Thorgeir Ljósvetningagoði (who was himself a pagan). He went under a cloak for a day and a night without speaking. What did he announce?
answer: All Icelanders should be baptized Christian — but private pagan practice was allowed for the time being
choices: All Icelanders should be baptized Christian — but private pagan practice was allowed for the time being
All Icelanders should remain pagan — Christianity was rejected at the assembly by a single binding vote
All Icelanders should divide by district — northern districts pagan, southern districts Christian forever
All Icelanders should consult Norway — the king was to decide for them in a binding manner
context: Thorgeir's compromise — Christianity as official religion, with private pagan practice allowed — kept the peace. Within a generation, pagan practice faded. The conversion was relatively peaceful, in striking contrast to the Christianizations of Norway (forcible under Olaf Tryggvason and Olaf Haraldsson), Sweden (slow, resistant), and Saxony (Charlemagne's massacre at Verden). Thingvellir is where the conversion was decided.

question: Eirik the Red — banished from Iceland for manslaughter — sailed west and discovered a land he called 'Greenland' (a marketing name to attract settlers). He founded the Greenland colony around 985 AD. His son was even more famous as an explorer. Who, and what did he do?
answer: Leif Eriksson — sailed further west around 1000 AD and reached Vinland (most likely Newfoundland, Canada)
choices: Leif Eriksson — sailed further west around 1000 AD and reached Vinland (most likely Newfoundland, Canada)
Bjarni Herjólfsson — actually sighted the American coast in 986 AD but did not land; Leif made the first landing
Thorvald Eiriksson — actually Leif's brother; killed by Skraelings (native Americans) in a later Vinland voyage
Eirik himself — actually died in Greenland; his son Leif made the further voyages and discoveries
context: Leif Eriksson's voyage (c. 1000 AD) is recorded in the Vinland Sagas (Saga of the Greenlanders, Eirik's Saga). He landed at three places: Helluland ('Flat-stone Land,' probably Baffin Island), Markland ('Forest Land,' probably Labrador), and Vinland ('Wine Land,' probably Newfoundland). L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland (excavated 1960s) confirmed Norse presence in North America 500 years before Columbus. The Vinland colony was abandoned within a generation.

question: The Talmud — central text of rabbinic Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple (70 AD) — was compiled over centuries from oral discussions among rabbis. There are actually two Talmuds, both built around the Mishnah (redacted c. 200 AD by Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi). What are the two Talmuds?
answer: Babylonian Talmud (c. 500 AD) and Jerusalem Talmud (c. 400 AD) — the Babylonian is more authoritative for tradition
choices: Babylonian Talmud (c. 500 AD) and Jerusalem Talmud (c. 400 AD) — the Babylonian is more authoritative for tradition
Eastern Talmud and Western Talmud — geographic split but not the standard rabbinic categorization
Old Talmud and New Talmud — temporal split that scholars never use; this is not the rabbinic distinction
Greater Talmud and Lesser Talmud — refers to length but again not the standard rabbinic categorization
context: The Babylonian Talmud (Bavli) — compiled in Mesopotamian academies, especially at Sura and Pumbedita — and the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi) are the two major rabbinic compilations. The Bavli is longer, more authoritative for traditional practice, more frequently studied. Together they contain the Gemara (rabbinic commentary on the Mishnah). The Talmud became the central text of Jewish religious life from the 6th century onward.

question: Adolf Eichmann — Nazi bureaucrat in charge of the logistics of deportation to death camps — escaped to Argentina after the war. Mossad agents captured him in Buenos Aires in 1960 and brought him to Israel. He was tried in Jerusalem 1961, found guilty, hanged 1962. The trial was covered by the German-Jewish philosopher Hannah Arendt for the New Yorker. What phrase did she coin?
answer: 'The banality of evil' — describing Eichmann's ordinary careerist mediocrity as the human face of monstrous bureaucratic evil
choices: 'The banality of evil' — describing Eichmann's ordinary careerist mediocrity as the human face of monstrous bureaucratic evil
'The radical evil' — actually her earlier (post-war 1945) phrase, abandoned by 1961 as inadequate to the actual phenomenon
'The bureaucratic evil' — actually a coinage of later scholars; Arendt's phrase emphasized ordinariness more than bureaucracy
'The lying evil' — actually Eichmann's own self-description, not Arendt's analytic phrase about his banality
context: Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil (1963) provoked intense controversy among Jewish intellectuals. Her thesis: Eichmann was not a fanatic monster but a thoughtless careerist, 'incapable of thought' in any deep sense. Critics argued she underestimated his antisemitism and agency. The phrase 'banality of evil' has become foundational for modern reflection on totalitarian crime. Her work raised lasting questions about responsibility, conscience, and bureaucratic complicity.

question: Islam's basic religious practice is summarized in the Five Pillars (arkan al-Islam). These are the obligations every Muslim is expected to fulfill. What are they?
answer: Shahada (declaration), Salat (5 daily prayers), Zakat (alms), Sawm (Ramadan fasting), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca)
choices: Shahada (declaration), Salat (5 daily prayers), Zakat (alms), Sawm (Ramadan fasting), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca)
Quran, Hadith, Ijma, Qiyas, Jihad — these are sources of Islamic law, not the Five Pillars of practice
Tawhid, Risala, Akhira, Imama, Adala — actually basic Shia theological principles, not Sunni Five Pillars
Faith, Charity, Justice, Knowledge, Service — generic religious virtues, not the specific Five Pillars
context: The Five Pillars are practical religious duties. The Shahada (la ilaha illa Allah; Muhammad rasul Allah — 'there is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the messenger of Allah') is recited at conversion and daily. Salat — 5 daily prayers at dawn (fajr), midday (zuhr), afternoon (asr), sunset (maghrib), and night (isha). Zakat — 2.5% annual wealth tax. Sawm — dawn-to-sunset fast during Ramadan. Hajj — once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage to Mecca if physically and financially able.

question: On March 26-27, 1997, in Rancho Santa Fe, California, 39 members of a UFO-cult called Heaven's Gate committed mass suicide. They were led by Marshall Applewhite (and the late Bonnie Lu Nettles, who had died in 1985). What did they believe?
answer: That a UFO followed the Hale-Bopp comet; they would shed their bodies (containers) to be transported to the 'Next Level'
choices: That a UFO followed the Hale-Bopp comet; they would shed their bodies (containers) to be transported to the 'Next Level'
That Christ was returning to California by March 27, 1997; they would meet him in their resurrected bodies
That nuclear war was imminent; their suicide was a protest against the inevitable destruction of humanity
That the IRS was tracking them; their suicide ended a tax-protest movement that had run for thirty years
context: Heaven's Gate's belief system blended UFO conspiracy theory, science fiction, and gnostic Christianity. The 39 dead wore identical black sweat-suits and Nike sneakers, with $5 bills and quarters in their pockets. They drank phenobarbital with applesauce and vodka, then placed plastic bags over their heads. Eight male members had been castrated voluntarily in 1996. The Hale-Bopp comet was visible in late March 1997; the suicides were timed to its passage.

question: On April 19, 1993, a fire consumed the Branch Davidian compound at Mount Carmel near Waco, Texas. The site had been under FBI siege for 51 days after a botched ATF raid on February 28 (in which four ATF agents and six Davidians died). The fire on April 19 killed 76 Davidians including their leader David Koresh. What was the Branch Davidian movement?
answer: Apocalyptic offshoot of Seventh-day Adventism — Koresh claimed to be the Lamb of Revelation 5; tensions with federal authorities over weapons led to the raid
choices: Apocalyptic offshoot of Seventh-day Adventism — Koresh claimed to be the Lamb of Revelation 5; tensions with federal authorities over weapons led to the raid
Quaker pacifist commune — the raid was a federal mistake on a peaceful religious group with no weapons stockpile
Mormon splinter group — the Branch Davidians were polygamous and Koresh had multiple young wives at the compound
Satanist black mass movement — the FBI raided to free children allegedly being abused in occult ceremonies
context: The Branch Davidians traced their origin to a 1955 split from the Seventh-day Adventists (themselves a 19th-century millenarian offshoot). David Koresh (Vernon Howell) took control in the late 1980s. Allegations of child abuse and weapons stockpiling led to the ATF raid. The 51-day siege ended with the FBI's tear-gas assault and the catastrophic fire. The cause of the fire was disputed (Davidians blamed the FBI; the FBI investigation concluded Davidians set it). Waco became a touchstone for right-wing distrust of federal government.

question: In late summer 386 AD a 31-year-old North African rhetoric professor wept in a Milan garden, torn between his Manichaean past and the Christianity of his mother Monica. He heard a child chanting tolle, lege — take up and read. He opened Paul's Romans at random and was converted. He would become bishop of Hippo and write the Confessions. What is its civilizational significance?
answer: It founded Western autobiography — the first sustained narrative of a self examining its motives before God, the model every later confessional writer worked within
choices: It founded Western autobiography — the first sustained narrative of a self examining its motives before God, the model every later confessional writer worked within
It founded systematic Christian moral theology — the virtues-and-vices framework medieval scholastics later elaborated into the seven deadly sins and cardinal virtues
It founded Christian engagement with Greek philosophy — translating Plato's metaphysics into a Christian register that shaped later Western theological synthesis
It founded Christian historical apologetics — answering pagans who blamed the old gods' abandonment for the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 AD
context: Augustine wrote Confessions around 397-400 AD. Rousseau, Newman, Merton, and countless secular memoirists worked in its shadow. He went on to write City of God (begun 410) and died at Hippo in August 430 as Vandals besieged the city.

question: On April 17-18, 1521, in the imperial city of Worms, a 37-year-old Augustinian friar from Wittenberg stood before Emperor Charles V and the assembled princes. His books were piled on a table; the papal envoy demanded he recant. Returning April 18, he declared his conscience captive to the word of God. What words have traditionally been attached to his closing statement?
answer: Here I stand, I can do no other, God help me — though the precise 'Hier stehe ich' is not in the earliest transcripts, the substance was unmistakable
choices: Here I stand, I can do no other, God help me — though the precise 'Hier stehe ich' is not in the earliest transcripts, the substance was unmistakable
Sola scriptura, sola fide, sola gratia — Luther condensed his position into the three Latin phrases that became the Reformation's rallying cry
Pereat mundus, fiat justitia — let the world perish, let justice be done — the Roman maxim the Reformers applied to their cause against Rome
Ad fontes — back to the sources — the humanist slogan of Erasmus that had inspired his return to the Greek New Testament against the Vulgate
context: The Edict of Worms (May 1521) declared Luther an outlaw. Frederick the Wise staged a kidnapping; Luther spent ten months at the Wartburg disguised as Junker Jörg, translating the New Testament into a German that became foundational for the modern language.

question: On December 6, 1273 a 48-year-old Dominican friar — already the most influential theologian in Europe, midway through Part III of his Summa Theologiae — celebrated mass at Naples. He emerged changed. He stopped writing. His secretary Reginald pleaded with him to finish. Thomas replied that compared with what he had seen, all he had written seemed to him as straw. What is the mainstream Catholic interpretation?
answer: A mystical experience of God so direct that theology's language, however precise, became inadequate to him — all theology approaches a reality it cannot fully capture
choices: A mystical experience of God so direct that theology's language, however precise, became inadequate to him — all theology approaches a reality it cannot fully capture
A breakdown from exhaustion caused by the Summa's scale, the modern biographer's diagnosis that rejects the mystical interpretation as legend
A loss of faith from his exposure to Averroes, whose secular rationalism the elderly Thomas could no longer answer within his theological system
A repudiation of scholastic method for the apophatic mysticism of Pseudo-Dionysius, anticipating the via negativa that would flower in Meister Eckhart
context: The Summa Theologiae (begun 1265) is the most influential work of Christian theology after Augustine. Its Five Ways, its synthesis of Aristotle with Christian doctrine, and its account of natural law remain central. Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris (1879) made Thomism quasi-official.

question: Around 1098 the Benedictine monk Anselm of Canterbury — by then archbishop, in exile after quarreling with William II Rufus — completed a dialogue with a fictional questioner named Boso. Its title asked: cur deus homo, why did God become man? Anselm rejected the older 'ransom' theory in which Christ's death paid a debt to the devil. He proposed sin offended God's infinite honor. What is this theory called?
answer: The satisfaction theory of atonement — refined by the Reformers into penal substitution (Christ bears the punishment owed to sinners) and dominant in Western theology
choices: The satisfaction theory of atonement — refined by the Reformers into penal substitution (Christ bears the punishment owed to sinners) and dominant in Western theology
The moral influence theory — Christ's death moves human hearts to repentance rather than paying any debt, the position later linked to Peter Abelard and liberal Protestants
The Christus Victor theory — Christ's death and resurrection defeated sin, death, and the devil in cosmic combat, revived by Gustaf Aulén in 1931
The governmental theory — Christ's death upheld the moral order of the universe as public demonstration rather than satisfying a private debt
context: Anselm also gave us the ontological argument — the being than which nothing greater can be conceived must exist. He died at Canterbury in 1109. The satisfaction theory maps medieval feudal categories (honor, debt, vassalage) onto God, and dominates evangelical Protestant atonement theology.

question: On October 27, 1553, at Champel near Geneva, a Spanish physician and theologian named Michael Servetus was burned at the stake on a pyre of green wood with one of his own books chained to his leg. He had denied the Trinity and infant baptism. The man who had pressed prosecution most vigorously was John Calvin. What does this event reveal that honest history must name?
answer: Religious liberty was not a Reformation principle in 1553 — both Catholic and Protestant authorities held civil power should enforce orthodoxy, far from later liberty
choices: Religious liberty was not a Reformation principle in 1553 — both Catholic and Protestant authorities held civil power should enforce orthodoxy, far from later liberty
Calvin's distance from the execution — he had requested beheading as more humane, the burning being ordered against his preference, the Reformed defenders' detail
The unique blame of the Catholic Inquisition — Servetus had been condemned at Vienne in April 1553 and escaped, the Geneva execution being a Catholic continuation
The establishment of religious pluralism in Geneva under Calvin — the case being an aberration, with Geneva famous for tolerating refugees within a decade
context: Sebastian Castellio's De Haereticis (1554) responded: 'To kill a man is not to defend a doctrine, it is to kill a man.' Castellio is now seen as a founder of religious toleration. The Reformation's eventual contribution to liberty came through the breakup of Christendom.

question: From 1618 to 1648 central Europe was consumed by the bloodiest conflict in early modern European history. It began with the Defenestration of Prague (May 23, 1618). It drew in Sweden, France (Catholic, fighting Habsburgs), Spain, Denmark. Modern estimates: 4.5-8 million dead, perhaps 20-30 percent of Germany. What treaty ended it?
answer: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) — treaties at Münster and Osnabrück that established state sovereignty, recognized Calvinism, and ended European religious wars
choices: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) — treaties at Münster and Osnabrück that established state sovereignty, recognized Calvinism, and ended European religious wars

The Treaty of the Pyrenees (1648) — ending the Franco-Spanish portion and setting the French-Spanish border, leaving Empire's religious settlement to later congresses
The Convention of Frankfurt (1648) — a meeting of Imperial Estates producing the German constitutional structure of religious toleration
context: Westphalia's significance is hard to overstate. State sovereignty and non-interference in domestic religious affairs is the foundation of modern international law. Honest history records both that the Reformation generated religious freedom AND that the road cost central Europe a third of its population.

question: From 1309 to 1377 the popes ruled from Avignon rather than Rome — Clement V and six French successors. Petrarch called it the Babylonian Captivity. A 30-year-old illiterate Dominican tertiary from Siena, dictating to secretaries, traveled to Avignon in 1376 and confronted Pope Gregory XI face to face. He returned to Rome. Who was she?
answer: Catherine of Siena — Doctor of the Church (Paul VI, 1970), co-patron of Europe (John Paul II, 1999), whose Dialogue and 380 letters made her one of the most influential late medieval voices
choices: Catherine of Siena — Doctor of the Church (Paul VI, 1970), co-patron of Europe (John Paul II, 1999), whose Dialogue and 380 letters made her one of the most influential late medieval voices
Bridget of Sweden — Doctor of the Church (John Paul II, 1991), founder of the Bridgettine order, whose Revelations recorded visions and prophecies that shaped Scandinavian devotion
Joan of Arc — the French peasant visionary who played a parallel role in the Hundred Years War a generation later, ending the English siege of Orleans before being burned in 1431
Margery Kempe — the English mystic whose Book (c. 1430s) is the first autobiography in English and records travels to Jerusalem, Rome, and Compostela without political influence
context: Catherine died at 33 in 1380, exhausted from austerities and the Western Schism struggles that broke out immediately after Gregory's return. She is buried at Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome; her severed head is preserved in Siena.

question: On July 15, 1099, after a five-week siege, the army of the First Crusade broke into Jerusalem. Eyewitness Raymond of Aguilers wrote of riding through blood up to his horse's knees. The Jewish community took refuge in their synagogue, which the crusaders burned with them inside. Muslim inhabitants were slaughtered for two days. What does honest Catholic history say?
answer: Genuine response to four centuries of Islamic conquest AND execution including atrocities — the Jewish massacres of 1096, the Jerusalem massacre — that cannot be defended
choices: Genuine response to four centuries of Islamic conquest AND execution including atrocities — the Jewish massacres of 1096, the Jerusalem massacre — that cannot be defended

The crusades began as response to specific threats (Manzikert 1071, Seljuk advances) but the violence that followed — including the 1204 sack of Constantinople by fellow Christians — must be named.

question: On Holy Thursday, April 21, 1519, Hernán Cortés landed at Veracruz. By November 8 he stood in Tenochtitlán face to face with Moctezuma II. Within three years the largest city in the Americas had been razed. Cortés found temples where, by some estimates, 20,000 prisoners had been sacrificed in a single 1487 dedication. What does honest Catholic history say?
answer: Both halves — the genuine Aztec horror the Spanish witnessed (Templo Mayor mass sacrifice) AND the conquest's atrocities and ~90% demographic catastrophe within a century
choices: Both halves — the genuine Aztec horror the Spanish witnessed (Templo Mayor mass sacrifice) AND the conquest's atrocities and ~90% demographic catastrophe within a century

context: Bartolomé de Las Casas (Dominican, 1484-1566) was the great Spanish voice condemning conquest violence; his Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542) prompted the New Laws abolishing the encomienda. Templo Mayor archaeology (1978 onward) has confirmed extensive sacrifice.

question: In 1206 in the cathedral square of Assisi, a 24-year-old merchant's son stripped naked before his father, the bishop, and the town. He had been giving away his father's goods to repair the chapel of San Damiano, where a painted crucifix had spoken: 'Francis, repair my house.' He would die October 3, 1226 bearing the wounds of Christ — the stigmata. What pattern did Francis's life establish?
answer: Voluntary radical poverty as Christian witness against the wealthy medieval Church — embodied by the Franciscan order through spiritual-conventual struggle for centuries
choices: Voluntary radical poverty as Christian witness against the wealthy medieval Church — embodied by the Franciscan order through spiritual-conventual struggle for centuries
The contemplative monastic ideal in opposition to scholastic university theology — setting Franciscans against Dominicans across the medieval universities for centuries
The veneration of saints as miracle-workers — the stigmata being the first of a sequence of physical phenomena defining late medieval popular Catholicism against Protestantism
Lay apostolate independent of clerical hierarchy — Francis's refusal of ordination setting precedent for lay movements leading through the Beguines toward the Reformation
context: Francis received papal approval from Innocent III in 1210. He composed the Canticle of the Sun (1224) and the Rule of 1223. His feast day is October 4. Chesterton's biography (1923) rehabilitated him for modern Protestants; John Paul II made him patron of ecology (1979); Pope Francis (2013) took his name.

question: In October 451 AD over 500 bishops met across the Bosphorus from Constantinople at Marcian's request. The issue: Eutyches held Christ had only one nature after the incarnation, the divine having absorbed the human. The council produced a definition built on Pope Leo I's Tome, which Eastern bishops cried 'Peter has spoken through Leo!' upon hearing read. What did the Chalcedonian Definition state?
answer: Christ is one person in two natures — fully divine and fully human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation, orthodox for Rome and the Reformation
choices: Christ is one person in two natures — fully divine and fully human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation, orthodox for Rome and the Reformation
Christ is one person of one nature after the incarnation — divine and human united into a single theandric nature, later defended by the Oriental Orthodox churches
Christ is two persons indwelling one human body — the divine Son in the human Jesus as in a temple, the position taught by Nestorius and condemned at Ephesus in 431

context: Chalcedon's formula remains standard Christology for Catholics, Eastern Orthodox, and most Protestants. The Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac Orthodox, and Indian Malankara churches rejected it (Oriental Orthodoxy). Modern dialogue has shown the historical separation was as much linguistic as substantive.

question: In Trinity term 1929 a 31-year-old Oxford English tutor — a former WWI officer wounded at Arras, an atheist — admitted in his Magdalen rooms that God was God. He knelt and prayed, 'perhaps the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.' Two years later, September 19, 1931, a long walk with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson finished his journey to Christianity. What was Tolkien's argument?
answer: The dying-rising god pattern Lewis loved in Norse and Greek was, in Christ, 'myth become fact' — the archetype embodied in history rather than only in story
choices: The dying-rising god pattern Lewis loved in Norse and Greek was, in Christ, 'myth become fact' — the archetype embodied in history rather than only in story
From 'sub-creation' — human myth-making participates in God's primary creative act — Christianity is the true myth all others imperfectly reflect
The 'trilemma' from Lewis's later Mere Christianity — Christ must be liar, lunatic, or Lord, the historical record making the first two implausible
That Lewis's Belfast rationalism was incoherent on its own terms, requiring an Augustinian-Thomist natural theology Lewis had dismissed as Catholic pleading
context: Lewis later wrote the conversation up in 'Mythopoeia' (Tolkien's poem in response to Lewis's view that myths were 'lies breathed through silver'). Lewis became the central twentieth-century English Christian apologist: Mere Christianity, Screwtape Letters, Narnia. He died November 22, 1963 — the same day as Kennedy.

question: On May 20, 1521, during the French siege of Pamplona, a 30-year-old Basque hidalgo and military officer named Íñigo López de Loyola was struck by a cannonball that shattered his right leg. During the long convalescence he asked for novels of chivalry but the household had only a Life of Christ and a collection of saints' lives. Reading them, he was converted. He would spend the next twenty years preparing — Manresa cave, Jerusalem pilgrimage, Paris masters degree. What did he found?
answer: The Society of Jesus (Jesuits) — approved by Paul III in 1540 with Ignatius as first Superior General, organized as a quasi-military religious order
choices: The Society of Jesus (Jesuits) — approved by Paul III in 1540 with Ignatius as first Superior General, organized as a quasi-military religious order

The Capuchins — a reformed Franciscan order that returned to the strictest interpretation of Francis's original rule of poverty and that became
The Theatines — the original Counter-Reformation reformed clerical order founded by Gaetano da Thiene and Gian Pietro Carafa (the future Paul IV)
context: Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises (1548) is among the most influential works of Western spirituality — a four-week retreat structure that has shaped Catholic interior life for five hundred years. The Jesuits reached Japan (Xavier 1549), Brazil, China (Ricci 1583), and the Iroquois (Jogues 1640s). Pope Francis (2013) is the first Jesuit pope.

question: In 999/1000 AD, the Icelandic Althing was bitterly divided. Norway's King Olaf Tryggvason was pressing Iceland to accept Christianity, sending missionaries and threatening trade sanctions and the relatives of pagan Icelanders held in Norway. Pagan and Christian factions were on the edge of civil war. The lawspeaker was Thorgeir Thorkelsson, a respected pagan priest from Ljósavatn. He withdrew under a cloak for a full day to think. He emerged with a binding judgment. What did he rule?
answer: All Icelanders would formally accept Christian baptism and Iceland would have Christian law — but private pagan practice would be permitted to continue at home, along

Adam of Bremen reports that he threw his pagan god images into a waterfall (still called Goðafoss, 'Waterfall of the Gods') in northern Iceland after his judgment. Iceland's Christianization was substantially peaceful by European standards.

question: Around 28-29 AD a wild prophetic figure appeared in the Judean wilderness near the Jordan River. He wore a camel-hair garment with a leather belt; he ate locusts and wild honey; he baptized those who came confessing sin. He told the religious leadership: brood of vipers, the axe is at the root. When his disciples asked who he was, what was his self-identification?
answer: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord — quoting Isaiah 40 and declaring himself not the Messiah but the forerunner of one greater coming after him
choices: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord — quoting Isaiah 40 and declaring himself not the Messiah but the forerunner of one greater coming after him

The reincarnated prophet Jeremiah weeping for Jerusalem — the identification matching the eccentric appearance and prophecies of doom on the temple complex he denounced

context: Matthew 3, Mark 1, Luke 3, John 1. John baptized Jesus around 29 AD. Herod Antipas imprisoned John at Machaerus for denouncing his marriage to Herodias (his half-brother Philip's wife); Salome's dance led to John's beheading. Jesus called him the greatest born of women.

question: Fifty days after Passover (Jewish Shavuot) in roughly 30 AD, about 120 disciples were gathered in Jerusalem. There came a sound like a rushing wind; tongues as of fire rested on each; they began to speak in other languages. Devout Jews from across the diaspora — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Cretans, Arabs — each heard them in their own native language. Peter then preached. What was the result?
answer: About 3000 were baptized that day, marking the traditional birth of the church and the reversal of Babel — divided languages now united in the proclamation of the gospel
choices: About 3000 were baptized that day, marking the traditional birth of the church and the reversal of Babel — divided languages now united in the proclamation of the gospel

The 120 number connects to the minimum for a synagogue council (a minyan-multiple) and to Israelite-tribal symbolism.

question: Around 34 AD a deacon serving widows in the Jerusalem church was hauled before the Sanhedrin on charges of speaking against Moses and the temple. Filled with the Spirit, he delivered a long survey of Israelite history climaxing in accusing his hearers of betraying the Righteous One. Looking up he saw heaven opened. They covered their ears. What was his death cry?
answer: Lord, do not hold this sin against them — paralleling Jesus's prayer from the cross, and a young Pharisee named Saul stood by approving the stoning, holding the witnesses' coats
choices: Lord, do not hold this sin against them — paralleling Jesus's prayer from the cross, and a young Pharisee named Saul stood by approving the stoning, holding the witnesses' coats
Lord, into your hands I commit my spirit — repeating Jesus's final cry, the deliberate doubling becoming the early template for martyr accounts in the Acts of the Martyrs
Behold, I see the Son of Man on the right hand of God — which the Sanhedrin treated as the same blasphemy charge that had condemned Jesus, immediately ordering execution
May Israel never forget the prophets it has killed — the curse-formula echoing Jesus's lament over Jerusalem in Matthew 23 and prophesying the temple's destruction in 70 AD
context: Acts 6-7. Stephen's speech (the longest in Acts) recasts Israel's history as a pattern of resisting God. The post-stoning persecution scattered Hellenist Christians who founded the church in Antioch — the launching pad of Paul's missions. The 'protomartyr' Greek title made Stephen the model of every later martyrology.

question: Between 328 and 373 AD a deacon (later bishop) of Alexandria fought a 45-year battle for the Nicene faith. Constantine, Constantius II, Julian, and Valens each drove him into exile — five times in total, totaling 17 years away from his see. He hid with the desert monks; he wrote the Life of Antony that launched Western monasticism. What Latin phrase summarizes his stance?
answer: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world; even as emperors and most bishops embraced Arianism or its compromises, he refused homoiousios and held to homoousios at any cost
choices: Athanasius contra mundum — Athanasius against the world; even as emperors and most bishops embraced Arianism or its compromises, he refused homoiousios and held to homoousios at any cost
Roma locuta, causa finita — Rome has spoken, the case is closed; the formula the later papal tradition applied to Athanasius's appeals to successive bishops of Rome for support
Extra ecclesiam nulla salus — outside the church there is no salvation; the formula Cyprian had coined and Athanasius extended into a defense of the visible Catholic Church
Credo quia absurdum — I believe because it is absurd; the formula Tertullian had used and that Athanasius applied to the philosophical impossibility of orthodox Christology
context: Athanasius died in his see at Alexandria in 373 AD, his Nicene party finally vindicated. The Council of Constantinople in 381 ratified the homoousios formula and added the third article on the Spirit, producing the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed recited at Sunday liturgies to this day.

question: Around 529 AD an Italian abbot in his late 40s founded a monastery on a hill in central Italy between Rome and Naples. Born around 480 at Nursia in Umbria, he had fled Roman education for the cave at Subiaco, gathered disciples, and now established his definitive house. He wrote a short Rule of 73 chapters. What is the famous Benedictine motto?
answer: Ora et labora — pray and work; the balance of liturgical prayer (the Divine Office, eight times daily), sacred reading, and manual labor that organized Western monasticism for 1500 years
choices: Ora et labora — pray and work; the balance of liturgical prayer (the Divine Office, eight times daily), sacred reading, and manual labor that organized Western monasticism for 1500 years
Solus Christus — Christ alone; the formula that would later become a Reformation sola but that Benedictine spirituality applied to the monk's renunciation of secondary attachments
Lex orandi, lex credendi — the law of prayer is the law of belief; the patristic formula Prosper of Aquitaine had articulated in the prior century, central to liturgical theology
Pax et bonum — peace and good; the formula Francis of Assisi would adopt seven centuries later as the Franciscan greeting, mistakenly retrojected onto Benedictine tradition
context: Montecassino was destroyed by Lombards (c. 580), Saracens (883), an earthquake (1349), and Allied bombing in February 1944 — each time rebuilt. The Rule's moderation made it dominant: the older, harsher Rules of Pachomius and Basil could not sustain Western monastic life as Benedict's did.

question: In 726 AD the Byzantine emperor Leo III ordered the great Christ icon over Constantinople's Chalke Gate destroyed. For the next 60 years the Eastern empire smashed icons, persecuted monks, and split itself from Rome. In 787 AD the Empress Irene convened a council to settle the question. What did the Seventh Ecumenical Council establish?
answer: Veneration (proskynesis) of icons is licit — distinguishing it from worship (latreia) due to God alone; the honor passing to the prototype, the Word's incarnation justifying material images
choices: Veneration (proskynesis) of icons is licit — distinguishing it from worship (latreia) due to God alone; the honor passing to the prototype, the Word's incarnation justifying material images
Veneration of icons is permitted in private homes but forbidden in public churches — the compromise Charlemagne's Frankish theologians had pushed in the Caroline Books of 794
Icons may be displayed for instruction but must not be kissed, censed, or carried in procession — the Reformed Protestant position read backward into the seventh ecumenical council
Only icons of Christ and the Virgin are permitted — those of saints being abolished as concessions to popular piety, the iconophile compromise iconoclasts had offered after 754
context: The defenders of icons — John of Damascus (writing from Muslim-ruled Palestine, beyond Byzantine reach) and Theodore the Studite — argued that the Incarnation justified material images; otherwise God could not be depicted. The Triumph of Orthodoxy (first Sunday of Lent, 843) commemorates the final restoration of icons.

question: Around 1205 a 35-year-old Castilian canon traveling through Languedoc saw the Cathar heresy and was scandalized. Papal legates rode with retinues; the Perfecti walked barefoot. Dominic chose poverty. By 1215 he had a small group at Toulouse preaching among the Cathars. On December 22, 1216 Honorius III confirmed the Order of Preachers. What was its mission?
answer: Combat heresy by study and preaching — the friars trained in theology, owned nothing, walked town to town, occupied chairs at the new universities, and produced Aquinas in the next generation
choices: Combat heresy by study and preaching — the friars trained in theology, owned nothing, walked town to town, occupied chairs at the new universities, and produced Aquinas in the next generation
Combat heresy by inquisitorial process and judicial sentence — the function the order would later acquire under Gregory IX (1233) but was not the original founding purpose
Maintain the daily liturgy in cathedral churches at the highest standard — the Cistercian competence repositioned to urban contexts where Benedictine cloisters had limited reach
Care for the sick and bury the dead in plague-stricken cities — the diakonia originally entrusted to the Antonines and Trinitarians but absorbed by the Dominicans after 1250
context: Dominic died 1221 in Bologna, canonized 1234. By 1300 the Order had 600 houses, produced Aquinas, Albert the Great, Eckhart, Catherine of Siena (Third Order). The black-and-white habit and the rosary devotion (traditionally attributed to him) became Dominican hallmarks across Catholic Europe.

question: From 1519 onward, the people's priest at the Grossmunster in Zurich led the Swiss Reformation through expository sermons. He removed organs from churches, abolished the Mass in 1525, and instituted a simple Lord's Supper. In October 1529 he met Luther at Marburg. They agreed on 14 of 15 articles. What did they disagree on?
answer: The Eucharist — Luther held the real bodily presence ('this is my body' literally), Zwingli held a memorial view ('is' meaning 'signifies'); the breach split the Protestant Reformation permanently
choices: The Eucharist — Luther held the real bodily presence ('this is my body' literally), Zwingli held a memorial view ('is' meaning 'signifies'); the breach split the Protestant Reformation permanently
Predestination — Luther held the bondage of the will against Erasmus, Zwingli a softer line; the disagreement was real but came later and was not the Marburg topic
Infant baptism — both held it but for different reasons; the Anabaptist movement that rejected it split off in 1525 in Zurich, distinct from the Luther-Zwingli dispute
Church-state relations — Luther held the doctrine of two kingdoms, Zwingli sacralized the city-republic; the disagreement was real but secondary to Marburg's main subject
context: Zwingli died at the Battle of Kappel (October 11, 1531) fighting against Catholic Swiss cantons — a Protestant clergyman killed in a religious war. His writings include the 1525 Of True and False Religion. His Eucharistic position dominates much later Reformed Protestantism through Calvin's modification of it.

question: On the evening of May 24, 1738, a 34-year-old Oxford-educated Anglican priest, who had returned from a failed Georgia mission disillusioned, attended a Moravian meeting at Aldersgate Street in London. Someone read from Luther's preface to Romans. At about a quarter before nine, his heart was 'strangely warmed.' What movement did he found?
answer: Methodism — through field-preaching to colliers and tinners; rejected by Anglican pulpits, he and George Whitefield preached outdoors; by his death (1791) about 80,000 Methodists with itinerant lay preachers covered Britain
choices: Methodism — through field-preaching to colliers and tinners; rejected by Anglican pulpits, he and George Whitefield preached outdoors; by his death (1791) about 80,000 Methodists with itinerant lay preachers covered Britain
The Quaker movement — founded by George Fox a century earlier (1647); Wesley admired but did not join Quakers, and Methodism became a separate evangelical movement
The Plymouth Brethren — founded by John Nelson Darby in the 1820s; Wesley predated this movement and its premillennial dispensationalism conflicted with his theology
The Salvation Army — founded by William and Catherine Booth in 1865; Wesleyan in inspiration but a century later than Wesley's own ministry and organizationally distinct
context: Wesley rode an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback and preached 40,000 sermons. His brother Charles wrote about 6500 hymns. Methodism formally separated from the Church of England after his death. The Methodist Episcopal Church in America (1784, ordained by Wesley's lay-ordination of Asbury and Coke) preceded the British separation.

question: From 1854 to 1892 a Calvinist Baptist preacher in London drew the largest regular Christian audiences of the 19th century. He began at 19 at New Park Street Chapel; by 1861 the Metropolitan Tabernacle seating 5000 was built for him. His 3500+ sermons outsold any other Victorian Christian author. He battled the 'Down-grade Controversy' against liberal theology. Who?
answer: Charles Haddon Spurgeon — 'Prince of Preachers', whose sermons remain the longest single-author homiletic series in Christian publishing history; left the Baptist Union 1887 over modernism

He founded the Stockwell Orphanage, the Pastors' College, and the Colportage Association. His Treasury of David (7 volumes on the Psalms) remains a standard devotional commentary.

question: Jesus taught a long sermon on a hill. What is this famous teaching called?
context: Matthew 5-7 contains Jesus' longest sermon, given on a hillside in Galilee. It includes the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and the Golden Rule.

question: Jesus began his big sermon with eight blessings. Each one starts with what word?
context: The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12) each begin 'Blessed are...' — the meek, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, those who mourn, and others.

question: Jesus said, 'Blessed are the peacemakers.' What will they be called?
context: Matthew 5:9: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.' One of the eight Beatitudes.

question: In the Lord's Prayer, Jesus taught us to call God by what name?
context: 'Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.' The Lord's Prayer is part of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13).

question: Jesus said, 'Do to others as you would have them do to you.' What is this called?
context: Matthew 7:12. The Golden Rule sums up the Law and the Prophets in one sentence.

question: Jesus taught his friends to pray. What is this short prayer called?
context: Matthew 6:9-13. Also called the 'Our Father' from its opening words.

question: Jesus said his followers are the salt of the earth and the what of the world?
context: Matthew 5:13-14. Salt flavors and preserves; light shines. Jesus said his people should do the same in the world.

question: How many blessings begin the Beatitudes in Matthew 5?
context: Matthew 5:3-12 lists eight 'Blessed are...' statements. Luke 6 gives a parallel set with four blessings and four woes.

question: Jesus said, 'Blessed are the meek.' What will they inherit?
context: Matthew 5:5: 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.' Meekness here means humble strength, not weakness.

question: Jesus told his hearers to love whom besides their friends?
context: Matthew 5:44: 'Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.' One of the hardest commands in the Sermon.

question: In the Sermon on the Mount, where did Jesus tell his hearers to store up treasure?
context: Matthew 6:19-20: 'Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.'

question: Jesus taught against worry. What flowers did he say grew without working or spinning?
context: Matthew 6:28-30. The lilies neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of them.

question: Jesus told a story about a man beaten by robbers on the road. Who helped him?
context: The Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37). A priest and a Levite walked past, but a despised Samaritan stopped to help.

question: In one parable, a son ran away and spent all his money. His father did what when he came home?
context: The Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32). The father saw him from far off, ran to meet him, and threw a feast.

question: Jesus told a story of a farmer planting seeds. Some fell on the path, on rocks, among thorns, and on good ground. What is this called?
context: Mark 4:1-20. The seed is the word of God; the soils are different kinds of hearers.

question: Jesus told a story of a shepherd who left 99 sheep to find one. What was lost?
context: The Parable of the Lost Sheep (Luke 15:3-7, Matthew 18:12-14). God seeks the one who is lost.

question: In one parable, a woman lost a coin and swept her whole house. How many coins did she have at the start?
context: The Parable of the Lost Coin (Luke 15:8-10). She had ten silver coins, lost one, and rejoiced when she found it.

question: In Jesus' story, a wise builder built his house on what?
context: Matthew 7:24-27. The wise man's house on the rock stood; the foolish man's house on the sand fell. Jesus closed the Sermon on the Mount with this.

question: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, two religious men passed by the wounded man before the Samaritan stopped. Who were they?
choices: a tax collector and a scribe
context: Luke 10:31-32. Jesus chose the two religious leaders most expected to help, then made the despised Samaritan the hero.

question: When the prodigal son came home, what did the father put on his hand?
context: Luke 15:22: 'Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.' The ring restored his status as son.

question: In the Parable of the Sower, what does the seed stand for?
context: Mark 4:14. The seed is the word; the soils are the kinds of hearts that receive it.

question: Christians believe Jesus died on the cross to save people from what?
context: The heart of Christian belief: Christ died for sinners (Romans 5:8). His death pays the cost of sin.

question: Christians teach that we are saved by grace through what?
context: Ephesians 2:8-9: 'By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God.'

question: John 3:16 begins 'For God so loved the world.' What did he give?
context: John 3:16 is the most-quoted verse in Christian faith: 'For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.'

question: Christians say God is one in being but three in what?
context: The doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Each is fully God, yet there is one God.

question: The doctrine of the Trinity names three Persons: Father, Son, and what third?
context: The third Person of the Trinity is the Holy Spirit (also called the Paraclete or Helper). Jesus promised to send the Spirit to the disciples.

question: Which Christian creed begins 'I believe in one God, the Father Almighty'?
context: The Nicene Creed was written in 325 AD at the Council of Nicaea to defend the Trinity against Arianism.

question: Jesus said to love your neighbor as you do what?
context: Mark 12:31: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' Jesus called this the second greatest command, after loving God.

question: Peter asked Jesus how many times to forgive a brother. Jesus said not seven, but how many?
context: Matthew 18:21-22. Forgiveness is not a small thing; it has no limit Jesus told his friends.

question: Jesus said, 'Let the little children come to me' and not to do what?
context: Matthew 19:14. The disciples tried to turn the children away. Jesus rebuked them and blessed each child.

question: In Jesus' teaching, who should we love besides our friends?
context: Matthew 5:44. Jesus taught radical love: even those who hurt you should be loved and prayed for.

question: Jesus said, 'Blessed are the merciful.' What will they receive?
context: Matthew 5:7: 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.' One of the Beatitudes.

question: Jesus said when you give to the poor, your left hand should not know what?
