context: Matthew 6:3-4. Give in secret. Don't make a show of being good.

question: Jesus said the greatest in his kingdom must be the what of all?
context: Mark 10:43-44. Jesus turned the world upside down: the greatest are those who serve, not those who rule.

question: Jesus said you should not judge others. What will be done to you with the measure you use?
answer: the same will be measured to you
choices: the same will be measured to you
context: Matthew 7:1-2: 'Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged.'

question: Jesus quoted two great commands: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself. From which book of the Old Testament does the first come?
context: Deuteronomy 6:5 is the Shema, the great Jewish prayer. Jesus paired it with Leviticus 19:18 to sum up the law.

question: Jesus told his followers to turn the other cheek when struck. What chapter of Matthew contains this?
context: Matthew 5:39 is part of the Sermon on the Mount. 'Resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.'

question: What does the apostle Paul say is the greatest of faith, hope, and love?
context: 1 Corinthians 13:13: 'And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.'

question: Jesus said that whoever wants to save their life will lose it. What must one do instead?
answer: lose their life for his sake
choices: lose their life for his sake
keep it safe at all costs
context: Mark 8:35: 'For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it.'

question: The Bible says God loves a cheerful what?
context: 2 Corinthians 9:7: 'Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.'

question: Micah 6:8 sums up what God requires: do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with whom?
context: Micah 6:8: 'He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?'

question: Jesus told the rich young ruler to sell what he had and give to whom?
context: Mark 10:21. The young man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God.

question: James 1:27 says true religion is to visit orphans and widows, and to keep oneself how?
context: James 1:27 defines pure religion as care for the helpless plus personal holiness — not mere ritual.

question: Jesus' Golden Rule says, 'Do to others what you would have them do to you.' Which two parts of the Old Testament did he say this sums up?
context: Matthew 7:12: 'Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.'

question: God promised Abraham a son even in his old age. What did Abraham's wife do when she heard?
context: Genesis 18:12. Sarah laughed behind the tent flap. God named the son 'Isaac' — Hebrew for 'he laughs'.

question: What was the name of the place where Abraham was told to offer Isaac?
context: Genesis 22:2. Moriah is later identified with the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Tradition links it to where Solomon built the Temple.

question: What did God provide at the last moment instead of Isaac, caught in a thicket by its horns?
context: Genesis 22:13. Abraham named the place 'The LORD will provide' (Jehovah-Jireh). The ram became the substitute offering.

question: God told Moses to take off his shoes because he stood on what kind of ground?
context: Exodus 3:5, at the burning bush on Mount Horeb. God's presence makes a place holy.

question: What was the name of Moses's brother, who spoke for him to Pharaoh?
context: Exodus 4:14-16. Moses was slow of speech, so God appointed Aaron as his mouthpiece. Aaron became Israel's first high priest.

question: Joshua's army marched around Jericho. How many times on the seventh day?
context: Joshua 6. They marched once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day. Then the trumpets blew and the walls fell down.

question: Who was the woman judge of Israel who led an army with Barak?
context: Judges 4. Deborah was a prophet and judge. She told Barak to attack Sisera; Sisera was killed by Jael.

question: On the first day of creation God said 'let there be...' what?
context: Genesis 1:3. God spoke light into being before the sun or stars. Christians read this as a sign that all creation begins from God's word.

question: God created the world and rested on the seventh day. The work took how many days?
context: Genesis 1. The seventh day God rested � establishing the Sabbath. Christians keep Sunday as the Lord's Day in memory of the resurrection.

question: In the garden of Eden, what fruit-tree did God forbid Adam and Eve to eat from?
context: Genesis 2:17. The tree of knowledge of good and evil stood at the centre of the garden alongside the tree of life. The serpent tempted Eve to eat its fruit.

question: Who tempted Eve in the garden to eat the forbidden fruit?
context: Genesis 3. Christian tradition reads the serpent as Satan in disguise. Revelation 12 calls him 'that ancient serpent who deceives the whole world'.

question: Where did God place a flaming sword after sending Adam and Eve away?
context: Genesis 3:24. Cherubim guarded the way back to the tree of life. Adam and Eve and all their children were now east of Eden.

question: Who built a great wooden ship to save his family from a worldwide flood?
context: Genesis 6-8. The ark held two of every kind of animal. After the flood Noah offered a sacrifice and God set the rainbow as a covenant sign.

question: How many of each animal did Noah take into the ark of clean kinds?
context: Genesis 7:2. Seven pairs of clean animals (and one pair of unclean). The numbers allowed for sacrifices after the flood ended.

question: How many days and nights did the rain fall on Noah's ark?
context: Genesis 7:12. Forty becomes a recurring biblical number for testing � Moses on Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Jesus in the desert.

question: After the flood, what sign did God set in the clouds as his covenant promise?
context: Genesis 9:13. Christians and Jews read the rainbow as a sign God will never again destroy the earth with water.

question: In Genesis, a tower was built to reach heaven. What was it called?
context: Genesis 11. God scattered the builders by confusing their speech. The story explains the origin of different languages and human pride's limits.

question: God called a man from Ur to leave his country and found a great nation. Who?
context: Genesis 12. Originally 'Abram'. God renamed him Abraham � 'father of many'. He is honoured as the father of the Jewish people and Christians too.

question: Abraham's nephew settled near the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. Who?
context: Genesis 13. Lot chose the well-watered plain near the cities. Angels later rescued him from God's judgment on the cities.

question: Lot's wife disobeyed the angels and looked back at the burning cities. What did she become?
context: Genesis 19:26. Jesus told his disciples 'remember Lot's wife' (Luke 17:32) as a warning against looking back to a sinful life.

question: Abraham's only son by his wife Sarah was named what?
context: Genesis 21. 'Isaac' means 'he laughs' in Hebrew � because Sarah laughed when God promised her a son in her old age. He was born when she was 90.

question: God tested Abraham by telling him to sacrifice his son on a mountain. What stopped him?
context: Genesis 22. An angel called from heaven; God provided a ram caught in a thicket. Christians read the story as a picture of God offering his Son.

question: Isaac's wife bore him twin sons. The elder sold his birthright for what?
context: Genesis 25. Esau came in famished from hunting. The red stew gave him his nickname 'Edom' (red). The birthright meant double inheritance.

question: Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels on it. Where?
context: Genesis 28:12. He named the place Bethel � 'house of God'. Christ later refers to the ladder image when he tells Nathanael he is its fulfilment (John 1:51).

question: Jacob wrestled a mysterious being all night by a river. What new name did he get?
context: Genesis 32:28. 'He who strives with God'. The name became the name of the whole people. Jacob walked with a limp afterward where the man touched his hip.

question: Jacob's favourite son was given a coat of many colours. Who was the son?
context: Genesis 37. His brothers were jealous and sold him into Egyptian slavery. God used the betrayal to save the family during famine years later.

question: Joseph was sold into slavery in which country?
context: Genesis 37-39. Joseph rose from slave to vizier of Egypt � second only to Pharaoh. He saved his brothers and father from famine.

question: Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dream about seven fat and seven skinny what?
context: Genesis 41. The dream warned of seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Joseph stockpiled grain and saved both Egypt and his own family.

question: Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys killed. Whose basket-cradle was found in the Nile?
context: Exodus 2. Pharaoh's daughter rescued the baby; Moses's own mother became his nurse. Moses grew up an Egyptian prince but knew his Hebrew origin.

question: Moses saw God in a bush that was on fire but did not what?
context: Exodus 3 on Mount Horeb. God revealed his name 'I AM' to Moses and sent him back to Egypt to free the Hebrews.

question: What did God tell Moses to do because he stood on holy ground?
context: Exodus 3:5. The ground was holy because God's presence was there. Christians remember this when they treat church buildings as sacred space.

question: Who spoke for Moses to Pharaoh because Moses said he was 'slow of speech'?
context: Exodus 4. Aaron was Moses's elder brother and became Israel's first high priest. His descendants served at the altar.

question: God sent plagues on Egypt to free the Hebrews. The plagues numbered how many?
context: Exodus 7-12. The plagues climbed in severity, ending with the death of every firstborn � passing over Hebrew homes marked with lamb's blood.

question: Hebrews painted their doors with lamb's blood so the destroyer would do what?
context: Exodus 12. Passover (Pesach) became the great Jewish festival. Christians see Jesus as the Passover Lamb whose blood saves them from judgment.

question: Moses raised his staff and God split a sea so the Hebrews could cross. Which?
context: Exodus 14. Pharaoh's chariots followed but the waters crashed back. Miriam led the women in song afterward � the oldest song in the Bible.

question: In the wilderness God sent bread from heaven each morning. What was it called?
context: Exodus 16. White flakes like coriander seed. Jesus called himself 'the true bread from heaven' � the fulfilment of manna.

question: On which mountain did Moses receive the Ten Commandments?
context: Exodus 19-20. Cloud, thunder, fire. The two stone tablets sat in the Ark of the Covenant in Israel's most holy place.

question: On Mount Sinai God gave Moses commandments inscribed on stone. The commandments numbered how many?
context: Exodus 20. Christians divide the ten between duties to God (1-4) and duties to neighbour (5-10). Jesus summarised them as love God and love neighbour.

question: The first commandment says 'You shall have no other ___ before me.'
context: Exodus 20:3. Christians read it as the basis of monotheism � the worship of the one true God.

question: Which commandment forbids stealing?
context: Exodus 20:15. 'You shall not steal' is the eighth commandment in Christian counting (seventh in Jewish/Reformed counting).

question: Which commandment honours one's father and mother?
context: Exodus 20:12. The first commandment with a promise (Ephesians 6:2): 'that your days may be long in the land'.

question: After the Hebrews left Egypt they wandered the wilderness for how many years?
context: Numbers 14. One year of wandering for each day the spies scouted the promised land. The generation that doubted God died in the desert.

question: Who took over from Moses to lead Israel into the promised land?
context: Deuteronomy 31. Joshua's name in Hebrew is the same as 'Jesus' � both mean 'the LORD saves'. He led the conquest of Canaan.

question: Israel marched around which Canaanite city seven times before its walls fell?
context: Joshua 6. Trumpets and a great shout brought the walls down. Rahab the Jericho innkeeper hid the spies and was spared.

question: Who hid Israel's spies in her house and was spared when Jericho fell?
context: Joshua 2. Rahab tied a scarlet cord in her window. Matthew 1 names her as an ancestor of King David and of Jesus.

question: Which judge of Israel was a woman and a prophet?
context: Judges 4-5. She held court under a palm tree and rode with Barak to defeat Sisera. Her victory song is one of the oldest poems in the Bible.

question: Whose strength came from his uncut hair until Delilah cut it?
context: Judges 16. Samson was a Nazirite � consecrated to God. His hair grew back and his final act brought down a Philistine temple.

question: A young Moabite widow followed her mother-in-law to Bethlehem. Who?
context: Ruth 1. 'Whither thou goest, I will go.' Ruth married Boaz and became great-grandmother of King David � and an ancestor of Jesus.

question: Hannah prayed for a child and dedicated him to serve at the tabernacle. Who?
context: 1 Samuel 1. Samuel grew up under the priest Eli. He anointed both Saul and David as kings.

question: How tall was Goliath, the giant David killed with a sling?
context: 1 Samuel 17 says about six cubits and a span � roughly nine feet (2.7m). One smooth stone from David's sling hit him in the forehead.

question: What weapon did the boy David use against Goliath?
context: 1 Samuel 17. David took five smooth stones from a brook. He used one. Then he cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword.

question: Whose love for David made him risk his royal succession to save him?
context: 1 Samuel 18-20. Saul's son saw God's favour on David. He gave David his robe, sword, bow, and belt � symbolic acts. He died fighting beside his father.

question: David sinned by taking the wife of which loyal soldier?
context: 2 Samuel 11. Bathsheba was bathing on a rooftop. David had Uriah killed in battle to cover the affair. Psalm 51 is his cry of repentance.

question: Which prophet confronted David with the words 'you are the man'?
context: 2 Samuel 12. Nathan told a story of a rich man stealing a poor man's lamb. David condemned the rich man, then Nathan turned the story on him.

question: David's son built God's first stone temple in Jerusalem. Who?
context: 1 Kings 6. Solomon asked God for wisdom, not riches. The temple stood for nearly 400 years until Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC.

question: A southern queen brought gifts of gold and spices to test Solomon's wisdom. Who?
context: 1 Kings 10. She came from southern Arabia or Ethiopia. Jesus mentions her as a witness against unbelief in his own day (Matt 12:42).

question: On Mount Carmel a prophet called fire from heaven against 450 priests of Baal. Who?
context: 1 Kings 18. The water-soaked sacrifice burned up; the priests were taken away and killed. Elijah was later carried to heaven in a fiery chariot.

question: How did Elijah leave the earth at the end of his life?
context: 2 Kings 2. A chariot of fire separated him from Elisha. He appeared with Moses on the Mount of Transfiguration with Jesus centuries later.

question: Who was thrown into the lions' den for praying to God?
context: Daniel 6. King Darius mourned all night. The angel of God shut the lions' mouths. Daniel served four world emperors as adviser.

question: Three young men were thrown into a fiery furnace by Nebuchadnezzar. How many?
context: Daniel 3. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to worship the king's golden idol. A fourth figure walked with them in the flames.

question: Who was swallowed by a great fish for three days and three nights?
context: Jonah 1-2. He fled God's call to preach to Nineveh. Jesus called the three days in the fish a sign of his own three days in the tomb.

question: Esther was a Jewish girl who became queen of which empire?
context: Esther 2. Her cousin Mordecai raised her. She risked her life to expose Haman's plot to destroy her people. Purim is celebrated for her courage.

question: In Bethlehem there was no room for Mary and Joseph in the what?
context: Luke 2:7. The baby Jesus was laid in a manger � a feeding trough for animals. Christians remember this each Christmas Eve.

question: Angels announced Jesus's birth to a group of what?
context: Luke 2:8-14. The angels sang 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace'. Shepherds were among the lowliest workers in Bethlehem.

question: Three wise men brought Jesus three gifts: gold, frankincense, and what?
context: Matthew 2:11. Gold for a king, frankincense for a god, myrrh for burial. Tradition gave them names: Caspar, Melchior, Balthasar.

question: The wise men followed what to find the baby Jesus?
context: Matthew 2. They came from 'the east' � probably Persia or Babylon. King Herod tried to use them to find Jesus to kill him; they were warned in a dream.

question: Mary and Joseph fled to which country to escape King Herod's soldiers?
context: Matthew 2:13-15. An angel warned Joseph in a dream. They stayed in Egypt until Herod died, fulfilling Hosea 11:1: 'Out of Egypt I called my son'.

question: Jesus was raised in which Galilean town?
context: Matthew 2:23. 'He shall be called a Nazarene.' Nazareth was a small town in Galilee. Nathanael said 'can anything good come out of Nazareth?'

question: Who baptized Jesus in the river Jordan?
context: Matthew 3. John saw the Spirit descend like a dove on Jesus and heard a voice from heaven: 'this is my beloved Son'.

question: How long did Jesus fast in the wilderness when the devil tempted him?
context: Matthew 4, Mark 1, Luke 4. Three temptations: bread from stones, jumping from the temple, kingdoms of the world. Jesus answered each from Scripture.

question: What was the first miracle Jesus performed in John's Gospel?
context: John 2. At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turned six stone jars of water into the best wine of the feast. His mother Mary asked him to act.

question: Jesus called a group of close followers to be his apostles. The disciples numbered how many?
context: Mark 3:14. They became the twelve apostles. Their number echoed the twelve tribes of Israel � a new people of God.

question: Which two disciples were fishermen brothers, sons of Zebedee?
context: Matthew 4:21. Jesus nicknamed them 'sons of thunder'. John lived the longest of the twelve and wrote a Gospel, three letters, and Revelation.

question: What was Peter's job before Jesus called him?
context: Matthew 4:18-19. 'Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.' Peter became the leader of the apostles after the resurrection.

question: Which disciple was a tax collector before Jesus called him?
context: Matthew 9:9. Tax collectors were hated as collaborators with Rome. Matthew left his table and followed Jesus, and wrote one of the four Gospels.

question: Jesus told a story of a man who built his house on what to face the storm?
context: Matthew 7:24-27. The wise man's house on the rock stood; the foolish man's house on the sand fell. Jesus ended his Sermon on the Mount this way.

question: In the Lord's Prayer, what do we ask for daily?
context: Matthew 6:11. 'Give us this day our daily bread.' The Greek word for 'daily' is unusual � it can also mean 'for tomorrow' or 'needed for life'.

question: Jesus blessed children and said 'of such is the kingdom of...' what?
context: Matthew 19:14. 'Let the little children come to me'. Jesus's welcome of children scandalised his disciples � children had low status in the ancient world.

question: Jesus healed a blind man by rubbing what on his eyes?
context: John 9. He made the mud with his own spittle and sent the man to wash in the pool of Siloam. The healed man said 'one thing I know: I was blind, now I see'.

question: Whose tomb did Jesus reach four days too late, then call him out alive?
context: John 11. 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35) is the shortest verse. The miracle stirred such a crowd that the chief priests began plotting Jesus's death.

question: A short tax collector climbed a tree to see Jesus. Who?
context: Luke 19. He gave back four times what he had cheated. Jesus said 'today salvation has come to this house, for this man too is a son of Abraham'.

question: Who walked on water beside Jesus and began to sink in fear?
context: Matthew 14. He cried 'Lord, save me!' Jesus reached out his hand. 'O you of little faith, why did you doubt?'

question: Jesus entered Jerusalem on a young donkey. What feast was coming?
context: Matthew 21. Christians remember this as Palm Sunday � crowds laid palm branches and cried 'Hosanna!' The same crowd cried 'crucify him' five days later.

question: Which apostle betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver?
context: Matthew 26. Judas threw the silver back in the temple and hanged himself. The priests bought a potter's field with it for foreigners' burial.

question: Before the cock crowed Peter denied Jesus this many times.
context: All four Gospels. Jesus had warned him at the Last Supper. The risen Jesus later restored Peter with three calls: 'feed my sheep'.

question: Who washed his hands and let the crowd condemn Jesus?
context: Matthew 27. The Roman governor of Judea AD 26-36. The Apostles' Creed names him: 'suffered under Pontius Pilate' � fixing the crucifixion in history.

question: On what hill was Jesus crucified, outside Jerusalem's walls?
context: John 19:17. Aramaic 'Place of the Skull'. The Latin name is 'Calvary'. Roman crucifixions were carried out by main roads to maximise public horror.

question: How long did Jesus hang on the cross before he died?
context: Mark 15. From the third hour (9am) to the ninth hour (3pm). Darkness covered the land from noon. The temple curtain tore from top to bottom.

question: Who carried Jesus's cross part of the way to Golgotha?
context: Mark 15:21. He was the father of Alexander and Rufus � names known to Mark's first readers. The Stations of the Cross commemorate his help.

question: In whose tomb was Jesus buried after his crucifixion?
context: Matthew 27. A rich disciple who had not consented to Jesus's death. The tomb was new and cut from rock.

question: On the third day, who was the first person to see the risen Jesus?
context: John 20. She thought he was the gardener until he called her name. She brought the news to the apostles � early tradition called her 'apostle to the apostles'.

question: Which disciple doubted until he could touch the nail-prints?
context: John 20. A week later Jesus appeared again and told him 'reach your hand here'. Thomas answered 'my Lord and my God!' � the highest confession in the Gospels.

question: Fifty days after Easter the disciples received the Holy Spirit. What is this day called?
context: Acts 2. Tongues of fire rested on each. The disciples spoke in languages they did not know. About 3000 were baptised � the church's first day.

question: The first Christian martyr was stoned outside Jerusalem. Who was he?
context: Acts 7. Stephen forgave his attackers as he died: 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them'. A young Pharisee named Saul stood by approving.

question: Who was knocked off his horse on the road to Damascus and saw the risen Jesus?
context: Acts 9. He became blind for three days, then was healed by Ananias. Saul became the apostle Paul � writer of thirteen letters in the New Testament.

question: What new name did Saul of Tarsus take after his conversion?
context: Acts 13:9. 'Saul, also called Paul'. Paul wrote about a third of the New Testament. He was beheaded in Rome about AD 67 under Nero.

question: On which Aegean island was the apostle John exiled to write Revelation?
context: Revelation 1:9. Tradition says he died in Ephesus in old age � the only one of the twelve apostles not martyred. His visions close the New Testament.

question: Who saw a cross in the sky before winning the Battle of the Milvian Bridge?
context: AD 312. The next year Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, legalising Christianity throughout the Roman Empire. His mother Helena helped find the holy sites.

question: From Jesus's death to the Edict of Milan, Christianity was banned in the Roman Empire for roughly how long?
context: From around AD 30 (the crucifixion) until AD 313 (Edict of Milan). Persecutions came in waves under emperors like Nero, Decius, and Diocletian.

question: The first great church council met in 325 AD. Where?
context: Constantine called the council to settle the Arian controversy. The bishops affirmed Christ as 'true God from true God' � the Nicene Creed.

question: Which fifth-century bishop wrote 'Confessions' about his life and conversion?
context: Augustine of Hippo, 354-430. Born in North Africa, converted under the preaching of Ambrose in Milan. His 'City of God' shaped Western political theology.

question: Which thirteenth-century theologian wrote a vast 'Summa' on Christian doctrine?
context: Thomas Aquinas, c. 1225-1274. A Dominican friar. His Summa Theologica is the great Catholic systematic theology. He died on his way to a church council.

question: A young Italian stripped naked in Assisi square in 1206 to follow Christ in poverty. Who?
context: Francis of Assisi, 1181-1226. Founded the Franciscan order. Preached to birds. Received the stigmata � the wounds of Christ � two years before he died.

question: Who nailed 95 theses to a Wittenberg church door in 1517?
context: Luther protested the sale of indulgences. The act sparked the Protestant Reformation. He later translated the Bible into German for ordinary readers.

question: Which English king broke with Rome to divorce his queen Catherine?
context: 1534. Henry made himself supreme head of the Church of England. Thomas More was beheaded for refusing to swear the oath supporting it.

question: From a Bedford prison cell a Baptist preacher wrote 'Pilgrim's Progress'. Who?
context: Published 1678. Bunyan was a Baptist preacher jailed for preaching without a licence. The book has never been out of print � after the Bible, the most-read English Christian book.

question: In the 1700s an Anglican priest founded the Methodist movement with his brother Charles. The elder Wesley brother was who?
context: John Wesley, 1703-1791. He rode 250,000 miles on horseback preaching across England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. Charles wrote thousands of hymns.

question: Which 20th-century pastor was hanged by the Nazis in April 1945?
context: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, 1906-1945. Lutheran pastor. Hanged at Flossenburg concentration camp for his part in the resistance plot against Hitler. 'The Cost of Discipleship'.

question: An Oxford don wrote the 'Chronicles of Narnia' (1950-1956) with Aslan the lion as a Christ figure. The author was who?
context: Seven books. Lewis converted to Christianity in 1931 after long resistance. He also wrote 'Mere Christianity' and 'The Screwtape Letters'.

question: In which city did King David rule and Solomon build the temple?
context: Jerusalem was captured by David around 1000 BC and made his capital. The temple stood there for 400 years before Babylon destroyed it in 586 BC.

question: Christians remember Jesus's last meal with bread and what?
context: The Eucharist (or Lord's Supper, or Communion). At the Last Supper Jesus said 'this is my body' and 'this is my blood' over the bread and wine.

question: The four Gospels tell the story of Jesus. How many are there?
context: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Matthew, Mark, and Luke share a common storyline (the 'synoptic Gospels'); John tells the story differently.

question: The first four books of the New Testament are called the what?
context: 'Gospel' means 'good news' (Old English 'godspell'). Each gives a portrait of Jesus � the same person seen from different angles.

question: How many books are in the Bible (Protestant count)?
context: Thirty-nine Old Testament books and 27 New Testament. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add the 'deuterocanonical' books (Tobit, Judith, Maccabees, etc.).

question: Christians say the Holy Spirit is the third person of what?
context: Christians believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in three persons. The Spirit lives in believers and gives them gifts to serve God and others.

question: What word names Jesus's twelve closest students?
context: 'Apostle' means 'one sent out'. After Judas's betrayal, Matthias was chosen by lot. Paul is also counted an apostle though not one of the original twelve.

question: In the Old Testament, who replaced Saul as king of Israel?
context: 1 Samuel 16. The prophet Samuel anointed David in secret while Saul still reigned. David spent years on the run before becoming king at age 30.

question: The book of Psalms has how many psalms?
context: Tradition gives David as author of many but not all. Psalms are still sung in Jewish and Christian worship after 3000 years. Psalm 23 is the most famous.

question: Which Psalm begins 'The Lord is my shepherd'?
context: Traditionally attributed to David, who himself was a shepherd boy. 'Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil'.

question: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus on which date?
context: Christmas Day in Western tradition. Orthodox Christians who use the old calendar celebrate on January 7. Both date back to the 4th century.

question: Christians celebrate Jesus's resurrection on which day?
context: The date moves each year � the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. Christians worship on Sunday because the resurrection happened on a Sunday.

question: Forty days before Easter begins on Ash Wednesday. What is this season called?
context: Christians often give up something during Lent to prepare for Easter. The forty days mirror Jesus's forty days in the wilderness before his ministry.

question: Christians say grace before meals to thank God. Which gospel records Jesus blessing the loaves and fish?
context: The feeding of the 5000 is the only miracle (other than the resurrection) in all four Gospels. Jesus 'took the loaves, gave thanks, and broke them'.

question: Who is the Father of the prodigal son?
context: In Jesus's parable (Luke 15) the father stands for God � running to meet the wayward child. The brother who stayed home stands for the religious who don't see God's mercy.

question: Jesus said the greatest commandment is to love God with your what?
context: Mark 12:30. 'With all your heart, all your soul, all your mind, and all your strength.' The second is like it: love your neighbour as yourself.

question: Who do Christians believe is the great healer?
context: Christians ask God to heal them. Medicine is also seen as a gift from God � Luke (a doctor) is one of the Gospel writers.

question: In the parable of the sheep and goats, who comes to judge the world?
context: Matthew 25:31-46. He divides people by how they treated 'the least of these my brothers' � the hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, imprisoned.

question: The Apostles' Creed begins 'I believe in God, the Father Almighty, ___ of heaven and earth.'
context: The Creed shapes baptismal confession in Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, and many other churches. Each Sunday it summarises the Christian faith in three articles.

question: Genesis 1:1 begins 'In the beginning God ___ the heaven and the earth.'
context: Christians read this as the founding affirmation: everything exists because God made it. Hebrew 'bara' � a verb used only for divine creation.

question: Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead on which day after his death?
context: Friday afternoon to Sunday morning, counting inclusively. The Apostles' Creed: 'crucified, dead, and buried; the third day he rose again from the dead'.

question: How many books of the Old Testament are 'Major Prophets' in Christian counting?
context: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel. The 'Minor Prophets' are the twelve shorter books at the end of the OT � called minor only for length.

question: Christians often say a short prayer to remember God before sleep. What is it called?
context: Jesus taught it in Matthew 6 and Luke 11. Christians of every tradition use it. Many say it daily or even more often.

question: Who said 'Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world'?
context: John 1:29. John pointed at Jesus walking by. Christians repeat the words at every Eucharist � the priest holds up the bread and quotes John.

question: On which day of the week did God rest in Genesis?
context: Genesis 2:2-3. The Sabbath in Hebrew tradition is Saturday. Christians moved their day of worship to Sunday � the day of the resurrection.

question: Jesus told a parable about a sower who sowed seed on what kinds of ground?
context: Mark 4:3-9. Path, rocky, thorny, and good soil. Jesus then explained that the seed is the word and the soils are kinds of hearers.

question: Jesus said his kingdom is not of this what?
context: John 18:36. Said to Pilate at his trial. Christians read it as meaning the church's authority is not the same as political power � though it shapes life on earth.

question: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse appear in which book?
context: Revelation 6. White (conquest), red (war), black (famine), pale (death). Each rides forth as a seal of the scroll is opened by the Lamb.

question: Which patient man lost everything but refused to curse God?
context: One of the oldest books in the Bible � the poetry of suffering. Job refuses to curse God despite losing children, wealth, and health. 'I know that my Redeemer lives'.

question: The Beatitudes begin 'Blessed are the ___ in spirit.'
context: Matthew 5:3. Eight blessings open the Sermon on the Mount. The 'poor in spirit' are those who know they need God � the opposite of pride.

question: Mary's song of praise in Luke 1 is called the what?
context: Latin 'magnificat anima mea Dominum' � 'my soul magnifies the Lord'. Set to music by Bach, Vivaldi, and others. Sung at evening worship for centuries.

question: How old was Jesus when he started his public ministry?
context: Luke 3:23. The same age Aaron was when he began as priest (Numbers 4:3). Jesus's ministry lasted about three years before his crucifixion.

question: What did Jesus do at twelve years old in the Jerusalem temple?
context: Luke 2:46-47. Mary and Joseph had thought he was with the caravan. They found him in the temple three days later. 'Did you not know I must be about my Father's business?'

question: Who was Jesus's adoptive father, who taught him carpentry?
context: Matthew 1:18-25. Joseph nearly divorced Mary quietly until an angel told him the child was from the Holy Spirit. He died before Jesus's public ministry.

question: How old was Mary, traditionally, when she conceived Jesus?
context: Luke gives no age but ancient Jewish women typically married young. Christian tradition has long imagined Mary as a young teenager when Gabriel came to her.

question: Whose body would Joseph of Arimathea ask Pilate for after the crucifixion?
context: Matthew 27:57-60. The Roman policy was to leave crucified bodies on the cross. Joseph's request was risky but Pilate granted it.

question: In Genesis 17 God renamed a 99-year-old wandering shepherd 'father of many nations' and gave him circumcision as a covenant sign. Who?
context: The covenant of circumcision marked all male descendants. Christians read it as a sign of God's faithful self-binding to a particular people � widened to all the world through Christ.

question: Genesis 18 has three travelers eat at Abraham's tent and tell aged Sarah she will bear a son. She laughed. The travelers were what?
context: Christians have long read this scene as a hint of the Trinity (Andrei Rublev's icon shows it). Sarah's laughter gave Isaac his name. Genesis 19 has the two angels go on to Sodom.

question: Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed by fire from heaven in Genesis 19. Whose family was warned out by angels first?
context: Lot's wife disobeyed and looked back, becoming a pillar of salt. The cities sit in Christian tradition as warnings against unrepentant injustice and sexual violence.

question: Abraham sent his servant back to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac. The young woman who watered the camels at the well was who?
context: Genesis 24. Daughter of Bethuel, granddaughter of Nahor. She would mother Esau and Jacob � the twins struggling in her womb a sign of nations at strife.

question: Genesis 27: blind old Isaac was tricked into blessing the younger son who wore goat-skin gloves to feel hairy. Who deceived him?
context: Genesis 27. Jacob got the blessing of the firstborn. Esau wept and begged for any blessing left. The deceit shaped the next generations of the family.

question: Genesis 29: Jacob worked seven years for Laban's daughter Rachel, but was tricked into marrying her sister first. Who was the sister?
context: Then he worked seven more years for Rachel. The two sisters and their handmaids together bore the twelve sons whose names became the tribes of Israel.

question: Joseph in Egypt rose from slave to second-in-command after he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams. The seven years of plenty were followed by what?
context: Genesis 41. Joseph's grain storage saved Egypt � and eventually his own family who came begging from Canaan. He revealed himself to his brothers in a famous scene of forgiveness.

question: Exodus 2: Moses fled Egypt after killing an overseer and tended sheep in Midian for forty years. Whose daughter did he marry?
context: Zipporah was his wife. Jethro (also called Reuel) was a Midianite priest. He later visited Moses in the wilderness and advised him to delegate judging to lesser leaders (Ex 18).

question: On the night of the tenth plague, Hebrew families ate roast lamb with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, ready to flee. What feast is this?
context: Exodus 12. Jews still keep Passover (Pesach) each spring. Christians read Jesus's Last Supper as a Passover meal � making him 'our Passover Lamb' (1 Cor 5:7).

question: After the Red Sea crossing, Moses's sister led the women in song with timbrels and dance. She was the prophetess Miriam, sister of whom?
context: Exodus 15. Miriam's song is one of the oldest pieces of Hebrew poetry. She later opposed Moses's Cushite wife and was struck briefly with leprosy (Numbers 12).

question: On Sinai while Moses received the law, the people lost patience and asked Aaron to make them a god of gold. What was the idol?
context: Exodus 32. Moses broke the stone tablets in anger and ground the calf to powder. The story is the great biblical paradigm of idolatry.

question: Numbers 13: Moses sent twelve spies into Canaan. Only two brought back a faithful report. Who were they?
context: The other ten said the giants were too strong. Their fear cost Israel forty years in the wilderness. Caleb at 85 still asked for the hill country Hebron � and got it.

question: Numbers 21: when Israelites complained, fiery serpents bit them. Moses lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole; those who looked at it lived. Jesus referenced this in which gospel?
context: John 3:14. 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up'. The verse leads directly into John 3:16.

question: Joshua 6: Israel marched around Jericho once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day. What brought the walls down?
choices: a sapping tunnel under the walls
a battering ram at the gate
context: The story is rich in symbol � seven (completeness), trumpet (proclamation), shout (worship). Modern archaeology debates the dating; the theological point is God gives victory, not Israel's strength.

question: Joshua 10: the sun stood still in the sky so Israel could finish a battle. Where?
context: Joshua had marched all night to rescue Gibeon from a coalition. The 'long day of Gibeon' is one of the Bible's most striking miracles. Christians have variously read it as literal, observational, or rhetorical.

question: Judges 6: an angel called a winemaking farmer 'mighty man of valor' while he hid threshing wheat in a winepress. Who was the farmer?
context: Gideon set out a fleece to test God's call. He defeated 135,000 Midianites with just 300 men carrying torches in jars and trumpets. He refused to be made king � 'the LORD shall rule over you'.

question: Judges 13: an angel announced a son's birth to a barren wife and forbade him to cut his hair. Who was the strongman born?
context: Samson was a Nazirite � a lifelong vow. His Philistine lover Delilah betrayed him; his hair grew back; his last act collapsed Dagon's temple on his enemies, killing more in death than in life.

question: Ruth 1: a young Moabite widow refused to leave her destitute mother-in-law. 'Whither thou goest, I will go.' She is named what?
context: Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz (a kinsman). They married. Their great-grandson was King David. Matthew 1 names Ruth in Jesus's genealogy.

question: 1 Samuel 3: a young boy serving the priest Eli heard a voice in the night and at last answered 'speak, LORD'. Who was the boy?
context: Samuel grew into the last judge and the prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings. Eli's own sons were corrupt; God's word came through the apprentice instead.

question: 1 Samuel 16: God told Samuel to anoint a new king from Jesse's sons. Seven elder brothers passed before God chose the youngest. Who?
context: 'Man looks on the outward appearance; the LORD looks on the heart.' David was tending sheep when his father called him in. He was anointed in secret while Saul still reigned.

question: 1 Samuel 17: a young shepherd faced a 9-foot Philistine champion with five smooth stones from a brook. Who was the champion?
context: One stone hit Goliath's forehead. David then cut off his head with the giant's own sword. The story shaped Western imagination of the small-against-great battle ever after.

question: 1 Kings 3: Solomon asked God for what gift instead of riches or long life?
context: God gave him all three. Solomon's famous judgment � proposing to cut a baby in half to find its true mother � comes shortly after. Proverbs and Ecclesiastes are attributed to him.

question: 1 Kings 18: a prophet challenged 450 priests of Baal on Mount Carmel. The contest: whose god could send fire to burn the sacrifice?
context: Baal failed; Elijah doused his sacrifice with water and then God's fire fell. Elijah had the Baal priests slain afterward. He fled the next day from Queen Jezebel's wrath into the desert.

question: 2 Kings 5: a Syrian general was healed of leprosy after dipping seven times in the river Jordan, at Elisha's word. Who?
context: Naaman at first refused � 'are not the rivers of Damascus better?' His servants persuaded him. He returned converted to Israel's God. Jesus cites him in Luke 4:27.

question: Daniel 5: a disembodied hand wrote four Aramaic words on a Babylonian palace wall during a feast. Daniel translated them. Whose feast was it?
context: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN � 'numbered, numbered, weighed, divided'. That very night Belshazzar was slain and the Medo-Persian empire took the throne.

question: Daniel 6: King Darius reluctantly threw a faithful Jewish official into a den of lions for praying to God. Who was the official?
context: An angel shut the lions' mouths. Darius watched the rescue with relief and decreed all his empire honour Daniel's God. Tradition counts Daniel's age in his 80s by this point.

question: Esther became queen of Persia and risked her life to save the Jews. Her uncle who raised her was who?
context: Esther fasted three days before going to King Ahasuerus uninvited. Haman's scheme to kill the Jews was reversed; Haman hanged on his own gallows. Purim still celebrates the deliverance.

question: Isaiah 6: a young prophet saw the LORD enthroned and crying 'holy, holy, holy'. The seraphim each had how many wings?
context: Two cover face, two cover feet, two for flying. A burning coal touched the prophet's lips to cleanse him. Christians repeat 'holy, holy, holy' at every Eucharist.

question: Jeremiah was called by God while still young. What did God touch to commission him as a prophet?
context: Jeremiah 1:9. 'Behold I have put my words in your mouth.' Jeremiah preached judgment for forty years; he was beaten, jailed, and dropped in a cistern. Tradition says he was finally stoned to death in Egypt.

question: Ezekiel 37 has a vision of dry bones reassembling, then growing flesh, then receiving breath � becoming an army. What does the vision foretell?
context: Christians have also read the vision as foreshadowing resurrection. The valley of dry bones is among the most striking images in prophetic literature.

question: Jonah ran from God's call to preach to which great pagan city?
context: Nineveh was the capital of Assyria. After three days in the fish Jonah preached judgment � and the city repented. Jonah sulked under a withering plant. The book ends with God's question of mercy.

question: Matthew 5-7: Jesus's longest recorded teaching, given on a Galilean hillside, is called what?
context: It contains the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule, and much else. Christians of every century have read it as the heart of the Christian moral vision.

question: Mark 4: Jesus told a parable of a sower whose seed fell on four kinds of ground. The good ground bore fruit how much?
context: Mark 4:8. Jesus then explained: path = those who hear and Satan steals the word; rocky = quick joy then withering; thorny = choked by cares and riches; good ground = the word bears fruit.

question: Luke 10: a despised Samaritan stopped to help a man left for dead while a priest and a Levite passed by. Which gospel records the parable?
context: Jesus told it to answer 'who is my neighbor?' The Samaritan paid for the man's care at an inn. 'Go and do likewise.' The story has shaped Western charity for two millennia.

question: Luke 15: three parables of lost things end the same way � rejoicing. They are the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost what?
context: The prodigal son squandered his inheritance, came home in rags, was met by his father running. The elder brother resented the feast. Christians read both sons as types of how people receive God's mercy.

question: John 4: Jesus broke convention by speaking to a Samaritan woman at a well at noon. Where was the well?
context: She brought her village to hear him; he stayed two days. Modern site identification is debated. The dialogue contains 'God is spirit; those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth'.

question: John 6: after Jesus fed the 5000, the crowd wanted to make him king. He withdrew to a mountain alone. What did he say of himself the next day?
answer: I am the bread of life
choices: I am the bread of life
I am the way and the truth
I am the door of the sheep
context: First of the seven 'I am' sayings in John (echoing Exodus 3:14: 'I AM has sent me'). Many disciples left at this teaching: 'this is hard, who can hear it?'

question: John 8: Jesus saved a woman caught in adultery from stoning with a famous line about her accusers. What did he tell them to do first?
answer: let the sinless throw the first stone
choices: let the sinless throw the first stone
report the man as well as the woman
show the witnesses required by law
say the words of accusation aloud
context: Then he stooped and wrote on the ground. One by one the accusers left, beginning with the eldest. To the woman: 'neither do I condemn you. Go and sin no more.'

question: John 11: Jesus stood at his friend's tomb and wept before calling him out alive. The friend had been dead how many days?
context: Lazarus of Bethany. His sisters Mary and Martha had sent word; Jesus delayed two days. The miracle drew such a crowd that the priests began plotting Jesus's death.

question: The Transfiguration on a high mountain has Jesus's face shining like the sun. Moses and which other figure appear beside him?
context: Matthew 17, Mark 9, Luke 9. Three apostles � Peter, James, John � witnessed it. A voice from the cloud said 'this is my beloved Son; listen to him'.

question: Matthew 26: at the Last Supper Jesus took bread, blessed it, and gave it to the disciples saying 'this is...' what?
context: He then took the cup: 'this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins'. Christians repeat these words at every Eucharist (or Communion or Lord's Supper).

question: Mark 14: in Gethsemane Jesus prayed three times that the cup might pass � but added what?
answer: not what I will, but what you will
choices: not what I will, but what you will
if it be your good pleasure, Father
I lay down my life of my own accord
I have finished the work you sent me
context: Hebrews 5:7 says he prayed 'with strong crying and tears'. His sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44). The disciples slept; he was arrested at the kiss of Judas.

question: Luke 23: on the cross Jesus prayed for his enemies. What was his first word from the cross?
choices: today you will be with me
context: Luke 23:34. Seven sayings of Christ from the cross are remembered in Christian devotion. Stephen the first martyr echoes this prayer in Acts 7.

question: Acts 1: Jesus was lifted up into a cloud forty days after his resurrection. Christians call this the what?
context: Two angels told the apostles: 'this same Jesus shall so come in like manner as you have seen him go'. The Apostles' Creed says: 'he ascended into heaven; sitteth on the right hand of God'.

question: Acts 2: ten days after the Ascension, the disciples were gathered in Jerusalem when a sound like wind filled the house and tongues of fire rested on each. What feast?
context: About 3000 were baptised that day � the church's birthday. The disciples spoke languages they did not know. Peter preached the gospel of the risen Christ.

question: Acts 6: seven men were chosen to oversee the daily distribution to widows so the apostles could focus on preaching. What were they called?
context: From Greek 'diakonos' � 'servant'. Stephen and Philip were among the first seven. The office still exists in most Christian traditions as a ministry of practical care.

question: Acts 8: Philip met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah on a desert road. After Philip explained the prophecy, what did the Ethiopian ask?
answer: what prevents me from being baptised
choices: what prevents me from being baptised
may I follow you back to Jerusalem
where can I purchase a copy of Christ's words
would you teach my queen also of this Jesus
context: Philip baptised him at a roadside pool. The Ethiopian official is sometimes counted the first African convert. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church traces its origins partly to him.

question: Acts 9: Saul was struck blind on the road to Damascus. What did the risen Jesus say?
answer: Saul, why do you persecute me
choices: Saul, why do you persecute me
come and follow me, Saul of Tarsus
depart from me, doer of evil works
knock and the door shall be opened
context: Acts 9:4. Ananias was sent (with some reluctance) to lay hands on Saul. Scales fell from Saul's eyes. He was baptised and immediately began preaching Jesus in the synagogues.

question: Acts 10: Peter had a vision of unclean animals lowered in a sheet and was told to kill and eat. The vision prepared him to baptise the first Gentile. Who?
context: Cornelius was a Roman centurion in Caesarea. Peter went, preached, the Holy Spirit fell on all listening, and they were baptised. The Jerusalem church was scandalised but Peter said 'God showed me I should not call any man unclean'.

question: Acts 16: Paul and Silas sang hymns in a Philippian prison at midnight when an earthquake opened the doors. Who was converted afterward?
context: The jailer was about to kill himself, assuming the prisoners had fled. Paul stopped him. 'What must I do to be saved?' Paul: 'believe on the Lord Jesus'. The jailer's whole household was baptised that night.

question: Acts 17: Paul preached on the Areopagus to philosophers in Athens. What altar inscription did he use as his starting point?
choices: to all the gods of Olympus
to the chief god of the city
to the god who hears prayers
context: Acts 17:23. Paul quoted Greek poets to make his case. Some mocked, some said 'we will hear you again', some believed � including Dionysius the Areopagite, traditionally counted Athens's first bishop.

question: 1 Corinthians 13: 'though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not ___, I am nothing.'
context: King James 'charity' translates Greek 'agape' � self-giving love. Modern translations often render 'love'. Paul wrote it to a Corinthian church divided over spiritual gifts.

question: Romans 8: nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Paul names ten things that try. Which begins his list?
context: Romans 8:35. The chapter is among the most beloved in Paul's letters � the long argument that ends with God's unbroken commitment to those in Christ.

question: Philippians 2: Christ Jesus emptied himself, taking the form of a what?
context: Philippians 2:7. The 'Christ hymn' (vv 5-11) is one of the oldest pieces of Christian poetry. Paul cites it to teach humility: 'have this mind in you'. It ends with every knee bowing at Jesus's name.

question: Ephesians 6: Paul lists the armour of God. The shield is for the shield of what?
context: Ephesians 6:10-18. Belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the gospel of peace, shield of faith, helmet of salvation, sword of the Spirit (the word of God). Christians have leaned on this image for prayer in trouble.

question: Hebrews 11 lists the 'great cloud of witnesses' of faith. Who is named first?
context: Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain. 'By his faith, though dead, he still speaks.' The chapter walks through Israel's history of faith, climaxing at Christ in chapter 12.

question: James, the brother of Jesus, taught that 'faith without works is what'?
context: James 2:17. James balances Paul's 'justified by faith' with 'faith without works is dead'. The Reformation read them as complementary; Luther initially called James 'an epistle of straw' but kept it.

question: 1 John 4:16: 'God is love; he that dwells in love dwells in God.' What is God said to be at the heart of this letter?
context: 1 John 4:16. The same letter says: 'we love because he first loved us'. Christians have read 1 John as the most concentrated New Testament treatment of love as the test of true faith.

question: Revelation 21: John saw a new heaven and a new earth, and a holy city descending from God. What was the city called?
context: Revelation 21:2. A cube of pure gold, 1500 miles each side. No temple, for the Lord himself is its temple. No need of sun or moon, for the glory of God lights it. No more tears or pain.

question: After Constantine legalized Christianity in 313 AD, the first great church council met in 325 to settle the question of Christ's divinity. Where?
context: The Council of Nicaea produced the first form of the Nicene Creed: 'true God from true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father'. Arius's view was condemned as heresy.

question: The Apostles' Creed begins 'I believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ his only ___ our Lord.'
context: The Apostles' Creed is the baptismal confession of the Western church. It comes in twelve articles, traditionally counted one per apostle. Most Christian traditions still use it.

question: Augustine of Hippo wrote a long autobiography of his conversion in the form of prayer. What is the book called?
context: Augustine, 354-430. Book 8 records his garden-conversion scene reading Romans 13:14 after a child's voice said 'tolle, lege' (take and read). Among the most influential books in Western literature.

question: In 432 AD a Roman Briton enslaved in Ireland as a youth returned to evangelise the island. Who is celebrated each March 17?
context: His own 'Confession' survives. Tradition credits him with using the shamrock to teach the Trinity, banishing snakes from Ireland, and lighting a paschal fire that challenged the High King's authority.

question: In 597 AD an Italian Benedictine monk landed in Kent to convert the English. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. Who?
context: Different Augustine from Augustine of Hippo � sent by Pope Gregory the Great. King Ethelbert of Kent was the first English king to be baptised. Augustine's shrine survived at Canterbury until the Reformation.

question: In 1095 a pope preached the First Crusade at Clermont with the words 'Deus vult'. What does the phrase mean?
context: Pope Urban II called Western knights to liberate Jerusalem from Seljuk Turkish rule. The crusaders took the city in 1099 with a notorious massacre � a complex moral legacy Christians have wrestled with ever since.

question: In 1209 a young Italian heard a voice from a roadside crucifix say 'rebuild my church'. He gathered followers in poverty and preached to all creation. Who?
context: Francis, 1181-1226. He preached to birds. He received the stigmata two years before his death. His order, the Franciscans, became one of the great medieval missionary orders.

question: Martin Luther translated the Bible into German while hidden as a fugitive in which castle?
context: 1521-22. After the Diet of Worms condemned him, Frederick the Wise had Luther 'kidnapped' to safety. The German Bible reshaped the language as the King James Bible later shaped English.

question: John Calvin systematized Reformed theology in his 'Institutes of the Christian Religion'. He led the church in which Swiss city?
context: Calvin's Geneva became a model Reformed city � austere, disciplined, missionary. Calvin trained pastors who went out across France, Scotland, the Netherlands. His thought shaped Anglo-American Puritanism.

question: In 1534 Henry VIII broke from Rome to divorce his queen Catherine of Aragon. Which act made him supreme head of the Church of England?
context: Thomas More was beheaded for refusing to swear it. Thomas Cranmer became Archbishop of Canterbury. The English Reformation was at once a religious revolution and a political one.

question: John Knox, fierce Scottish reformer, returned from exile in 1559 to lead Scotland's break with Rome. He had been a galley slave of which navy?
context: Knox was captured during the siege of St Andrews in 1547 and rowed in a French galley for 19 months. His 'Monstrous Regiment of Women' (1558) attacked female rulers. Mary Queen of Scots feared his preaching.

question: Charles Wesley wrote thousands of hymns including 'Hark the Herald Angels Sing'. His elder brother was the founder of the Methodist movement. Who?
context: John, 1703-1791. He rode 250,000 miles on horseback preaching. The Methodist movement began as a renewal inside the Church of England and only later became a separate church.

question: In 1738 at a Moravian meeting on Aldersgate Street a 35-year-old Anglican priest felt his heart 'strangely warmed'. Who?
context: Wesley dated his real conversion to that meeting. He was already a missionary returned from Georgia. Aldersgate is sometimes called the birth-date of the Methodist movement.

question: William Wilberforce led the British parliamentary campaign to abolish the slave trade. He was converted under the preaching of which evangelical?
context: Newton had himself been a slave-ship captain before his conversion. He wrote 'Amazing Grace'. The British Slave Trade Act passed 1807; Wilberforce died days after the act ending slavery itself in 1833.

question: A young American to be hanged for tax-resistance turned the Civil War song into the great abolitionist hymn 'Mine Eyes Have Seen the Glory'. Whose body was 'a-mouldering in the grave'?
context: John Brown was hanged in 1859 for the Harpers Ferry raid. The melody became Julia Ward Howe's 'Battle Hymn of the Republic' � still sung in many churches and at presidential inaugurations.

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran pastor, was hanged by the Nazis in April 1945 for his part in the plot against Hitler. His best-known book is called what?
context: Bonhoeffer's German title was 'Nachfolge' (Following After). His attack on 'cheap grace' � forgiveness without repentance � has shaped two generations of Christian ethics.

question: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity to serve the dying poor of which Indian city?
context: Mother Teresa, 1910-1997. Albanian-Indian Catholic nun. Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. Canonised in 2016. Her private letters showed she lived for decades in 'spiritual darkness' � feeling God's absence.

question: Martin Luther King Jr was a Baptist pastor from which American state?
context: Born in Atlanta, Georgia, 1929. Pastored Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, Alabama, during the 1955 bus boycott. Assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1968. His Christian preaching shaped the American civil rights movement.

question: Christians say there is one God in three persons. What word is used for this teaching?
context: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit � each fully God, yet there is one God. The doctrine took its first creedal form at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). It is the foundational Christian doctrine.

question: Christ is fully God and fully human, the church teaches. This doctrine took its mature form at the Council of Chalcedon in what year?
context: Chalcedon, 451 AD. Christ is 'in two natures � without confusion, change, division, or separation'. The Coptic, Ethiopian, and Armenian churches rejected the formula; the rest of Christendom received it.

question: Christians celebrate Jesus's death and resurrection over a special weekend each year. The Sunday is Easter; the Friday is what?
context: The most solemn day of the Christian year. Many churches keep three-hour services of meditation on the seven last words from the cross. Holy Saturday between is a day of silence.

question: Thomas Aquinas's 'Five Ways' argue for God's existence. The first way reasons from what we see around us � change. It is the argument from what?
context: Summa Theologica, Question 2. Everything that changes is changed by something already actual; an infinite regress is impossible; therefore there is an unmoved mover. 'And this all men call God.'

question: Christians have prayed a daily cycle of psalms and prayers since the earliest centuries. The morning prayer is often called what?
context: From Latin 'matutinus' � 'of the morning'. The Benedictine pattern of seven prayer-times shaped the medieval church. Anglicans simplified to Morning and Evening Prayer. Many Christians still keep some pattern of daily prayer.

question: Christmas Day was set on December 25 in the fourth century. It celebrates Jesus's birth. What is its season of preparation called?
context: Four weeks before Christmas. From Latin 'adventus' � 'coming'. The Advent wreath has four candles, lit one per week, with a white Christ candle at the centre lit on Christmas Eve.

question: Christians traditionally observe forty days of preparation before Easter. The forty days mirror Jesus's fast in the wilderness. What is the season called?
context: From Old English 'lencten' � 'spring'. Many Christians give up something for Lent or take on a discipline. It begins on Ash Wednesday and ends on Easter Eve. Sundays are not counted.

question: Christians have read Psalm 22 ('my God, my God, why have you forsaken me') as foretelling Christ's crucifixion. The psalm is traditionally attributed to which king?
context: Jesus cried this verse from the cross in Mark 15:34. The psalm describes detail by detail what happened � piercing of hands and feet, casting lots for clothing � written centuries earlier.

question: Easter is the most important Christian feast. The English name comes from a pre-Christian spring season; most other languages use a name from which Jewish festival?
context: Spanish 'Pascua', French 'Paques', Greek 'Pascha' � all from 'Pesach'. Christians read Christ as the true Passover Lamb whose blood saves them, fulfilling the Exodus story.

question: Christians celebrate seven main feasts of Mary in the Catholic tradition. The Annunciation (Gabriel announcing Jesus's coming) is celebrated nine months before Christmas. On which date?
context: Nine months back from December 25. The Annunciation in Luke 1 is the moment Christians count Jesus's incarnation � not his birth. Many old calendars began the year on March 25.

question: The largest Christian denomination in the world is the Roman Catholic Church. The second-largest tradition is what?
context: Roman Catholic c. 1.3 billion; Eastern Orthodox c. 260 million; Protestant c. 800 million (across thousands of denominations). The Orthodox churches separated from Rome at the Great Schism of 1054.

question: The Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches officially split in 1054. Who excommunicated whom?
answer: the Pope and Patriarch each other
choices: the Pope and Patriarch each other
context: Pope Leo IX (through his legate) and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicated each other. The excommunications were lifted in 1965 by Paul VI and Athenagoras � but the churches remain separate.

question: In the Christian liturgical year, the Sundays after Pentecost (or after Trinity) make up the season called what?
context: 'Ordinary' from 'ordinal' (numbered), not 'common'. The longest season � from Pentecost through November. The liturgical color is green (growth). The cycle of readings walks through the Bible.

question: Christians read the four gospels in church on Sundays. The first gospel in the New Testament arrangement is which?
context: Matthew was placed first because it bridges Old and New Testaments with the genealogy of Jesus tracing back to Abraham. Mark is shortest and probably written earliest. John is most distinct from the others.

question: Saint Patrick used a three-leaf plant to teach the Trinity, says tradition. What was the plant?
context: Each leaf one person, all one plant. The shamrock has been Irish national symbol ever since. Patrick's actual writings (his 'Confession' and 'Letter to Coroticus') survive but make no mention of it.

question: The Hebrew Bible (Old Testament) was originally written mostly in Hebrew. A small portion is in which related language?
context: Parts of Ezra, Daniel, and one verse of Jeremiah. Aramaic was the common language of Jews returning from Babylon. Jesus spoke Aramaic in daily life � traces survive in the gospels ('talitha cumi', 'eloi eloi').

question: The New Testament was originally written in which language?
context: Koine Greek � the common Greek of the Hellenistic world. The Greek New Testament has been translated into more languages than any other text. Latin took over in the West only with Jerome's Vulgate (c. 400).

question: The Greek translation of the Old Testament made by Jewish scholars in Alexandria c. 250 BC was used by the early church. What is it called?
context: Tradition says seventy (or seventy-two) translators worked separately and produced identical translations � hence 'LXX', the seventy. Paul quotes the Septuagint in his letters. Eastern Orthodox Christians still use it.

question: Jerome translated the Bible into Latin around 400 AD. His translation became the standard Bible of the Western church for over a thousand years. What is it called?
context: Latin 'vulgata' � 'common' (everyday language). Jerome worked from the Hebrew text for the OT (controversially), not just the Greek. The Council of Trent (1546) declared the Vulgate the authoritative Latin Bible.

question: Pope John Paul II was the first non-Italian pope in over 450 years. From which country did he come?
context: Karol Wojtyla, 1920-2005. Elected 1978. Survived a 1981 assassination attempt; later forgave the gunman in his cell. His support for Polish Solidarity helped bring down European communism.

question: Genesis 1: light, sea/sky, land/plants, sun/moon/stars, sea/sky creatures, land animals/man. After how many days did God rest?
context: Genesis 2:2-3. God blessed the seventh day and made it holy. The Sabbath rest is one of the great gifts of biblical religion to the world. Jesus said 'the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27).

question: Genesis 4: Cain killed his brother in a field after God favoured the brother's offering. What was the killer's punishment?
context: Genesis 4:12-16. God put a mark on Cain to protect him from murder. He settled east of Eden in the land of Nod ('wandering'). Christians have long read Cain and Abel as the founding story of human violence and God's costly mercy toward the violent.

question: Genesis 11: humanity built a tower to reach heaven. God scattered them by confusing their what?
context: Genesis 11. The Tower of Babel. Acts 2 reverses Babel at Pentecost � the Spirit gives a different gift, the gift of being understood across language. Christians see this as a foretaste of the kingdom 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation' (Revelation 7:9).

question: Exodus 19: God descended on Sinai in fire, smoke, and thunder. He told Moses 'tell the people to wash their clothes and be ready for the third day'. What was about to happen?
context: Exodus 19-20. Israel was to be 'a kingdom of priests, a holy nation'. The covenant was the central event of OT religion. Peter applies the language to the church in 1 Peter 2:9: 'you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation'.

question: Leviticus 16: once a year the high priest entered the holiest place of the tabernacle (or temple) to make atonement for the people. What is this day called?
context: Hebrew 'Day of Atonement'. The high priest sprinkled blood on the mercy seat. A goat 'for Azazel' (the scapegoat) was sent into the wilderness with the people's sins. Hebrews 9 reads Christ's once-for-all sacrifice as the fulfilment of Yom Kippur.

question: Numbers 21: Moses lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole; whoever looked at it lived. Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent because the people had begun to worship it. What name did he give the broken pieces?
context: 2 Kings 18:4. 'Nehushtan' means 'a piece of bronze'. Hezekiah's reform was thorough: he removed high places, broke down pillars, cut down sacred poles. The bronze serpent had been a relic of Israel's wilderness wandering but became an idol when worshipped in itself.

question: Joshua 1: when Moses died, God called Joshua to lead Israel. What command did God give him three times?
context: Joshua 1:6,7,9. 'Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land.' God promised: 'as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you.' Joshua's leadership took Israel across the Jordan and into the conquest.

question: Judges 2: a recurring pattern in Israel's judges. Israel sinned, was oppressed, cried out, God raised a judge to deliver them. Then the people did what?
context: The cycle repeats through the book of Judges. The last verse summarises: 'in those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes' (Judges 21:25). The cycle prepares the way for Israel's request for a king in 1 Samuel.

question: Ruth's harvest gleaning brought her to the field of a kinsman of her late father-in-law. She and Boaz married. Their son Obed was the father of whom?
context: Ruth 4:17. 'Obed who is the father of Jesse, the father of David.' Matthew's genealogy of Jesus lists Ruth specifically. The book's quiet story turns out to be part of the great line that climaxes at Bethlehem with David's greater son.

question: 1 Samuel 25: a foolish wealthy man named Nabal refused to give provisions to David's men. His wife rode out with food and saved her household. What was her name?
context: 1 Samuel 25:14-35. Abigail's wise speech turned David from rash vengeance. Within days Nabal had a stroke and died. David married Abigail. Her speech is one of the great pieces of OT wisdom literature embedded in narrative.

question: 2 Samuel 1: David received news of Saul's and Jonathan's deaths at Gilboa. He tore his clothes, fasted, and composed a song. What did he name in the song?
context: 2 Samuel 1:21. 'Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon.' David's lament includes one of the most famous lines in OT love poetry: 'Jonathan, my brother, very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women'.

question: Psalm 23: 'The LORD is my ___, I shall not want.'
context: Psalm 23:1. Traditionally attributed to David, himself a shepherd boy. 'He leadeth me beside the still waters; he restoreth my soul.' Probably the best-known psalm in any language. It has been at countless deathbeds and funerals across two thousand years.

question: Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon. Chapter 31 closes with a famous portrait of a 'wife of valor'. What kind of woman does she resemble?
context: Proverbs 31:14. She brings food from far away. She rises while still night, considers a field, plants a vineyard, makes linen garments. 'Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband, and he praises her'. The poem is acrostic � each verse begins with the next Hebrew letter.

question: Isaiah 40: 'comfort, comfort my people, says your God'. The chapter goes on to picture a way being prepared in the desert. John the Baptist later applied this prophecy to himself. What voice cries in the desert?
context: Isaiah 40:3. All four gospels quote this verse about John the Baptist. The chapter ends with one of the greatest passages in scripture: 'they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles' (40:31).

question: Ezekiel 36: a prophecy of cleansing. God promises 'I will sprinkle clean water on you; and I will give you a new heart, and put a new ___ within you'.
context: Ezekiel 36:25-27. 'I will take away the stony heart and give you a heart of flesh.' The prophecy is often read as fulfilled in Pentecost and the new covenant. Christians have read it as the OT background for the New Testament theology of regeneration.

question: Mary's song in Luke 1 is called the Magnificat. It begins 'My soul ___ the Lord.'
context: Luke 1:46. Mary's song echoes Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2 (about the prophet Samuel). 'He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts; he has put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.' Sung at evening prayer for centuries.

question: Simeon's song in Luke 2 is called the Nunc Dimittis (its first two Latin words). The old man held the infant Jesus and said 'now you let your servant ___'.
context: Luke 2:29-32. Simeon had been told by the Holy Spirit he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. He saw, he held, he blessed. The song is sung at the close of day in many Christian traditions � the soul releasing the day with peace.

question: Matthew 2: Herod ordered the killing of all baby boys in Bethlehem under age two. The slaughter is remembered each year. The commemoration is called what?
context: Feast of the Holy Innocents, December 28. The slaughter was not on the scale of Herod's other crimes (he killed his own sons) but in Bethlehem itself probably twenty or thirty children died. Christians remember them as the first martyrs � witnesses to Christ without yet knowing him.

question: Jesus performed his first public miracle at a wedding in Cana. What did he do?
context: John 2:1-11. Six stone jars, each holding 20-30 gallons. Jesus's mother Mary asked him to act, though it 'was not his hour'. The master of the feast was astonished: 'you have saved the best wine until now'. Christians have read the sign as foreshadowing the messianic banquet.

question: Mark 5: a desperate woman with a chronic bleeding condition pushed through the crowd to touch the hem of Jesus's cloak. What happened?
choices: she was rebuked by the crowd
she was honored by the elders
she was given gifts of silver
context: Mark 5:25-34. Jesus turned and asked 'who touched me?' The disciples thought the question silly � a crowd was pressing on every side. Jesus knew power had gone out of him. The woman trembling came and told him. 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'

question: Luke 18: Jesus told a parable of a Pharisee and a tax collector praying in the temple. The Pharisee thanked God he was not like others. The tax collector beat his breast and said one short prayer. What was it?
answer: God, be merciful to me a sinner
choices: God, be merciful to me a sinner
Lord, you know how I have served
Father, hear thy son in his need
context: Luke 18:13. 'I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.' The tax collector's prayer became part of the Eastern Christian 'Jesus Prayer'. The parable warns against contempt for those we think beneath us.

question: Acts 8: Simon Magus offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit. Peter rebuked him sharply. From his name comes which sin's English label?
context: Simony � the sin of buying or selling sacred things (especially church offices). It became a major issue in the medieval church. Dante consigned simonists to the third pouch of the eighth circle of hell, inverted in rock.

question: Christian baptism in the early church usually meant immersion in a river or pool. Believers came up out of the water. What did they put on at the same time?
context: The white baptismal robe symbolised Christ-clothing (Galatians 3:27). 'White Sunday' (Whitsun) is the old English name for Pentecost, when baptisms were often performed. The white christening gown for infants still preserves the tradition in many Christian families.

question: The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) condemned the teaching of an Alexandrian presbyter named Arius. What was Arius teaching about Christ?
answer: the Son was a created being
choices: the Son was a created being
the Son had two natures conjoined
the Son was only a divine man
context: Arius taught 'there was a time when the Son was not'. Nicaea answered with 'homoousios' � the Son is of one substance with the Father, eternally begotten not made. Most Christians today receive the Nicene Creed without realising what it was forged against.

question: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. What did the great cathedral of Hagia Sophia become for the next 481 years?
context: Sultan Mehmed II added minarets and covered the mosaics in plaster. The dome continued to inspire Islamic architecture (Suleymaniye, Selimiye). Ataturk made it a museum in 1934; in 2020 Turkey reverted it to active mosque use. Orthodox Christianity has not regained the building.

question: In 1095 Pope Urban II preached a sermon at Clermont calling for a crusade. The crowd shouted back a Latin phrase, which became the crusader cry. What did they shout?
context: Latin 'God wills it'. The First Crusade (1096-99) recovered Jerusalem with notorious massacre. Christian assessment of the crusades has been complex � John Paul II expressed deep sorrow in 2000 while not condemning the original defensive purpose.
