question: Martin Luther published 95 theses for academic debate in 1517. He posted them on the door of which church?
context: Wittenberg Castle Church door served as the university notice board. Luther wrote in Latin � not initially aimed at the general public. Within weeks the theses had been translated into German and circulated across the empire. The Reformation had begun.

question: Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and insisted on believer's baptism. Their name in Greek means 'rebaptisers'. The Swiss Brethren first did adult baptism on January 21, 1525, in which city?
context: Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock by pouring; Blaurock baptised the rest. The Zurich council ordered them all to recant. They refused; many were drowned, burned, or fled. Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites trace their roots to this movement.

question: In 1605 a small group of English Catholics tried to blow up Parliament and King James I. The plot was discovered. Guy Fawkes was caught in the cellar. The event is celebrated each November 5 in Britain. What is it called?
context: Or 'Guy Fawkes Night'. The plot reflected continued tensions between Catholic and Protestant after the Reformation. Anti-Catholic feeling shaped British politics for centuries afterward. The Catholic Emancipation Act came only in 1829.

question: Methodism began with John Wesley's Aldersgate experience on May 24, 1738. Wesley said his heart was 'strangely ___ ' while listening to Luther's preface to Romans being read.
context: Aldersgate has been called the birthday of Methodism. Wesley was already an Anglican priest and former missionary to Georgia � but had not yet had the experience of personal trust in Christ. Methodism became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States by the early 19th century.

question: Christians celebrate the resurrection of Jesus on Easter Sunday. How is the date of Easter set?
answer: first Sunday after first full moon after spring equinox
choices: first Sunday after first full moon after spring equinox
the second Sunday of April each year
the closest Sunday to March 25 each year
the first Sunday after Roman calends of April
context: The Council of Nicaea fixed the calculation in 325. Eastern and Western churches use slightly different methods, so they often differ by a week or more. Easter can fall any Sunday between March 22 and April 25.

question: Christians read Romans 6 at baptisms: we are 'buried with Christ in baptism, into death; that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in ___'.
context: Romans 6:4. Paul's argument: the Christian's baptism is union with both Christ's death and his resurrection. The new life is the moral and spiritual life of one who has died with Christ and risen with him. This vision shapes Christian moral teaching about discipleship.

question: Christians have always read Genesis 1 as foundational. The verse 'God created humans in his image' has shaped Western dignity-claims. The image of God in Hebrew is 'tselem ___ '.
context: Genesis 1:27. 'In the image of Elohim he created them; male and female he created them.' Christians have argued for centuries about what the image consists of � rationality, dominion, relationality, holiness. The doctrine grounds opposition to all forms of human degradation.

question: Christians have prayed for the dead in many traditions. What is the medieval doctrine that some are purified before heaven?
context: Catholic doctrine teaches purgatory as a state of cleansing for those who die in grace but still need preparation for heaven's holiness. Protestants since the Reformation have rejected the doctrine as lacking clear scriptural warrant; Orthodox have a different but related teaching. The disagreement remains.

question: Christian doctrine of the church (ecclesiology) has been disputed for centuries. The Nicene Creed says the church is one, holy, catholic, and what?
context: 'One, holy, catholic, and apostolic'. Catholic from Greek 'kath-holos' � 'according to the whole' (i.e., universal, not 'Roman'). Apostolic � founded on the apostles and continuing their faith. Christians read these four notes in different ways but most affirm them together.

question: Genesis 14: four eastern kings raided Sodom and carried off Abraham's nephew Lot. Abraham mustered 318 retainers, pursued, defeated them by Damascus, and recovered the captives. On his return a mysterious king-priest of Salem blessed him with bread and wine. Who?
context: Hebrews 7 reads Melchizedek as a type of Christ � 'priest forever' without genealogy. Christians have long puzzled over who this Salem king-priest of God Most High actually was.

question: Genesis 16: Sarah, still childless, gave her Egyptian handmaid to Abraham. The handmaid bore a son, was treated harshly, and fled to a desert well where the angel of the LORD found her. She named God 'the God who sees me'. Who?
context: Hagar's son was Ishmael � the angel told her he would be 'a wild donkey of a man'. Arabs trace descent from Ishmael through tradition. Hagar's well is the first place in scripture God is given a personal name by a human.

question: Genesis 19: God told Abraham he was going to investigate Sodom. Abraham bargained him down � if fifty righteous, would he spare it? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Finally how few?
context: There weren't ten. Only Lot and his family were dragged out by the angels. The story shows two great themes together: God's openness to a man's prayer, and the heavy reality of judgment when justice goes unanswered.

question: Genesis 25: Isaac's wife had a troubled pregnancy and asked the LORD what was happening. God answered that two nations were in her womb, and the older would serve the younger. The boys were twins. Who was firstborn?
context: Esau came out hairy and red; Jacob followed gripping his heel ('Jacob' puns on 'heel-grasper'). The struggle continued their whole lives � Esau gave up his birthright for stew, Jacob stole his blessing dressed in goatskins.

question: Genesis 33: after twenty years of exile, Jacob returned to Canaan in terror of his brother. He sent gifts ahead and divided his camp. Then he saw Esau coming with 400 men. What did Esau do?
answer: ran to embrace him in tears
choices: ran to embrace him in tears
context: Genesis 33:4. Esau forgave him. Jacob said 'seeing your face is like seeing the face of God'. The story is one of the great biblical pictures of reconciliation � a brother's offered forgiveness exceeding what Jacob had any right to expect.

question: Genesis 39: Joseph the Hebrew slave in Egypt rose to manage Potiphar's whole household. Then Potiphar's wife began trying to seduce him. He fled, leaving his garment in her hand. What happened next?
answer: she accused him; he was jailed
choices: she accused him; he was jailed
she let him return to Canaan
she repented and went to the temple
she gave him a higher post
context: Genesis 39. Joseph said 'how can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?' � the OT pattern for resisting sexual temptation. The jail became the next step in God's plan; in prison he met Pharaoh's officials.

question: Exodus 14: when Pharaoh's chariots pursued Israel to the Red Sea shore, the people complained bitterly to Moses. What did Moses tell them?
answer: stand still and see God save you
choices: stand still and see God save you
take up your swords and form ranks
send your women across by night
context: Exodus 14:13-14. 'The LORD will fight for you; you have only to be still.' Then God told Moses to raise his staff. The east wind blew all night and the sea parted. The Hebrews crossed; Pharaoh's chariots were drowned.

question: Exodus 17: in the wilderness Israel grumbled for water. God told Moses to strike a rock; water flowed. The place got two names from the quarrel. What were they?
context: Massah � 'testing'. Meribah � 'quarrelling'. Psalm 95 cites the place as a warning: 'do not harden your hearts as at Meribah'. Paul reads the rock as Christ in 1 Corinthians 10:4.

question: Numbers 16: Korah led 250 leading men against Moses, claiming all the people were holy. What happened to them?
context: Numbers 16:31-32. The ground opened; the rebels fell in alive. Their incense pans were hammered into a bronze covering for the altar � a permanent warning. Korah's sons survived (mentioned in Numbers 26:11 and as Psalmists).

question: Deuteronomy 6:4-5: Israel's central confession of faith � 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one � and you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, and might.' What is this prayer called?
context: From the Hebrew first word 'shema' � 'hear'. Pious Jews say it morning and evening. Jesus cited it as the first and great commandment (Mark 12:29). It is recited at death and in the daily prayers of observant Jews.

question: 1 Samuel 4: the Philistines defeated Israel and captured the Ark of the Covenant. Eli, hearing the news, fell off his chair and broke his neck. His pregnant daughter-in-law gave birth and died, naming her son for the loss. The boy was named what?
context: 1 Samuel 4:21. 'Ichabod' means 'the glory has departed'. The Ark spent seven months wreaking havoc in Philistine cities before they sent it back on a cart drawn by two cows.

question: 1 Samuel 28: King Saul, abandoned by God, sought out a forbidden woman who could call up the dead. She brought up the prophet Samuel. From which town was she?
context: 1 Samuel 28. Samuel rebuked Saul and announced his death in battle the next day. Saul fell on his own sword at Gilboa. The episode is the only place in the OT where necromancy actually works � and it does not help.

question: 2 Samuel 6: King David escorted the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem with great joy, dancing 'with all his might' before it. His wife Michal despised him from a window. Who was her father?
context: 2 Samuel 6:16. Michal was Saul's daughter, David's first wife. The text says she had no child to the day of her death � a quiet ending to the line of Saul as queen mother.

question: 1 Kings 19: after the Carmel triumph, Elijah fled in despair from Jezebel and lay down to die in the desert. He travelled forty days to which mountain to meet God?
context: Horeb is another name for Sinai � where Moses had received the law. God came not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in 'a still small voice' (KJV) or 'a sound of thin silence' (literal Hebrew). Then God recommissioned the prophet.

question: 2 Kings 2: Elijah and Elisha walked together east of the Jordan. Suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared. Elijah was carried away in a whirlwind. What did Elisha receive?
context: Elisha had asked for 'a double portion of your spirit' � the inheritance of the firstborn. He picked up the mantle, struck the Jordan, the waters parted. The disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration saw Elijah back from heaven (Mark 9:4).

question: 2 Kings 6: Elisha and his servant were surrounded by an Aramean army by night. The servant despaired. Elisha prayed: 'open his eyes that he may see.' What did he see?
answer: hills full of horses of fire
choices: hills full of horses of fire
the angel of the LORD with sword
all the armies of Israel marching
the prophet's mantle on the wall
context: 2 Kings 6:17. Christians have read this scene as a picture of the unseen spiritual reality behind the visible world. The chapter ends with Elisha leading the blinded enemy into Samaria and feeding them rather than killing them.

question: 2 Kings 22: a long-lost scroll was found while repairing the Jerusalem temple. The young king tore his clothes when it was read and led a great reform. Who was the king?
context: The book was probably Deuteronomy. Josiah destroyed pagan altars, killed false priests, kept a Passover the like of which had not been seen since the judges. He died in battle at Megiddo in 609 BC at age 39.

question: Isaiah 7: the prophet gave King Ahaz of Judah a sign. 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called...' what?
context: Hebrew 'Immanuel' � 'God with us'. Matthew 1:23 cites this verse as fulfilled in Jesus. Ahaz refused the sign and went his own way. He sacrificed his own children to pagan gods. He died young.

question: Jeremiah 18: God told the prophet to visit the workshop of a craftsman who was working with wet clay on a wheel. The clay was marred; the craftsman reshaped it. What did God say?
answer: I am like the potter with Israel
choices: I am like the potter with Israel
I am like the painter with canvas
I am like the carpenter with wood
I am like the smith with iron
context: Jeremiah 18:6. 'Can I not do with you as this potter has done?' Paul picks up the image in Romans 9:21. The metaphor has shaped Christian thinking about God's sovereignty in shaping individual lives ever since.

question: Jeremiah 31: God promises a new covenant � not like the one made at the exodus. What will be written on hearts?
context: Jeremiah 31:33. Hebrews 8 cites this prophecy as fulfilled in Christ. The new covenant is inward; God will be their God; they will all know him 'from the least to the greatest'. He will forgive their iniquity.

question: Daniel 2: King Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great statue with head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with what?
context: A stone cut without hands struck the feet and ground the statue to dust; the stone became a mountain that filled the earth. Daniel interpreted: the metals are successive kingdoms; the stone is God's everlasting kingdom.

question: Hosea 1: God told the prophet to marry a prostitute and have children as a sign-act. Whose name meant 'not pitied'?
context: Hosea 1:6. Lo-Ruhamah was the daughter; Lo-Ammi (not my people) the second son. Israel had broken the covenant by chasing other gods � but Hosea 2 promises the names will be reversed: 'I will say to Lo-Ammi, you are my people'.

question: The Bible's longest book is which?
context: 150 Psalms total. Tradition gives David as author of about half; others belong to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, and many unattributed. The Psalter is the prayer book of the church.

question: The shortest book of the Bible by verses is which?
context: 3 John is one chapter, 14 verses � a personal note from the apostle to Gaius. Obadiah is the shortest Old Testament book.

question: Which book of the OT does not mention the name of God?
context: Esther mentions kings, queens, edicts, Persian customs � but never God by name. Christian tradition has read God's hidden providence as the whole point of the book. The Septuagint added prayers to make the divine activity explicit.

question: The four Gospels were written in the second half of the first century. The first three are called what � for their shared common storyline?
context: Greek 'sun-optikos' � 'seen together'. Matthew, Mark, Luke share material and order in striking ways. John tells the story very differently. Scholars debate how Matthew, Mark, Luke are related to each other.

question: The shortest verse in most English Bibles is two words. Where is it?
context: 'Jesus wept.' He is standing at Lazarus's tomb. The early church saw deep theology in this short verse � God in the flesh weeping over death even while about to undo it.

question: Matthew 5:13: Jesus calls his disciples the salt of the earth. He then warns what will happen if salt loses its saltiness?
choices: it can only flavor the cooking
context: Matthew 5:13. 'Thrown out and trampled.' Salt preserved meat in the ancient world � a powerful image of God's people preserving the world from rot. Lewis used the image to describe Christian moral influence: 'be good salt'.

question: Matthew 13: Jesus told seven parables of the kingdom. The first compares the kingdom to a what?
context: Matthew 13:3-23. The kingdom is like a sower sowing on various soils. Jesus explained it privately to the disciples. The chapter is among the most concentrated teaching on the nature of the kingdom in the gospels.

question: Matthew 18: Jesus said unless we become like little children we cannot enter the kingdom. Peter asked how often he should forgive his brother � 'as many as seven times?' Jesus answered:
context: Matthew 18:22. Greek can mean 70x7 (490) or 77 � both pictures of limitless forgiveness. Jesus then told the parable of the unmerciful servant: forgiven millions, he choked a man for hundreds. God will not be mocked.

question: Mark 10: a rich young man came running and asked what to do for eternal life. Jesus, loving him, said one thing was lacking. What?
context: Mark 10:21. The man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God � 'easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye'. The disciples were astonished.

question: Luke 7: a sinful woman wept on Jesus's feet at a Pharisee's dinner and wiped them with her hair. The Pharisee was offended. What did Jesus say?
answer: her many sins are forgiven for she loved much
choices: her many sins are forgiven for she loved much
she has the faith for which I came
she shows what no rich man can show
she has done what was needed today
context: Luke 7:36-50. He pointed out that Simon the Pharisee had not even given the basic courtesies the woman lavished. The story has shaped Christian devotion through the figure of Mary Magdalene (whom Western tradition identified with this woman, though Luke doesn't name her).

question: Luke 19: Jesus wept over Jerusalem from the slope of the Mount of Olives. What did he foresee?
choices: the rise of a new prophet
context: Luke 19:41-44. 'They will dash you to the ground, you and your children with you, and they will not leave one stone upon another.' Fulfilled by the Romans in AD 70 under Titus. The temple has not been rebuilt since.

question: John 13: at the Last Supper, Jesus rose and did something startlingly humble for the disciples. What?
choices: broke bread with each by name
context: John 13:1-15. 'I have given you an example.' Foot-washing was the work of the lowest slave � the disciples were horrified. Peter at first refused; then asked to be washed all over. The act remains a Maundy Thursday liturgy.

question: John 20: the risen Jesus met Mary Magdalene in the garden by his tomb. She thought he was the gardener until he spoke one word. What?
context: John 20:16. 'Mary!' 'Rabbouni!' (teacher). She tried to embrace him; he sent her to tell the brothers. Early tradition called her 'apostle to the apostles'. She is the first witness of the resurrection in all four gospels.

question: Luke 24: two disciples walked toward a village seven miles from Jerusalem on Easter day. The risen Jesus walked beside them unrecognized until he broke bread at table. What village?
context: Luke 24:13-35. They had heard the women's news but did not believe. Jesus opened the Scriptures to them on the road. 'Did not our hearts burn within us?' The Emmaus road has shaped Christian art and devotion for two thousand years.

question: Acts 4: Peter and John, hauled before the Sanhedrin, were ordered to stop preaching Jesus. Their answer became a classic line of Christian dissent. What did they say?
answer: we must obey God rather than men
choices: we must obey God rather than men
we cannot help but speak of him
give us yet a season to think
let the people decide for themselves
context: Acts 4:19-20 and 5:29. The line has been quoted across history � by martyrs, by reformers, by civil-rights activists, by dissidents under tyrannies. Peter and John had been with Jesus; their courage came from that.

question: Acts 12: Peter was jailed by Herod Agrippa I, who had just beheaded James the brother of John. The night before execution, an angel woke Peter in his cell. What did the chains do?
context: Acts 12:7. Peter walked out past sleeping guards. He came to a friend's house where Rhoda the servant girl recognised his voice but was so excited she left him standing at the gate. Herod Agrippa died horribly soon after.

question: Acts 18: in Corinth Paul met a Jewish husband-wife team who had been expelled from Rome by Claudius. They became Paul's coworkers and tentmakers. Who were they?
context: Acts 18:2. They appear repeatedly in Paul's letters. In Romans 16 Paul says they 'risked their necks' for him. Priscilla taught the eloquent Apollos a fuller gospel in Ephesus. Christians ever since have read them as a model of partnership in ministry.

question: Acts 20: Paul preached late into the night at Troas. A young man named Eutychus fell asleep in a third-floor window and fell to his death. What did Paul do?
answer: embraced him; he came back to life
choices: embraced him; he came back to life
carried his body to the burial place
rebuked the disciples for their grief
context: Acts 20:9-12. Paul went on preaching till daybreak. Christians have read the story with affection � the early church kept long-winded preachers, but God was patient with them.

question: Acts 27: Paul travelled to Rome as a prisoner. A great storm � a 'northeaster' � tore the ship for fourteen days. At what island did they shipwreck?
context: Acts 27-28. All 276 aboard reached shore. A viper struck Paul as he gathered firewood; he shook it off; the Maltese expected him to die or to be hailed a god. He healed the chief's father, and Christians have been on Malta ever since.

question: Romans 12 opens with one of Paul's great calls: 'present your bodies a living ___, holy and acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service'.
context: Romans 12:1. The word is striking � sacrifice implies death, but it is a 'living' sacrifice. Christians read this as the whole of the moral life � body and mind given over to God as worship. Chapter 12 continues with the gifts and practical love.

question: Romans 5: Paul says we have peace with God through Christ. He then names the chain that suffering produces. The order is suffering, endurance, character, and finally what?
context: Romans 5:3-5. 'And hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.' The argument has been hugely formative for Christian thinking about suffering.

question: 1 Corinthians 13: Paul says love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and does what?
context: 1 Corinthians 13:7. The chapter is read at most Christian weddings � though it was written first to address a divided church arguing over which spiritual gifts mattered most. 'And now abides faith, hope, love � but the greatest is love.'

question: Galatians 5: Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit in opposition to the works of the flesh. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness � and what two more?
context: Galatians 5:22-23. Nine fruits. The list is among the best-known summaries of Christian character in scripture. Paul places them against eight 'works of the flesh' he had listed just before.

question: Ephesians 2:8-9: 'For by grace are you saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any...' what?
context: Ephesians 2:8-9. The verse is foundational for Reformation theology: grace alone, faith alone. Paul immediately adds verse 10: 'we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works'.

question: Hebrews 11:1: 'Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things...' what?
context: Hebrews 11:1. KJV. The chapter then walks through the heroes of OT faith � Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, the judges, David, the prophets � all believing in promises beyond their lifetime.

question: James 1: 'Pure religion and undefiled before God the Father is this, to visit the fatherless and ___ in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world.'
context: James 1:27. Care for the most vulnerable is named as the heart of pure religion. Throughout the OT widows and orphans symbolise those without legal standing � those whose claim is on God's mercy through his people.

question: In the second century, an aged bishop of Smyrna was arrested in old age and asked to curse Christ to save his life. He said 'eighty and six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong'. Who?
context: Polycarp, c. 69-155. A disciple of John. He was burned at the stake; tradition says the flames would not touch him, so a soldier stabbed him. His 'Martyrdom of Polycarp' is the earliest non-NT Christian martyrdom narrative.

question: Justin Martyr was a philosopher in Rome who converted to Christianity in the 130s and wrote 'Apologies' defending the faith to emperors. He was beheaded c. 165 AD. He wrote a long dialogue with a Jewish opponent. The opponent's name was what?
context: 'Dialogue with Trypho' � the earliest Christian sustained engagement with rabbinic Judaism. Justin had searched among Stoics, Aristotelians, Pythagoreans, and Platonists before meeting an old man by the sea who pointed him to the prophets.

question: Tertullian, the third-century North African church father, wrote 'the blood of the martyrs is the seed of...' what?
context: Tertullian, c. 155-220. Latin theologian, originally a lawyer, eventually a Montanist heretic in later life. The line comes from his 'Apologeticus' � defending the church against Roman accusations of secret crimes.

question: Origen of Alexandria, the third-century theologian, took Matthew 19:12 ('eunuchs for the kingdom') literally as a young man � with permanent results. He wrote a massive textual study of the OT in six parallel columns. What was it called?
context: Greek 'six-fold' � Hebrew, Hebrew transliterated, Aquila, Symmachus, Septuagint, Theodotion. Origen was the most influential biblical scholar of antiquity. Some of his theological speculations (universal salvation, pre-existent souls) were condemned after his death.

question: Athanasius defended the deity of Christ for fifty years against Arian opposition. He was exiled five times. He was bishop of which city?
context: Athanasius, c. 296-373. The saying 'Athanasius against the world' caught his lonely persistence. His 'On the Incarnation' remains a classic statement of why God became man. He also defended the canonical 27 New Testament books.

question: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus were three theologians from one region of Asia Minor � two brothers and a friend. What is the trio called?
context: Cappadocia, central Anatolia (modern Turkey). The Cappadocian Fathers (380s) hammered out the mature doctrine of the Trinity � one ousia (substance), three hypostases (persons). Their work shaped the Nicene Creed's final form at Constantinople 381.

question: John Chrysostom (the 'golden-mouthed') was patriarch of Constantinople around 400 AD. He preached against luxury at court. The Empress Eudoxia had him exiled. Where was he sent?
context: He died on the forced march to Pityus on the Black Sea (407). His liturgy is still used in the Eastern Orthodox Church. His sermons on Genesis, the Gospels, and Paul's letters remain among the great series of patristic biblical exposition.

question: Augustine's 'Confessions' records his conversion in a garden in Milan in 386 AD. What text did he read at random that brought him to faith?
context: 'Not in revelling and drunkenness, not in lust and licentiousness, not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ.' Augustine had heard a child's voice say 'tolle, lege' (take and read). He was 31. His mother Monica had been praying for him for years.

question: Anselm of Canterbury (1033-1109) wrote a famous proof for God's existence: God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in thought; therefore God exists. What is the proof called?
context: Anselm's 'Proslogion' (1078). Critics from Gaunilo (his contemporary) to Kant have challenged it; defenders from Descartes to Plantinga have refined it. The argument remains a standard topic of philosophy of religion.

question: Thomas Aquinas's 'Summa Theologica' began with five proofs of God's existence � the 'quinque viae'. The fifth way argues from purpose in nature. What is it called?
context: Things in nature act for ends though they lack knowledge � therefore there must be an intelligent designer. 'And this we call God.' The argument was sharpened by Paley (1802) and challenged by Hume and Darwin. Modern intelligent design takes it up again.

question: Francis of Assisi composed a hymn near the end of his life praising God through 'Brother Sun, Sister Moon'. The hymn is sometimes called the first poem in modern Italian. What is its name?
context: Also called Canticle of the Creatures. Francis added a final verse praising 'Sister Death' shortly before his own. The hymn shaped centuries of Christian creation-praise � most famously in 'All Creatures of Our God and King' by William Henry Draper.

question: Julian of Norwich was a fourteenth-century English anchoress (a religious recluse) who had sixteen 'shewings' � visions � from Christ during a near-fatal illness. Her account is the first book in English by a woman. What is it called?
context: Julian (c. 1342-1416). 'All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.' She wrote two versions � a short text and a longer 'long text' twenty years later. T S Eliot quoted her at the close of 'Four Quartets'.

question: Catherine of Siena (1347-1380) was an Italian Dominican tertiary (lay sister) who persuaded the pope to leave Avignon and return to Rome. She wrote a long mystical 'Dialogue' between her soul and God. What is her status in the Catholic Church?
context: Catherine was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970 (by Paul VI) � only the second woman so honoured (Teresa of Avila was first). She is co-patron of Italy. She died at age 33 of self-imposed fasting and exhaustion.

question: In 1431 a 19-year-old French peasant girl was burned at the stake in Rouen for heresy after leading the French army to victory and seeing the dauphin crowned at Reims. Who?
context: Joan claimed visions from saints Michael, Margaret, and Catherine. She was canonised in 1920. The trial transcripts survive; Pope Benedict XV reviewed them in detail. Her cross-dressing in armour was one of the charges; her devotion to Christ was undeniable.

question: In 1453 the city of Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks under Sultan Mehmed II, ending the Byzantine Empire. The great church of Hagia Sophia became what?
context: Hagia Sophia was built by Justinian in 537 AD. The Turkish conversion added minarets and plaster over the mosaics. Atatürk made it a museum in 1934; in 2020 Turkey reconverted it to a mosque. Eastern Orthodoxy lost its central liturgical space.

question: Martin Luther's 1517 Wittenberg theses challenged the sale of indulgences � written certificates of forgiveness or remission of penalty. The Dominican preacher selling them in Saxony was who?
context: Tetzel's slogan: 'as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs'. The indulgence money was for St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Luther's theses were copied and printed across Germany within weeks.

question: At the 1521 Diet of Worms, Luther was asked to recant. His reply included the famous line about conscience. What did he say?
answer: here I stand, I can do no other
choices: here I stand, I can do no other
the law alone shall judge me here
I will not depart from the truth
say what you will, my king
context: Luther probably said 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders, Gott helfe mir. Amen.' He was protected on the way home by Frederick the Wise. The diet condemned him; he was kidnapped to the Wartburg castle and translated the New Testament into German.

question: John Calvin's 'Institutes of the Christian Religion' first appeared in 1536 and was revised throughout his life. The final 1559 edition was structured around the Apostles' Creed. The fourth and last book is on what?
context: Book 1: God the Creator. Book 2: Christ the Redeemer. Book 3: Grace and Salvation. Book 4: The Church and its government. The 'Institutes' became the systematic theology of Reformed Protestantism for centuries.

question: Thomas Cranmer (1489-1556) was Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI. He compiled the Book of Common Prayer that shaped English-speaking worship for centuries. How did he die?
context: Mary Tudor restored Catholicism. Cranmer recanted under pressure, then retracted his recantation, then thrust into the flames the hand that had signed the recantations. His last words: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.'

question: In 1611 King James I authorized a new English translation of the Bible. The work was done by 47 translators in six companies. From which Hebrew source did the OT translators work?
context: The Masoretic Text � the Hebrew Bible as preserved and pointed by medieval Jewish scribes. The King James (or 'Authorised') Version became the dominant English Bible for 300+ years. Its prose shaped English literature from Bunyan to Lincoln.

question: John Newton (1725-1807) was the captain of a slave ship who eventually became an Anglican curate and wrote 'Amazing Grace'. The man he mentored in the antislavery campaign in Parliament was who?
context: Wilberforce led the Parliamentary fight against the slave trade for 20 years. The Slave Trade Act passed in 1807; Wilberforce died days after Parliament passed the act ending slavery itself in 1833. Newton lived to see the trade abolished.

question: In 1873 a Belgian Catholic priest volunteered to serve the lepers of Molokai in Hawaii. He contracted leprosy himself and died in 1889. Who?
context: Damien de Veuster (1840-1889). Canonised 2009. He learned the Hawaiian language, built a church, dressed sores, made coffins, dug graves. He wrote: 'I am the happiest missionary in the world'. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote a famous defence of him.

question: C. S. Lewis converted to Christianity in 1931 after long resistance, with the help of which fellow Oxford don and Catholic friend?
context: Tolkien (and Dyson) walked Lewis around Addison's Walk the night of September 19-20, 1931. Lewis was 32. He had been a theist for two years but did not yet believe in Christ. The conversation showed him 'myth become fact' in the gospel.

question: Corrie ten Boom and her Dutch family hid Jews in their Haarlem watch-shop during the Nazi occupation. She was sent to which concentration camp?
context: Corrie ten Boom (1892-1983). Her sister Betsie died there in 1944. Corrie was released by a clerical error a week before all the women her age were executed. Her 1971 memoir 'The Hiding Place' has shaped two generations of Christian readers.

question: Mother Teresa, founder of the Missionaries of Charity, won the Nobel Peace Prize in which year?
context: Born Anjeze Bojaxhiu in Skopje (now North Macedonia). She used the prize money to fund her work with the poor of Calcutta. She was canonised in 2016. Her order now runs hundreds of homes for the destitute, dying, and disabled across the world.

question: Billy Graham preached to vast crusades from the late 1940s until 2005. He counselled American presidents from Truman onward. Which crusade in 1957 lasted 16 weeks at Madison Square Garden?
context: Graham's New York crusade had 2.4 million attenders. He died 2018, aged 99. He preached to an estimated 215 million people in person over his career � more than any other Christian preacher in history.

question: The Christian doctrine of original sin teaches that Adam's fall affected all humanity. Augustine sharpened the doctrine against which fifth-century monk who taught humans could be sinless by their own free will?
context: Pelagius, a British monk in Rome (c. 360-420). The Council of Carthage 418 condemned his teaching. Christians have debated the exact relation of grace and free will ever since � Augustinian, Semi-Pelagian, Calvinist, Arminian camps each finding their root in this dispute.

question: Christians distinguish three uses of the Old Testament law: moral, ceremonial, and civil. Which use applies to Christians today, according to most Reformed teaching?
context: The Ten Commandments and the moral law remain binding (summarised in the great commandments to love God and neighbour). The ceremonial law (sacrifices, dietary rules) is fulfilled in Christ; the civil law applied specifically to OT Israel.

question: Christians traditionally call seven gifts 'gifts of the Holy Spirit' � drawn from Isaiah 11. They are wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and what?
context: Isaiah 11:2. The list shaped Catholic teaching on the spiritual life and is named in confirmation prayer. Aquinas devoted a substantial section of the Summa to these gifts as the highest workings of God in the soul.

question: The Beatitudes in Matthew 5 are eight blessings (or nine, counting verse 11). Which is the third?
context: Matthew 5:5. 'They shall inherit the earth'. The Beatitudes describe the citizens of the kingdom. They run counter to ordinary worldly values � power, wealth, pleasure. Augustine read them as a ladder of ascent in the spiritual life.

question: Christians have prayed the rosary since the medieval period (developed by Dominicans). The rosary has 'mysteries' � events from Christ's life. The Joyful Mysteries are Christmastide events. Which is the first?
context: Five Joyful Mysteries: Annunciation, Visitation, Nativity, Presentation, Finding in the Temple. John Paul II added the Luminous Mysteries (events from Christ's ministry) in 2002. The Sorrowful and Glorious Mysteries complete the cycle.

question: The traditional Christian liturgical colors are white (for feasts of Christ), red (for martyrs and Pentecost), green (for ordinary time), and what for penitential seasons?
context: Purple (or violet) marks Advent and Lent. Some traditions also use rose on the third Sunday of Advent (Gaudete) and fourth of Lent (Laetare). Black is sometimes used for funerals; gold can substitute for white at great feasts.

question: Christians have practiced spiritual disciplines for centuries. Which Russian Orthodox monastic prayer is repeated in synchrony with the breath: 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner'?
context: Practiced from at least the fifth century. The 'Philokalia' is the great anthology of texts on it. J D Salinger's 'Franny and Zooey' (1961) introduced it to a Western audience. Many Christians of all traditions now use it for daily devotion.

question: The four ancient Latin Doctors of the Church are Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and which fourth?
context: Gregory the Great (540-604) was pope, monk, and reformer. He sent Augustine of Canterbury to evangelise England. His 'Pastoral Rule' shaped medieval bishops. Gregorian chant is named for him. The Eastern Doctors are Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and John Chrysostom.

question: The Christian Eucharist (Lord's Supper) is celebrated weekly in most traditions. The Greek word 'eucharist' itself means what?
context: From Greek 'eucharistein' � 'to give thanks'. The verb is used at the Last Supper accounts: Jesus 'took the bread and gave thanks'. The Eucharist combines remembrance, communion with God and church, sacrifice (in some traditions), and presence of Christ.

question: The two major sacraments accepted by all major Christian traditions are baptism and the Eucharist. Catholic, Orthodox, and some Lutheran traditions count five more for a total of seven. Which of these is NOT among the seven?
context: The Catholic seven: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation (confession), anointing of the sick (last rites), holy orders (ordination), matrimony. Most Protestant traditions count only baptism and the Eucharist as sacraments instituted by Christ.

question: Many Christian traditions baptise infants. Others (Baptist, Pentecostal, most Anabaptist) practice 'believer's baptism' only. The largest argument for infant baptism appeals to which OT covenant sign?
context: Colossians 2:11-12 links baptism with circumcision. Acts 16 says Lydia 'and her household' were baptised. Christians have disputed for centuries; the disagreement remains central between paedobaptist and credobaptist traditions.

question: In Holy Week, Maundy Thursday commemorates the Last Supper. 'Maundy' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
context: From 'mandatum novum' � 'a new commandment'. John 13:34: 'A new commandment I give you, that you love one another.' Jesus said this at the Last Supper after washing the disciples' feet. The English king or queen distributes 'Maundy money' to the elderly on this day.

question: Christmas in Western Christianity is celebrated December 25. The Eastern Orthodox who use the Julian calendar celebrate on which day?
context: 13 days off from the Western calendar. Orthodox Christians using the Revised Julian Calendar (most of them) celebrate Christmas with Catholics on December 25. Old-calendarists keep January 7. Both date back to fourth-century traditions.

question: Easter Sunday is preceded by Holy Saturday and Good Friday. The day before Palm Sunday is sometimes called Lazarus Saturday in the Eastern Orthodox tradition. Why?
answer: Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead
choices: Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead
context: John 11. The miracle drew such a crowd that the priests began plotting Jesus's death. In Western Christianity the raising of Lazarus is read on the Fifth Sunday of Lent. The Orthodox dedicate the Saturday before Palm Sunday to the resurrection-foreshadowing miracle.

question: Christian hymn-singing has shaped daily devotion for two millennia. 'Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty' was written in 1826 by which Anglican bishop?
context: Bishop Heber, 1783-1826. He died in India aged 42, exhausted from missionary work. His hymn opens with the Sanctus from Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4. Sung often at Trinity Sunday across Anglican, Methodist, Lutheran, and other Christian traditions.

question: 'Be Thou My Vision' is an old Irish hymn translated into English in 1905 by Mary Byrne. The Old Irish original dates from roughly which century?
context: The Irish original 'Rop tu mo baile' is from c. 700-800 AD � the golden age of Celtic Christian poetry. The set tune is the Irish folk tune Slane. The hymn has become a beloved part of English-speaking Christian worship around the world.

question: 'Amazing Grace' was published in 1779 in the Olney Hymns collection. The tune most often paired with it ('New Britain') is from which country?
context: American shape-note hymnody. Newton's text and the 'New Britain' tune (first published 1835) were joined later in the 19th century. The combination has become perhaps the most beloved Christian hymn in English � used at presidential funerals, civil rights marches, and ordinary church services.

question: In Acts 11:26, the disciples were first called Christians in which city?
context: Antioch in Syria, the third-largest city of the Roman Empire. The label was probably from outsiders � 'partisans of Christ'. The church there sent out Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey, and bishop Ignatius wrote his famous letters from Antioch.

question: The first part of the Lord's Prayer in Greek begins 'Pater hemon ho en tois ouranois...' which translates as what?
answer: Our Father who art in heaven
choices: Our Father who art in heaven
Our Lord whose name we hallow
Our Lord who reigns in heaven
Our King whose throne is heaven
context: Matthew 6:9 and Luke 11:2. 'Pater' is the form of direct address. Jesus addressed God as 'Abba' (Aramaic, 'dear father') in his own prayer life. Paul says we can call God 'Abba' too because of the Spirit (Romans 8:15).

question: The Hebrew Bible Christians call the Old Testament is divided into Law, Prophets, and Writings. The first division contains how many books?
context: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy � the Pentateuch (Greek 'five scrolls') or Torah (Hebrew 'law'). Traditionally ascribed to Moses, though modern scholars see more complex composition. They make up the foundation of all subsequent OT books.

question: 'Soli Deo Gloria' � 'to God alone the glory' � was one of the five 'solas' of the Reformation. Bach inscribed the abbreviation 'SDG' at the end of his manuscripts. The other four solas include sola scriptura, sola fide, sola gratia, and what?
context: Christ alone. Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, glory to God alone. The five formulas became a shorthand for Protestant theology a century after Luther. They expressed the conviction that salvation rests in God's gift, not human achievement.

question: Polycarp of Smyrna was tied to the stake to be burned, but the flames did not consume him. The soldiers stabbed him instead. Above the flames a great voice from heaven was heard. What did the voice say?
answer: be strong, Polycarp, and play the man
choices: be strong, Polycarp, and play the man
come, take up your crown of life
blessed are those who endure to the end
your faith has saved you, my son
context: The 'Martyrdom of Polycarp' (mid-2nd century). The first Christian martyrdom narrative outside the New Testament. Polycarp was 86. His feast day is celebrated February 23 across Christian traditions.

question: Genesis 22 is the Akedah � the 'binding' � of Isaac. Abraham woke early, saddled his donkey, took two servants and his son, and travelled three days to Mount Moriah. He built an altar, bound Isaac, raised the knife. An angel of the LORD called from heaven 'Abraham! Abraham!' � stop. Now what was provided?
answer: a ram caught in a thicket
choices: a ram caught in a thicket
a sheep brought from the herd
context: Genesis 22:13. Abraham named the place 'the LORD will provide'. Jewish tradition reads Isaac as conscious participant; Christians have long read the binding as a foreshadowing of God offering his own Son. The location is identified by tradition with the Temple Mount.

question: Genesis 32: alone by the Jabbok river the night before meeting his estranged brother Esau, Jacob wrestled an unknown 'man' until dawn. The man asked to be released because day was breaking; Jacob refused unless blessed. The man asked Jacob's name, then renamed him 'Israel' � 'he who strives with God and prevails'. What did he touch?
context: Genesis 32:25. Jacob walked with a limp afterward. The story is one of the strangest in the Bible. Hosea 12 reads the wrestler as 'the angel'; Christians have read him as Christ pre-incarnate (a 'Christophany'). The name 'Israel' became the name of the whole nation.

question: Genesis 37-50 is the long Joseph cycle. Joseph's brothers sold him to a passing caravan for twenty pieces of silver. Joseph rose in Egypt, interpreted Pharaoh's dreams of seven cows and seven ears, became second-in-command, and stored grain through seven years of plenty. When his brothers came for grain during famine, he tested them. What did he hide in Benjamin's grain sack?
context: Genesis 44. The test was whether the brothers would now abandon Benjamin as they had once abandoned Joseph. They didn't � Judah offered his own life instead. Joseph then revealed himself in tears. 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (50:20) becomes a key text for biblical theology of suffering.

question: Exodus 32: Moses came down Sinai carrying two stone tablets and saw Israel dancing around a golden calf. He smashed the tablets, ground the calf to powder, scattered it on water, and made the people drink it. He then asked 'who is on the LORD's side?' Which tribe rallied?
context: Exodus 32:26. The Levites slew about 3000 of the idolaters that day. As a result, Moses said, the Levites were 'consecrated for the service of the LORD'. Aaron was a Levite; his sons became the priestly line; the rest of the tribe served at the tabernacle and temple.

question: Numbers 11: when Israel grumbled for meat, God sent vast flocks of quail. The Hebrews gorged. Many died of plague before the meat had been consumed. The place was named what?
context: Numbers 11:34. 'Graves of craving'. The story is one of several wilderness episodes about the danger of grumbling against God's provision. Paul cites this generation in 1 Corinthians 10 as 'examples for us, that we should not crave evil things, as they did'.

question: Numbers 22-24: Balaam son of Beor was a foreign prophet hired by Balak king of Moab to curse Israel. His donkey saw the angel of the LORD blocking the road three times and turned aside. Balaam beat her each time. Then the donkey did what?
context: Numbers 22:28. 'What have I done to you that you have struck me these three times?' Balaam's eyes were opened to see the angel. He then could only bless Israel, not curse � four times he blessed them. He was later killed when the Israelites attacked Midian (Numbers 31).

question: Joshua 7: after the spectacular victory at Jericho, Israel was crushed at little Ai. Joshua tore his clothes and lay before the Ark. God revealed that someone had violated the ban on plunder from Jericho. Lots were cast and identified the culprit. Who?
context: Joshua 7:18. Achan had stolen a Babylonian garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a gold bar, and buried them under his tent. He was stoned with his family in a place renamed 'Valley of Trouble' (Achor). The conquest then continued successfully.

question: Judges 4: Deborah summoned Barak son of Abinoam to lead Israel against Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army. Barak refused to go without her. Deborah came but said the glory of victory would go to a woman. After the battle Sisera fled and found shelter in the tent of a Kenite woman. What did she do?
answer: drove a tent peg through his skull
choices: drove a tent peg through his skull
lit a fire to bring help
sent word back to her people
context: Judges 4:21. Jael gave him milk to drink, covered him; he slept; she crept up with hammer and tent peg. The song of Deborah (Judges 5) is one of the oldest Hebrew poems. It celebrates the deliverance and the women who shared in it.

question: Judges 11: Jephthah, an outcast warrior recalled to lead Israel against Ammon, made a rash vow � if God gave him victory he would sacrifice whatever came first out of his house to greet him. Victory came. Who came out?
context: Judges 11:34. She came dancing to the timbrels. Jephthah tore his clothes. She accepted the vow and asked only two months to mourn her virginity in the hills. Christian and Jewish readers have debated for centuries whether Jephthah actually killed her or dedicated her to lifelong virginity.

question: 1 Kings 11: King Solomon had 700 royal wives and 300 concubines who turned his heart from the LORD to follow other gods � Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, Milcom of the Ammonites, Chemosh of the Moabites. God told Solomon that the kingdom would be torn from his son. What was kept for the sake of David?
context: 1 Kings 11:13. Judah remained loyal to Solomon's son Rehoboam; Jeroboam led the other ten northern tribes into a separate kingdom. The two kingdoms (Israel north, Judah south) lasted until Assyria destroyed Israel (722 BC) and Babylon destroyed Judah (586 BC).

question: 1 Kings 17-2 Kings 2: Elijah's ministry took place during the reign of which wicked king of the northern kingdom, husband of Jezebel?
context: Ahab's marriage to Phoenician princess Jezebel brought Baal worship to Israel. Elijah faced him repeatedly. After Naboth's vineyard incident, Elijah pronounced the destruction of Ahab's line. Ahab died in battle at Ramoth-Gilead; dogs licked his blood as Elijah had predicted (1 Kings 22).

question: 1 Kings 21: King Ahab coveted a vineyard adjoining his palace. Naboth refused to sell because it was his ancestral inheritance. Jezebel arranged false witnesses to accuse Naboth of blasphemy. Naboth was stoned. Elijah confronted Ahab in the vineyard. What did Elijah prophesy?
choices: ravens would feed on Ahab's flesh
context: 1 Kings 21:19. The prophecy was fulfilled at Ahab's death; an extension applied to Jezebel was fulfilled when Jehu had her thrown out the window and dogs ate her body (2 Kings 9:36). The Naboth story is the OT's clearest indictment of royal abuse of property rights.

question: 2 Kings 4: a Shunammite woman extended hospitality to the prophet Elisha. He prophesied that she would bear a son though her husband was old. When the boy was older he died in the field one day. The woman rode to Mount Carmel and clung to the prophet's feet. Elisha came, prayed twice, stretched himself over the boy. What happened?
choices: the boy opened his eyes wide
the boy spoke a single word
the boy stood at once unaided
context: 2 Kings 4:35. The resurrection of the Shunammite's son is one of the great Elisha miracles. The story foreshadows New Testament resurrections (Jairus's daughter, the Nain widow's son, Lazarus). It also foreshadows the central Christian claim of Jesus's own resurrection.

question: Isaiah 53 is the great 'Suffering Servant' chapter, read by Christians as foretelling Christ's crucifixion. The chapter says 'he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his ___ we are healed'.
context: Isaiah 53:5. The chapter has shaped Christian understanding of the atonement for two thousand years. Acts 8 has Philip explaining the chapter to the Ethiopian eunuch. The early church read Isaiah 53 with a centrality second only to the gospels themselves.

question: Daniel 9: the prophet calculated from Jeremiah's prophecy that the seventy years of Babylonian exile were nearly complete. He prayed a long prayer of confession on Israel's behalf. The angel Gabriel came in flight 'about the time of the evening offering' with a new revelation � the 'seventy weeks'. What did the seventy weeks foretell?
answer: the coming of an anointed one
choices: the coming of an anointed one
the fall of the Persian Empire
the conquest of the eastern lands
context: Daniel 9:25-27. The 'seventy weeks' (490 years) prophecy has been variously interpreted by Christians from the early church to today as referring to Christ's first coming, his second coming, or both. The chapter is among the most disputed in eschatology.

question: Ezekiel 1: the prophet by the Chebar canal in Babylon saw the heavens opened. Four 'living creatures' came out of a stormy cloud, each with four faces � man, lion, ox, and what?
context: Ezekiel 1:10. Each face symbolises a creaturely category. Christians from Irenaeus (c. 180) onward connected the four faces with the four gospels: Matthew (man), Mark (lion), Luke (ox), John (eagle). The four faces still appear on the central crossing of many old churches.

question: Jonah 1: the prophet fled God's call to preach to Nineveh by sailing west from Joppa toward Tarshish. A great storm hit. The sailors cast lots to find the cause; the lot fell on Jonah. He told them to throw him overboard. They first tried what?
choices: to pray to many gods at once
to cast lots a second time
context: Jonah 1:13. Their rowing failed. They threw Jonah overboard reluctantly with prayers to his God. The sea calmed; the sailors feared the LORD and offered sacrifices. Jonah was swallowed by a 'great fish' � the book never says whale. He spent three days and nights in its belly.

question: Matthew 4 has Jesus tempted in the wilderness by three temptations. Stones to bread; jumping from the Temple; kingdoms of the world. Jesus answered each from Deuteronomy. What was the third temptation's offer?
answer: all the kingdoms of the world
choices: all the kingdoms of the world
context: Matthew 4:8. Satan showed Jesus all the kingdoms 'in a moment of time' and offered them in exchange for worship. Jesus answered: 'thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve'. Then Satan left, and angels came and ministered to him.

question: Matthew 5 begins the Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes. The sixth Beatitude promises a vision of God to whom?
context: Matthew 5:8. 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.' The 'beatific vision' of God face-to-face has been the centre of Christian eschatological hope � the goal toward which the saints are formed. Aquinas devoted a long section of the Summa to it.

question: Matthew 6: Jesus taught the Lord's Prayer in seven petitions � hallowed name, kingdom come, will be done, daily bread, forgive debts, lead us not, deliver from evil. He then warned about three private practices people use to be seen by others. They are giving, praying, and what?
context: Matthew 6:1-18. 'When you fast, do not look gloomy as the hypocrites do. Wash your face, anoint your head, that your fasting may not be seen by others.' Jesus assumes his disciples will fast � he does not abolish the practice. He criticizes ostentatious display of fasting.

question: Mark 7: Jesus debated the Pharisees about ritual handwashing. He cited Isaiah 29 against them: 'this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men'. Jesus then declared all foods clean. What was the deeper teaching?
answer: what defiles comes from the heart, not food
choices: what defiles comes from the heart, not food
what blesses comes from the lips of the law
what stains comes from the look of the eye
what cleanses comes from the hand of priest
context: Mark 7:21-23. The list of evils that defile from within: evil thoughts, fornication, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. Mark adds the parenthesis: 'thus he declared all foods clean'. The teaching foreshadows the church's move beyond the kosher laws.

question: Mark 10: a rich young ruler ran to Jesus and knelt asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus said keep the commandments. The man said he had since youth. Then Jesus, looking at him, loved him and told him one thing was lacking. What?
answer: sell all and give to the poor
choices: sell all and give to the poor
love your neighbor more than yourself
fast for forty days in the desert
go to John the Baptist for baptism
context: Mark 10:21. The man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. The disciples were astonished at Jesus's teaching that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom. Peter said 'we have left everything to follow you'. Jesus promised hundredfold reward 'in this life � with persecutions'.

question: Luke 1 narrates the dual annunciations to Zechariah (for John the Baptist) and Mary (for Jesus). The angel Gabriel struck Zechariah dumb for disbelief. Mary's response showed faith � 'let it be done according to your word'. After hearing the news she travelled to visit her cousin Elizabeth. Where did Elizabeth live?
context: Luke 1:39. Tradition locates the visit at Ein Karem near Jerusalem. The Visitation produced Mary's Magnificat and Elizabeth's blessing. John leapt in his mother's womb at Mary's greeting � the unborn forerunner recognising the unborn Christ. The Visitation is the second Joyful Mystery of the Rosary.

question: Luke 16: Jesus told the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. After death the poor man was carried to Abraham's bosom; the rich man was in torment. Across an unbridgeable chasm the rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers. What was Abraham's answer?
answer: they have Moses and the Prophets
choices: they have Moses and the Prophets
they will surely listen to the dead
they cannot now be saved at all
they must be left to their fate
context: Luke 16:29-31. 'If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rose from the dead.' Christians have read these final words as foreshadowing those who rejected Jesus despite his actual resurrection. The parable is also the Bible's most vivid picture of the consequences of riches without compassion.

question: Luke 23 records three sayings from the cross. Jesus prayed for his enemies. He promised paradise to a repentant criminal. He commended his Spirit to the Father. The repentant criminal is known in tradition as which name?
context: Tradition names him Dismas, the other criminal Gestas. Dismas is patron saint of prisoners and the dying. Jesus told him 'today you will be with me in paradise' � the only direct promise of immediate post-death blessedness Jesus ever made. The faith of the dying thief has reassured Christian deathbeds for two thousand years.

question: John 17 is Jesus's 'high priestly prayer' before his arrest. He prays for himself, for the disciples, and for those who will come to faith through the disciples' word. What is his great petition for that future church?
answer: that they may all be one
choices: that they may all be one
context: John 17:21. 'That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they also may be one in us � that the world may believe that you have sent me.' Christian unity has often fallen short of this prayer; the ecumenical movements of the 20th century took it as their watchword.

question: Acts 13 begins the Christian missionary expansion. The Antioch church prayed and fasted, and the Holy Spirit set apart two men for the work. Who were they?
context: Acts 13:2. From this point the narrative follows Paul (Saul is renamed Paul in v9). The first journey took them to Cyprus and central Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Barnabas had earlier vouched for the recently converted Saul when the Jerusalem disciples were afraid of him (Acts 9:27).

question: Acts 15: the Jerusalem Council settled the great early-church dispute about whether Gentile converts had to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law. James presided. Peter spoke. Paul and Barnabas reported. The decision was what?
context: Acts 15:19-29. The council asked Gentile believers only to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality. The decision was foundational for the church's identity as the people of God drawn from every nation, not a sect of Judaism. James's quotation of Amos 9:11-12 shaped his argument.

question: Acts 18: at Athens Paul argued in the synagogue and in the marketplace daily. He met Epicurean and Stoic philosophers who invited him to the Areopagus. There he preached an unknown god using Greek poetic quotation. He cited Aratus's Phaenomena: 'we are also his...' what?
context: Acts 17:28. Paul also quotes Epimenides ('in him we live and move and have our being'). The sermon failed with most hearers but a few believed � Dionysius the Areopagite (later patron of Athens), a woman Damaris, and others. The Areopagus sermon has been studied as a model of cross-cultural communication of the gospel.

question: Romans 3: Paul concludes the long argument about universal sin and divine righteousness with a great paragraph (vv 21-26) on Christ as a 'propitiation' through faith. The Greek word 'hilasterion' is also the OT word for what?
context: The 'hilasterion' or 'kapporet' was the gold lid on the ark, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement. Paul calls Christ the new mercy seat � the place where God's wrath against sin and his mercy toward sinners meet. The metaphor is among the most concentrated in Paul.

question: Romans 9-11: Paul wrestles with the painful question why Israel has largely rejected its Messiah. He concludes with a great hope � 'all Israel shall be saved'. The whole argument climaxes in a hymn of praise. What is its first line?
answer: O the depth of the riches
choices: O the depth of the riches
O the wonder of the love
O the height of the grace
O the breadth of the kindness
context: Romans 11:33. 'Both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!' The hymn closes with 'for of him, and through him, and to him, are all things; to whom be glory for ever. Amen'. Christians have read these chapters as the highest treatment of God's mysterious purposes in salvation history.

question: 1 Corinthians 15 is the great resurrection chapter. Paul lists Christ's appearances: to Cephas, to the Twelve, to over 500 brothers at once, to James, to all the apostles. 'Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me'. The chapter ends with what?
answer: death is swallowed up in victory
choices: death is swallowed up in victory
Christ is high above every name
love is the greatest of these
context: 1 Corinthians 15:54-57. Quoting Isaiah 25 and Hosea 13: 'O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ'. The chapter is read at most Christian funerals.

question: 2 Corinthians 12: Paul described a man caught up to the third heaven and heard inexpressible things. Most readers conclude Paul meant himself. He then mentions a 'thorn in the flesh' � 'a messenger of Satan'. He prayed three times for its removal. What did the Lord say?
answer: my grace is sufficient for you
choices: my grace is sufficient for you
my mercy is enough for thee
my peace shall guard thy heart
context: 2 Corinthians 12:9. 'For my strength is made perfect in weakness.' The verse has been a great comfort to Christians under chronic illness or suffering. Paul ends 'when I am weak, then am I strong'. The specific nature of his thorn is debated � vision problems, headaches, opponents.

question: Ephesians 1-3: Paul opens with a vast hymn of praise for God's eternal plan in Christ � chosen before creation, redeemed by his blood, sealed by the Spirit, gathered into one in him. Chapter 2 includes the great verse about salvation by grace through faith. Verse 10 explains the purpose. What were we created for?
context: Ephesians 2:10. 'We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.' The verse balances vv 8-9: grace produces good works, not the other way around. Christians have used it to refute the charge that 'salvation by faith' produces laziness.

question: Philippians 4: Paul writes from Roman house-arrest about contentment. 'I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.' What's the source of this strength?
answer: I can do all things through Christ
choices: I can do all things through Christ
he gives strength to the weary one
he grants peace beyond all comprehension
I rest in the eternal arms of God
context: Philippians 4:13. Paul speaks specifically of contentment with little or much � not 'I can do anything'. The famous verse, often quoted out of its context, is actually about resting in Christ when life is hard or when life is comfortable.

question: Colossians 1:15-20 is one of the great Christological hymns of the NT. 'He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him were all things created � all things have been created through him and for him.' What is Christ called in verse 18?
answer: the head of the body, the church
choices: the head of the body, the church
the lord of the powers of the air
the king of all the saints of God
the prince of those who serve him
context: Colossians 1:18. Paul confronts a 'philosophy' that mingled Christ with other powers. He responds: Christ has supremacy in everything � creation, providence, the church, redemption. The hymn ranks among the loftiest meditations on Christ's identity in scripture.

question: Hebrews is anonymous but has been ascribed to Paul, Apollos, Barnabas, Luke, and Priscilla over the centuries. The letter's central argument is that Christ is superior � to the angels, to Moses, to the Levitical priesthood. He is the high priest of which order?
context: Hebrews 7. The mysterious priest-king of Genesis 14 (Melchizedek) is taken as foreshadowing a priestly order outside the Levitical line. Christ is the eternal priest of that order � 'not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life' (Heb 7:16).

question: 1 Peter is addressed to Christians scattered through Asia Minor under threat of persecution. Peter encourages them to follow Christ's example of unjust suffering. He cites Isaiah 53 explicitly. Which verb does he use for what Christ did for us on the cross?
answer: bore our sins in his body
choices: bore our sins in his body
context: 1 Peter 2:24. 'Who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness; by whose stripes ye were healed.' Peter writes from Rome (he calls it 'Babylon' in 5:13) shortly before his own martyrdom under Nero around AD 64.

question: Revelation 5: John saw a scroll sealed with seven seals in the right hand of him who sat on the throne. An angel cried 'who is worthy to open the scroll?' No one could. John wept. Then an elder said one was worthy. Who is described in two animal images?
answer: the Lion of Judah and the Lamb slain
choices: the Lion of Judah and the Lamb slain
the Star of David and the Ram of Aries
the Tribe of Levi and the Cup of Joseph
the Seed of Eden and the Vine of Israel
context: Revelation 5:5-6. The Lion who is also a Lamb is the great paradoxical Christ-image of Revelation. The Lamb opens the seals one by one through chapters 6-8. The whole book turns on this Lion-Lamb: powerful and slain, triumphant and crucified.

question: In 313 AD Constantine and Licinius issued an edict legalising Christianity throughout the Roman Empire. The edict took its name from the city where Constantine met Licinius. What city?
context: The Edict of Milan ended three centuries of intermittent persecution and confiscated property was restored. Constantine eventually defeated Licinius and reunified the empire. He moved the capital east to Byzantium and renamed it after himself � Constantinople, the 'New Rome'.

question: The Council of Constantinople in 381 AD completed the Nicene Creed by adding language about the Holy Spirit. Who is named in the creed as proceeding from the Father?
context: 'And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father.' The West later added 'and from the Son' (filioque) without consulting the East � a major cause of the 1054 Great Schism. The original Eastern form remains the official creed of the Orthodox churches.

question: Patrick of Ireland (c. 385-461) had been captured by Irish raiders at age 16 and spent six years as a slave tending sheep. He escaped, returned home, was called in a dream to preach to the Irish, was eventually consecrated bishop, and returned. His one indisputable autobiographical writing survives. What is it called?
context: Patrick's 'Confessio' is a defence of his ministry against critics who called him an uneducated 'unlearned rustic'. He also wrote a 'Letter to Coroticus' protesting a Welsh chieftain's raid that had killed and enslaved Patrick's recent converts. Both works are in clumsy late Latin � the testimony of a man who learned his Latin under duress.

question: Benedict of Nursia (c. 480-547) founded the Western monastic tradition at Monte Cassino in southern Italy. His Rule of Benedict became the template for Western monasticism for over a thousand years. The Rule's central principle is summarised in two Latin words. What are they?
context: 'Pray and work' (or 'Prayer and work'). Benedictine monks divided the day between prayer (the Daily Office in eight hours), manual labor, and study. The Rule shaped not only monasteries but the broader Christian sense of vocation � that ordinary daily work, done before God, is itself sacred.

question: Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540-604) sent missionaries to convert the pagan Anglo-Saxons in 597 AD. The leader was a Benedictine prior who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. Who?
context: Not Augustine of Hippo (different man, two centuries earlier). Augustine of Canterbury landed in Kent in 597 with about 40 monks. King Ethelbert was baptised, then his Frankish queen Bertha (already a Christian). Augustine became the first archbishop. English Christianity has a continuous line from this mission to today.

question: The 1054 Great Schism between East and West had been brewing for centuries. The immediate trigger was the placement of unleavened bread by the Latins on the altar at the Eucharist. Cardinal Humbert of the Pope laid an excommunication on whom?
context: Humbert placed his excommunication bull on the altar of Hagia Sophia on July 16, 1054. The Patriarch returned the favour. The mutual excommunications remained in force until Paul VI and Athenagoras lifted them in 1965 � but the churches remain in separation today.

question: In 1525 Conrad Grebel, a Zurich layman in the circle of Reformer Ulrich Zwingli, baptised George Blaurock by pouring water over his head � the first Anabaptist baptism. Anabaptists rejected infant baptism. Within months Felix Manz was drowned (1527) in the Limmat by which government?
context: Manz was the first Anabaptist martyr at Protestant hands. Anabaptists were drowned, beheaded, or burned across both Protestant and Catholic territories. The Mennonites (followers of Menno Simons), Amish, and Hutterites trace their origins to this radical wing of the Reformation.

question: Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament into German (1522) and the whole Bible (1534) was hugely influential. His Bible shaped what would become standard High German. From what Greek text did Luther translate the NT?
context: Erasmus had compiled the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516 from a handful of Byzantine manuscripts. Luther's German version multiplied the impact � a Bible in vernacular for ordinary readers. Within a generation New Testaments appeared in French, English, Dutch, Czech, and many other languages.

question: Ignatius of Loyola (1491-1556), a Basque soldier wounded at the siege of Pamplona in 1521, recovered during a long convalescence in which he read lives of Christ and the saints. He founded the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in 1540. His 'Spiritual Exercises' guides retreatants through a four-week pattern of meditation. What is the first week's focus?
context: Week 1: sin and mercy. Week 2: incarnation and ministry of Christ. Week 3: passion. Week 4: resurrection and contemplation of God's love. The Spiritual Exercises remain the founding spiritual classic of Jesuit life and are widely practiced by other Christians too.

question: John Wesley (1703-1791) and George Whitefield (1714-1770) led the 18th-century evangelical awakenings. They came to differ over predestination � Whitefield Calvinist, Wesley Arminian. What was the main institutional fruit of Whitefield's preaching in America?
context: Whitefield made seven preaching tours of the American colonies between 1738 and his death in 1770. His preaching at Boston, New York, Philadelphia, and the southern colonies helped spark the First Great Awakening (1730s-1740s). Jonathan Edwards, in Massachusetts, was the leading theologian of the awakening.

question: William Carey (1761-1834), often called 'the father of modern missions', went to India in 1793 with the Baptist Missionary Society. His Sermon on 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God' had stirred his fellow Baptists. He translated the Bible (or parts of it) into how many Indian languages?
context: Carey spent 40 years in India. He worked in Bengali, Sanskrit, Marathi, and many other languages. He also helped lead the campaign against sati (widow-burning) and infanticide. His example sparked the modern missionary movement that took Protestant Christianity around the world in the 19th century.

question: Hudson Taylor (1832-1905) founded the China Inland Mission in 1865. He pioneered the missionary approach of wearing Chinese dress, eating Chinese food, working in inland China rather than coastal cities. He was deeply formed by which Reformed Anglican who preached daily devotional living?
context: Simeon was vicar of Holy Trinity Cambridge for 54 years (1782-1836). His preaching and his Sunday gatherings ('Simeon's conversation parties') shaped a generation of evangelical Anglicans. The Simeon Trust still funds preaching ministries in Britain. Taylor's CIM became one of the largest missionary organisations in the world.

question: Karl Barth (1886-1968), Swiss Reformed theologian, was the chief author of the 1934 Barmen Declaration that opposed Nazi co-option of the German churches. His massive 'Church Dogmatics' covers over 8000 pages in 14 volumes. What is Barth's first theological move (against 19th-century liberalism)?
answer: God is wholly other; we know him only by his self-revelation
choices: God is wholly other; we know him only by his self-revelation
religious experience is the source of theological truth
the historical method must precede dogmatic inquiry
ethics provides the foundation for all theology
context: Barth's commentary on Romans (2nd ed 1922) was the explosive book that turned 20th-century theology. He insisted theology must begin with God's word, not human consciousness. His influence is felt across both Catholic and Protestant theology of the 20th century.

question: Karl Rahner (1904-1984), Jesuit theologian, was the most influential Catholic systematic theologian of the 20th century and a major figure at Vatican II (1962-65). His phrase 'anonymous Christianity' tried to describe what?
answer: those who follow Christ's pattern without naming him
choices: those who follow Christ's pattern without naming him
those who confess Christ but live wickedly
those who attend mass but do not believe
those who reject the church but believe in God
context: Rahner argued that the grace of Christ may reach those who, through no fault of their own, never hear the gospel � whose lives nonetheless show love and self-giving consistent with Christ. Conservatives accused him of relativising the gospel; he replied that he meant to honour Christ's universal saving will, not blur revealed truth.

question: Dietrich Bonhoeffer's letters from prison (1943-45) include reflections on what he called 'religionless Christianity'. He was hanged at Flossenburg on April 9, 1945, two weeks before American troops liberated the camp. His last words to his fellow prisoners were what?
answer: this is the end; for me, the beginning of life
choices: this is the end; for me, the beginning of life
may God have mercy on Germany
tell my fiancée I forgive everyone
remember me when I am gone
context: Bonhoeffer (1906-1945). He was hanged for his part in the resistance plot against Hitler. His prison letters were smuggled out by sympathetic guards and published in 1951 as 'Letters and Papers from Prison'. They have shaped two generations of Christian ethics, especially in the West.

question: In 1989-91, communism collapsed across Eastern Europe. The Polish trade union 'Solidarity' had been founded in 1980 with support from Pope John Paul II. His 1979 visit to Poland is sometimes credited with starting the long unravelling. He celebrated open-air masses to vast crowds. What was the size of his largest Polish mass?
context: Warsaw, June 2, 1979. About two million attended. The Polish state security service noted with alarm: 'the pope is more powerful than the Party'. By 1989 Polish Solidarity had won; by 1991 the Soviet Union itself had dissolved. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev later credited the pope.

question: The doctrine of the Trinity holds one God in three persons. Christians distinguish 'essential' attributes (those shared by all three persons) and 'personal' properties (unique to each person). Which is essential, not personal?
context: Father, Son, and Spirit are each fully God � all-knowing, all-powerful, all-good.
